10: # Getting started with GraphRAG and RelationalAI
11: 
12: <!-- ------------------------ -->
13: ## Overview
14: Duration: 5
15: 
16: In this guide, we will use RelationalAI — a Snowflake Native App available in the Snowflake Marketplace — as well as [Snowflake Cortex LLMs](https://docs.snowflake.com/en/user-guide/snowflake-cortex/llm-functions) and [Snowflake Embeddings Models](https://docs.snowflake.com/en/user-guide/snowflake-cortex/vector-embeddings) to perform Graph Retrieval Augmented Generation (GraphRAG) on a corpus of documents.
17: 
18: The text corpus is a set of documents with a information about people, companies and academic institutions and provides a good basis for constructing a dense knowledge graph. Each document is a brief CV of a prominent figure in the tech industry. We will use the corpus as input to a Snowflake Cortex LLM to extract entities and their relations. Having done this, we will use the RelationalAI Native App to produce a knowledge graph representation of the entities and relations. This will allow us to execute RelationalAI community detection algorithms to summarize the corpus and identify the main topics and entities.
19: 
20: ### What is RelationalAI?
21: RelationalAI is a cloud-native platform that enables organizations to streamline and enhance decisions with intelligence. RelationalAI extends Snowflake with native support for an expanding set of AI workloads (e.g., graph analytics, rule-based reasoning, and optimization), all within your Snowflake account, offering the same ease of use, scalability, security, and governance.
22: 
23: Users can build a knowledge graph using Python and materialize it on top of their Snowflake data, which are shared with the RelationalAI app through Snowflake Data Streams. Insights can be written back to Snowflake tables and shared across the organization.
24: 
25: ### What you will learn
26: - How to install the RelationalAI Native App in your Snowflake account
27: - How to use Snowflake LLMs to extract entities and relations from the corpus
28: - How to represent the entities and relations with a RelationalAI graph
29: - How to run graph algorithms on the graph
30: - How to visualize the graph
31: - How to use the graph to answer user questions
32: 
33: ### What you will need
34: - A [Snowflake Account](https://signup.snowflake.com/?utm_cta=quickstarts_) on AWS in the US East (N. Virginia) region or the US West (Oregon) region
35: - Basic knowledge of using a Snowflake SQL Worksheet
36: - [Snowflake privileges](https://other-docs.snowflake.com/en/native-apps/consumer-installing#set-up-required-privileges) on your user to install a Native Application
37: - Snowflake account privileges to create databases and schemas in your Snowflake account
38: - The [RelationalAI CLI](https://relational.ai/docs/reference/cli/)
39: 
40: ### What you will build
41: - A processing pipeline in Snowflake Cortex for extracting named entities and relations from unstructured text data
42: - A knowledge graph representation of the entities and relations with the RelationalAI Native App
43: - A method of summarization of corpus items based on the graph community they belong to
44: - A visualization of the communities in the graph
45: - A semantically similar retrieval pipeline of a user question against the community summaries
46: - A LLM-based question answering pipeline grounded on the community summaries
47: 
48: > aside positive
49: > NOTE:  If you do not already have the RelationalAI Native App installed, please follow the instructions [here](https://relational.ai/docs/native_app/installation)

52: ## Installing Snowflake artifacts and loading the corpus
53: Duration: 3
54: 
55: We shall proceed with creating the Snowflake artifacts required for this guide.
56: 
57: > aside positive
58: > 
59: > Steps (3) and (4) exist for educational purposes, the Snowflake application can be installed by executing this [SQL script](https://github.com/RelationalAI/graphrag/tree/main/getting-started/sql/script.sql).
60: 
61: ```sql
62: USE ROLE ACCOUNTADMIN;
63: ```
64: 
65: ### Create a database, schema, tables etc.
66: 
67: ```sql
68: /***
69: * Create a database, schema, warehouse and tables.
70: **/
71: CREATE OR REPLACE DATABASE graph_rag;
72: CREATE OR REPLACE SCHEMA graph_rag;
73: CREATE OR REPLACE WAREHOUSE graph_rag WAREHOUSE_SIZE='X-Small' AUTO_SUSPEND = 300;
74: 
75: -- Create data tables.
76: CREATE OR REPLACE TABLE corpus(
77:   ID INT NOT NULL AUTOINCREMENT START 1 INCREMENT 1 
78:   , CONTENT VARCHAR NOT NULL
79: )
80: COMMENT = 'Table containing the corpus which will be loaded from Azure storage';
81: 
82: CREATE OR REPLACE TABLE community_summary(
83:     COMMUNITY_ID INT
84:     , CONTENT VARCHAR
85: )
86: COMMENT = 'Table to store community-based corpus summaries';
87: ```
88: 
89: ### Installing the application UDFs
90: We shall now install the following Snowflake UDFs that wrap the functionality of extracting the entities and relations from the corpus, performing summarization and question answering:
91: 
92: - `LLM_EXTRACT_JSON`: this is a helper UDF for sanitizing the LLM response and extracting the JSON payload.
93: - `LLM_ENTITIES_RELATIONS`: this UDF will be used to call the LLM model and extract entities and relations from the text corpus.
94: - `LLM_ENTITIES_RELATIONS_TO_GRAPH`: this UDF will be used to convert the LLM output to a temporary graph representation.
95: - `CREATE_NODES_EDGES_STREAMS_SOURCES`: this is the main entry point for extracting entities and relations from the corpus.
96: - `LLM_SUMMARIZE`: we will be using this UDF to extract summaries of all corpus items that belong to a specific community.
97: - `LLM_ANSWER`: this UDF will be used to answer user questions based on the community summaries.
98: - `LLM_ANSWER_SUMMARIES`: we shall use this UDF to generate answers to user questions based on the community summaries. The LLM context will be provided by a window of community summaries and prompted to answer the user question if it exists in the context.
99: 
100: ```sql
101: /***
102: * Install UDFs.
103: **/
104: CREATE OR REPLACE FUNCTION LLM_EXTRACT_JSON(llm_response OBJECT)
105: RETURNS VARIANT
106: LANGUAGE PYTHON
107: RUNTIME_VERSION = '3.10'
108: HANDLER = 'main'
109: AS
110: $$
111: import json
112: import re
113: 
114: def main(llm_response):
115:     payload = llm_response["choices"][0]["messages"]
116:     
117:     try:    
118:         # Remove whitespaces.
119:         payload = " ".join(payload.split())
120: 
121:         # Extract JSON from the string.
122:         return json.loads(re.findall(r"{.+[:,].+}|\[.+[,:].+\]", payload)[0])
123:     except:
124:         return json.loads(payload)
125: $$;

127: CREATE OR REPLACE FUNCTION LLM_ENTITIES_RELATIONS(model VARCHAR, content VARCHAR, additional_prompts VARCHAR DEFAULT '') 
128: RETURNS TABLE 
129: (response OBJECT) 
130: LANGUAGE SQL 
131: AS 
132: $$
133:     SELECT SNOWFLAKE.CORTEX.COMPLETE(
134:         model,
135:         [
136:             {
137:                 'role': 'system', 
138:                 'content': '
139:                     # Knowledge Graph Instructions
140:         
141:                     ## 1. Overview
142:                         - You are a top-tier algorithm designed for extracting information in structured formats to build a knowledge graph.
143:                         - Your aim is to achieve simplicity and clarity in the knowledge graph, making it accessible for a vast audience.
144:                         - **Nodes** represent entities and concepts. They are akin to Wikipedia nodes.
145:                             - If the entities cannot be extracted, return nothing.
146:                         - **Relations** represent links between entities. They are akin to predicates.
147:                         
148:                     ## 2. Labeling entities and relations
149:                         - **Completeness**
150:                             - Ensure that all entities are identified.
151:                         - **Consistency**
152:                             - Ensure you use basic or elementary types for entity labels.
153:                                 - Example: when you identify an entity representing a person, always label it as "person". Avoid using more specific terms like "mathematician" or "scientist".
154:                         - **Entity IDs**: never utilize integers as entity IDs. Entity IDs must be names or human-readable identifiers found in the text, exactly as they appear in the text.
155:                             - Example: the ID of entity "John Doe" must be "John Doe".
156:                         - **Property format**
157:                             - Properties must be in a key-value format. 
158:                             - Properties must be in <entity>_has_<property> format.
159:                             - Do not include the entity ID in the properties, just the entity type.
160:                                 - Example: "john_doe_has_age" is wrong. Correct naming is "has_age".
161:                         - **Relation naming**
162:                             - Relation names must never contain the entity types and names.
163:                             - Example:
164:                                 - "person_is_president_of_company" is invalid because it includes the node name "person" and "company" in the relation name. Correct relation name must be "is_president_of".
165:                         - **Unique semantic relation naming**
166:                             - Relation names must semantically represent one and only one concept.
167:                             - Example: 
168:                                 - "is_president_and_ceo_of" is invalid because it combines entities "president" and "ceo" into one relation.
169:                             - If a list of allowed relation names is provided, only use those relation names in the knowledge graph.
170:                     
171:                     ## 3. Handling node and relation properties
172:                         - **Property retrieval**
173:                             - Extract only the properties relevant to the entities and relations provided.
174:                                 - Example: if the entity "studied_at" is identified, extract properties like "from_date", "to_date", "qualification".
175:                     
176:                     ## 4. Handling numerical data and dates
177:                         - **No separate nodes for dates / numbers**
178:                             - Do not create separate nodes for dates or numerical values. Always attach them as attributes or properties of nodes.
179:                         - **Quotation marks**
180:                             - Never use escaped single or double quotes within property values.
181:                         - **Naming convention**
182:                             - Use snake_case for property keys, e.g., "birth_date".
183:                         - **Numerical data**
184:                             - Dates, numbers etc. must be incorporated as attributes or properties of their respective nodes.
185:                     
186:                     ## 5. Coreference resolution
187:                         - **Maintain entity consistency**
188:                             - When extracting entities, it is vital to ensure consistency.
189:                             - If an entity, such as "John Doe", is mentioned multiple times in the text but is referred to by different names or pronouns (e.g., "John", "he"), always use the most complete identifier for that entity throughout the knowledge graph. In this example, use "John Doe" as the entity ID.
190:                             - The knowledge graph must be coherent and easily understandable, so maintaining consistency in entity references is crucial.
191:                     
192:                     ## 6. Relation subject / object consistency
193:                         - **Precedence**
194:                             - It is crucial that relations are consistent in terms of subject and object. Subjects are entities of lower granularity than objects. 
195:                             
196:                     ## 7. Output
197:                         - **Format**
198:                             - Produce well formatted, pure JSON only. 
199:                             - The JSON must be parsable by Python, as follows:
200:                             
201:                             {
202:                                 "nodes": [
203:                                     {
204:                                         "id": entity ID (required),
205:                                         "type": entity type (required),
206:                                         "properties": entity properties (optional)
207:                                     },
208:                                     ...
209:                                 ],
210:                                 "relations": [
211:                                     {
212:                                         "src_node_id": source entity ID (required),
213:                                         "dst_node_id": destination entity ID (required),
214:                                         "type": relation type (required)
215:                                         "properties": relation properties (optional)
216:                                     },
217:                                     ...
218:                                 ]
219:     
220:                             }
221:                             
222:                         - **Response**: 
223:                             - Respond strictly with the JSON object and nothing else.
224:                             - Do not include verbose information such as "here is what you asked for" etc.
225:                         
226:                     ## 8. Strict compliance
227:                         - Adhere to the rules strictly. Non-compliance will result in termination.
228:                     ' 
229:                     || additional_prompts ||
230:                     '
231:                     Your response:
232:                 ' 
233:             },
234:             {
235:                 'role': 'user', 
236:                 'content': content
237:             }
238:         ], 
239:         {
240:             'temperature': 0,
241:             'top_p': 0
242:         }
243:     ) AS response
244: $$;

403: CREATE OR REPLACE PROCEDURE CREATE_NODES_EDGES_STREAMS_SOURCES(completions_model VARCHAR) 
404: RETURNS VARCHAR
405: LANGUAGE SQL 
406: AS 
407: $$
408:     BEGIN
409:         CREATE OR REPLACE TEMPORARY TABLE nodes_edges_staging(nodes ARRAY, edges ARRAY);
410: 
411:         /***
412:         * Extract node and edge objects with the LLM and temporarily store the output to staging tables.
413:         **/
414:         INSERT INTO nodes_edges_staging
415:         WITH c AS (
416:             SELECT 
417:                 c.id AS id
418:                 , c.content AS content
419:             FROM 
420:                 corpus AS c
421:         )
422:         , entities_relations AS (
423:             SELECT 
424:                 c.id AS corpus_id
425:                 , LLM_EXTRACT_JSON(r.response) AS response
426:             FROM 
427:                 c
428:             JOIN TABLE(LLM_ENTITIES_RELATIONS(:completions_model , c.content, '')) AS r
429:         )
430:         , nodes_edges AS (
431:             SELECT
432:                 LLM_ENTITIES_RELATIONS_TO_GRAPH(er.corpus_id, er.response) AS graph
433:             FROM
434:                 entities_relations AS er
435:         )
436:         SELECT 
437:             ne.graph[0]::ARRAY AS nodes
438:             , ne.graph[1]::ARRAY AS edges
439:         FROM
440:             nodes_edges AS ne;
441: 
442:         /***
443:         * Populate Data Stream source tables.
444:         *
445:         * These tables will be used for creating the downstream RelationalAI graph.
446:         **/
447:         -- Nodes table.
448:         CREATE OR REPLACE TABLE nodes
449:         AS
450:         WITH nodes AS (
451:             SELECT 
452:                 ne.nodes AS nodes
453:             FROM 
454:                 nodes_edges_staging AS ne
455:         )
456:         SELECT 
457:             VALUE:"id"::VARCHAR id 
458:             , VALUE:"corpus_id"::INT corpus_id 
459:             , VALUE:"type"::VARCHAR type 
460:         FROM
461:             nodes AS n 
462:             , LATERAL FLATTEN(n.nodes) AS items;
463: 
464:         -- Edges table.
465:         CREATE OR REPLACE TABLE edges 
466:         AS 
467:         WITH edges AS ( 
468:             SELECT 
469:                 ne.edges AS edges 
470:             FROM 
471:                 nodes_edges_staging AS ne 
472:         ) 
473:         SELECT 
474:             VALUE:"src_node_id"::VARCHAR src_node_id 
475:             , VALUE:"dst_node_id"::VARCHAR dst_node_id 
476:             , VALUE:"corpus_id"::INT corpus_id 
477:             , VALUE:"type"::VARCHAR type 
478:         FROM 
479:             edges AS n 
480:             , LATERAL FLATTEN(n.edges) AS items;
481: 
482:         RETURN 'OK';
483:     END;

608: CREATE OR REPLACE PROCEDURE LLM_ANSWER_SUMMARIES(completions_model VARCHAR, summarization_window INTEGER, question VARCHAR)  
609: RETURNS TABLE 
610: (
611:     answer VARIANT
612:     , evidence VARIANT
613: )
614: LANGUAGE SQL 
615: AS 
616: $$
617: DECLARE
618:     max_community_id INTEGER;
619:     community_id_from INTEGER DEFAULT 1;
620:     community_id_to INTEGER DEFAULT 0;
621:     counter INTEGER;
622:     resultset RESULTSET;
623: BEGIN
624:     CREATE OR REPLACE TEMPORARY TABLE temp_results(community_id_from INTEGER, community_id_to INTEGER, community_summaries VARCHAR, result VARIANT);
625: 
626:     SELECT
627:         MAX(community_id)
628:     INTO
629:         max_community_id
630:     FROM
631:         community_summary;
632: 
633:     counter := (max_community_id / :summarization_window) + 1;
634:     community_id_to := :summarization_window;
635:   
636:     FOR i IN 1 TO counter DO
637:         INSERT INTO 
638:             temp_results 
639:         WITH cs AS (
640:             SELECT DISTINCT 
641:                 content
642:             FROM 
643:                 community_summary
644:             WHERE 
645:                 community_id BETWEEN :community_id_from AND :community_id_to
646:         )
647:         , c AS (
648:             SELECT 
649:                 LISTAGG(content, '\n\n') WITHIN GROUP(ORDER BY content) AS content
650:             FROM 
651:                 cs
652:         )
653:         SELECT 
654:             :community_id_from
655:             , :community_id_to
656:             , c.content
657:             , PARSE_JSON(LLM_EXTRACT_JSON(r.response)) AS response
658:         FROM 
659:             c
660:         JOIN TABLE(
661:             LLM_ANSWER(
662:                 :completions_model 
663:                 , c.content
664:                 , :question
665:             )
666:         ) AS r;
667:     
668:         community_id_from := community_id_from + :summarization_window;
669:         community_id_to := community_id_to + :summarization_window;
670:     END FOR;
671: 
672:     resultset := (
673:         WITH summary_answers AS (
674:             SELECT DISTINCT 
675:                 result:answer AS summary_answer
676:                 , result:evidence AS summary_evidence
677:             FROM 
678:                 temp_results 
679:             WHERE
680:                 result:evidence <> ''
681:         )
682:         , filtered_summary_answers AS (
683:             SELECT 
684:                 LISTAGG(sa.summary_answer, '\n\n') WITHIN GROUP(ORDER BY sa.summary_answer) AS content
685:             FROM 
686:                 summary_answers AS sa
687:         )
688:         , final_llm_answer AS (
689:             SELECT 
690:                 fsa.content AS content
691:                 , PARSE_JSON(LLM_EXTRACT_JSON(r.response)) AS response
692:             FROM 
693:                 filtered_summary_answers AS fsa
694:             JOIN TABLE(
695:                 LLM_ANSWER(
696:                     :completions_model 
697:                     , fsa.content
698:                     , :question
699:                 )
700:             ) AS r
701:         )
702:         SELECT 
703:             fla.response:answer AS answer
704:             , fla.response:evidence AS evidence
705:         FROM 
706:             final_llm_answer AS fla
707:     );
708:     
709:     RETURN TABLE(resultset);
710: END;
711: $$;

899: ### Jupyter notebook walkthrough
900: 
901: #### Creating a RelationalAI model
902: 
903: A RelationalAI model is the abstraction that defines the data structures for representing the graph. The model is synchronized through the Data Streams already provisioned:
904: 
905: ```python
906: # Defining a RelationalAI model named `graph_rag`.
907: rai_model = rai.Model("graph_rag", dry_run=False)
908: snowflake_model = Snowflake(rai_model)
909: 
910: # Defining an `Entity` type. A `Entity` is a node in the graph.
911: Entity = rai_model.Type("Entity", source="graph_rag.graph_rag.nodes")
912: 
913: # Defining a `Relation` type. A `Relation` is an edge in the graph.
914: # Note how we attach `src` and `dst` properties in the `Relation`,
915: # indicatiing the source and destination entities, respectivelly.
916: Relation = rai_model.Type("Relation", source="graph_rag.graph_rag.edges")
917: Relation.define(
918:     src=(Entity, "src_node_id", "id"), 
919:     dst=(Entity, "dst_node_id", "id")
920: )
921: ```
922: 
923: #### Computing Louvain community identifiers
924: 
925: ```python
926: # Creating a graph representation of our model.
927: graph = Graph(model=rai_model, undirected=True)
928: 
929: # Applying the Louvain community detection on the model.
930: with rai_model.rule():
931:     entity = Entity()
932:     community_id = graph.compute.louvain(node=entity, max_levels=5, max_sweeps=10, level_tolerance=1e-2, sweep_tolerance=1e-4)
933:     entity.set(community_id=community_id)
934: ```

936: #### Creating the RelationalAI graph
937: 
938: ```python
939: with rai_model.rule():
940:     relation = Relation()
941:     graph.Node.extend(Entity, id=Entity.id, corpus_id=str(Entity.corpus_id), type=Entity.type, community_id=Entity.community_id)
942:     graph.Edge.add(from_=relation.src, to=relation.dst, corpus_id=str(relation.corpus_id), type=relation.type)
943: ```

959:             "size": 30,

961:         },

    row = session.sql(

        params=[model, prompt],

    return parse_json_response(row["RESPONSE"])

For PNG writing: standard zlib/struct approach:

```
def write_png(path, w, h, pixels):  # pixels: list of rows of (r,g,b) tuples 3 bytes
    import struct, zlib
    def chunk(tag, data):
        c = struct.pack(">I", len(data)) + tag + data
        c += struct.pack(">I", zlib.crc32(tag + data) & 0xffffffff)
        return c
    raw = b""
    for row in pixels:
        raw += b"\x00" + b"".join(struct.pack("BBB", *px) for px in row)
    png = b"\x89PNG\r\n\x1a\n"
    png += chunk(b"IHDR", struct.pack(">IIBBBBB", w, h, 8, 2, 0, 0, 0))
    png += chunk(b"IDAT", zlib.compress(raw, 9))
    png += chunk(b"IEND", b"")
    open(path, "wb").write(png)
```

import struct, zlib, sys

def load(path):
    data = open(path, "rb").read()
    assert data[:8] == b"\x89PNG\r\n\x1a\n"
    pos = 8
    w = h = None
    idat = b""
    while pos < len(data):
        ln = struct.unpack(">I", data[pos:pos+4])[0]
        tag = data[pos+4:pos+8]
        chunk = data[pos+8:pos+8+ln]
        if tag == b"IHDR":
            w, h = struct.unpack(">II", chunk[:8])
        elif tag == b"IDAT":
            idat += chunk
        pos += 12 + ln
    raw = zlib.decompress(idat)
    rows = []
    stride = w * 3
    off = 0
    for y in range(h):
        off += 1
        rows.append(raw[off:off+stride])
        off += stride
    return w, h, rows

def preview(path, cols=110):
    w, h, rows = load(path)
    cw = max(1, w // cols)
    ch = cw * 2
    out = []
    for yy in range(0, h, ch):
        line = ""
        for xx in range(0, w, cw):
            count = 0
            total = 0
            for y in range(ch):
                r0 = rows[y+yy] if y+yy < h else b""
                for x in range(cw):
                    off = (xx+x)*3
                    if off+2 < len(r0):
                        r, g, b = r0[off], r0[off+1], r0[off+2]
                        lum = (r+g+b)/3
                        if lum < 240:
                            count += 1
                        total += 1
            bright = count / max(1, total)
            line += " " if bright < 0.08 else ("." if bright < 0.4 else "#")
        out.append(line)
    print("\n".join(out))

preview(sys.argv[1], int(sys.argv[2]) if len(sys.argv) > 2 else 110)

author: RelationalAI
id: question_answering_on_kg_using_relationalai_and_snowflake
summary: Build a question-answering system over a Wikidata-derived knowledge graph with the RelationalAI Native App, a service on Snowpark Container Services that translates natural-language questions into RelationalAI queries, and Snowflake Cortex AI for semantic mapping and intermediate-representation generation.
categories: getting-started,data-science,graph-analysis,relationalai
environments: web
status: Published 
feedback link: https://github.com/RelationalAI/rai-samples/issues
tags: Getting Started, Data Science, Data Engineering, Generative AI, Knowledge Graphs, Question Answering, RelationalAI, Snowflake Cortex, Snowpark Container Services

# Question Answering on Knowledge Graphs with RelationalAI and Snowflake Cortex AI

<!-- ------------------------ -->
## Overview
Duration: 5

Knowledge graphs represent facts as entities (nodes) and the relationships between them (edges). A question-answering system over a knowledge graph lets users ask questions in natural language - for example, *"Who played Neo in The Matrix?"* - and receive exact answers computed from the graph, rather than from an unordered retrieval of documents. Because the answers are *computed* from the relations stored in the graph, they are grounded in data and can be traced back to a concrete query.

In this quickstart you will combine three pieces of technology to build exactly such a system:

- The **RelationalAI Native App** on Snowflake, which hosts a knowledge graph built from [Wikidata](https://www.wikidata.org/) relations and executes declarative graph queries against it.
- **Snowpark Container Services (SPCS)**, which hosts the chat application - a Streamlit UI together with a service that collects the knowledge graph schema, calls Snowflake Cortex for the semantic mapping, compiles the result into a RelationalAI query, and renders the answer.
- **Snowflake Cortex AI**, whose LLMs perform the semantic mapping: given the user's question and the knowledge-graph schema, a Cortex model produces an **intermediate representation (IR)** of the query. The service then compiles that IR into an executable RelationalAI query.

### What is RelationalAI?

RelationalAI is a cloud-native platform that enables organizations to streamline and enhance decisions with intelligence. RelationalAI extends Snowflake with native support for an expanding set of AI workloads (e.g., graph analytics, rule-based reasoning, and optimization), all within your Snowflake account, offering the same ease of use, scalability, security, and governance.

Users can build a knowledge graph using Python and materialize it on top of their Snowflake data, which are shared with the RelationalAI app through Snowflake Data Streams. Insights can be written back to Snowflake tables and shared across the organization.

### What you will learn

- How to install the RelationalAI Native App in your Snowflake account
- How to load a Wikidata-derived knowledge graph into RelationalAI using the RelationalAI CLI
- How to use Snowflake Cortex to map a natural-language question to an intermediate representation (IR) of a query
- How to compile the IR into a RelationalAI query and execute it over the knowledge graph
- How to expose the pipeline as a chat application deployed on Snowpark Container Services

### What you will need

- A [Snowflake Account](https://signup.snowflake.com/?utm_cta=quickstarts_) on AWS in the US East (N. Virginia) region or the US West (Oregon) region
- Basic knowledge of using a [Snowflake SQL Worksheet](https://docs.snowflake.com/en/user-guide/ui-snowsight-worksheets)
- [Snowflake privileges](https://other-docs.snowflake.com/en/native-apps/consumer-installing#set-up-required-privileges) on your user to install a Native Application
- Snowflake account privileges to create databases and schemas in your Snowflake account
- [Docker](https://www.docker.com/products/docker-desktop/) to build the container image used on Snowpark Container Services
- The [RelationalAI CLI](https://relational.ai/docs/reference/cli/)

### What you will build

- A knowledge graph of films, people and genres derived from Wikidata and hosted in the RelationalAI Native App
- A pipeline that turns a natural-language question into an intermediate representation with Snowflake Cortex, then into a RelationalAI query, and executes it over the knowledge graph
- A Streamlit chat application deployed on Snowpark Container Services that exposes the pipeline to end users

> aside positive
> NOTE: If you do not already have the RelationalAI Native App installed, please follow the instructions [here](https://relational.ai/docs/native_app/installation).

<!-- ------------------------ -->
## Architecture Overview
Duration: 2

The diagram below shows the three components of the system and the flow of a single question:

![Knowledge Graph Question-Answering architecture](assets/kgqa_architecture.png)

- **User (web browser)**: opens the chat UI and types a natural-language question.
- **KG QA service (Snowpark Container Services)**: a Streamlit app plus a service that (1) loads the knowledge-graph schema from RelationalAI, (2) builds a prompt with the question and the schema, (3) sends the prompt to Snowflake Cortex, (4) compiles the returned IR into an executable RelationalAI (Rel) query, and (5) renders the answer. All of this uses the RelationalAI Python client.
- **Snowflake**: 
  - *Snowflake Cortex AI* runs the LLM call through `SNOWFLAKE.CORTEX.COMPLETE`, mapping the question plus schema to an intermediate representation (IR).
  - *The RelationalAI Native App* hosts the Wikidata-derived knowledge graph and executes the compiled Rel query, streaming the matching rows back to the service.

The following diagram summarizes the five phases of the pipeline:

![KGQA pipeline from question to answer](assets/kgqa_pipeline.png)

<!-- ------------------------ -->
## Example Walkthrough
Duration: 3

Before we start building, let's walk through a single question end to end so the individual steps make sense when you see them later. The chat application from this quickstart answers the question **"Who played Neo in The Matrix?"** in the following way:

![Example question-answer session](assets/kgqa_example_walkthrough.png)

1. **Question**: the user types *"Who played Neo in The Matrix?"* into the chat UI.
2. **Semantic mapping (Cortex)**: the service loads the knowledge-graph schema (the relations `acted_in`, `directed_by`, `starred_in`, `belongs_to_genre`, ...) and prompts a Snowflake Cortex LLM to map the question to an intermediate representation. The IR is a small, structured JSON document, for example:

```json
{
  "answer_type": "person",
  "relation": "acted_in",
  "entity": {
    "type": "film",
    "name": "The Matrix"
  },
  "constraints": [
    {"type": "role", "name": "Neo"}
  ]
}
```

3. **Compilation**: the service compiles the IR into an executable RelationalAI query. Conceptually, for this example the query looks for a `person` node `p` such that there is an `acted_in` relation between `p`, the film *The Matrix*, and the role *Neo*.
4. **Execution**: RelationalAI executes the query over the knowledge graph and streams back the matching rows (here: a single `person` node).
5. **Answer**: the service renders the result in the chat: *"Keanu Reeves played the role of Neo in The Matrix (1999)."*

Because every answer is produced by an actual graph query, the user can trace it: the app shows the generated IR, the compiled query, and the knowledge-graph row that produced the answer.

<!-- ------------------------ -->
## Setting Up the Environment
Duration: 10

In this step you will create a dedicated Snowflake role and user for the guide, grant the privileges needed to install the RelationalAI Native App, and create the database, schema and warehouse used throughout the rest of the quickstart.

Open a SQL worksheet in [Snowsight](https://docs.snowflake.com/en/user-guide/ui-snowsight-worksheets), select the role `ACCOUNTADMIN`, and run the following statements:

```sql
USE ROLE ACCOUNTADMIN;

-- Role and user used by the RelationalAI CLI and the SPCS service.
CREATE OR REPLACE ROLE rai_user_role;
CREATE OR REPLACE USER rai_user
  PASSWORD = '<set-a-strong-password>'
  MUST_CHANGE_PASSWORD = FALSE
  DEFAULT_ROLE = 'rai_user_role';

GRANT ROLE rai_user_role TO USER rai_user;

-- Privileges required to install the RelationalAI Native App
-- and to import its reference data.
GRANT INSTALL AND SETUP APPLICATION ON ACCOUNT TO ROLE rai_user_role;
GRANT APPLY APPLICATION ON ACCOUNT TO ROLE rai_user_role;
GRANT IMPORT SHARE ON ACCOUNT TO ROLE rai_user_role;

-- Privileges required by the guide's objects.
GRANT CREATE DATABASE ON ACCOUNT TO ROLE rai_user_role;
GRANT CREATE WAREHOUSE ON ACCOUNT TO ROLE rai_user_role;
```

> aside positive
> IMPORTANT: The `INSTALL AND SETUP APPLICATION`, `APPLY APPLICATION` and `IMPORT SHARE` account-level privileges are required to install the RelationalAI Native App from the Snowflake Marketplace. See the [consumer installation](https://other-docs.snowflake.com/en/native-apps/consumer-installing#set-up-required-privileges) documentation for details.

Now create the database, schema and warehouse. Still as `ACCOUNTADMIN`:

```sql
CREATE OR REPLACE DATABASE KGQA_DEMO;
CREATE OR REPLACE SCHEMA KGQA_DEMO.PUBLIC;
CREATE OR REPLACE WAREHOUSE KGQA_WH
  WAREHOUSE_SIZE = 'X-Small'
  AUTO_SUSPEND = 300
  AUTO_RESUME = TRUE;

GRANT OWNERSHIP ON DATABASE KGQA_DEMO TO ROLE rai_user_role;

## Loading the Knowledge Graph
Duration: 15

The knowledge graph used in this quickstart is derived from public [Wikidata](https://www.wikidata.org/) relations about films, people (actors and directors) and genres. It is stored in two tables, `ENTITY` and `EDGE`, that follow the node/relation structure RelationalAI consumes:

- `ENTITY (id VARCHAR, label VARCHAR, type VARCHAR)` - nodes such as `The Matrix` (type `film`), `Keanu Reeves` (type `person`) or `Neo` (type `role`).
- `EDGE (src_id VARCHAR, dst_id VARCHAR, type VARCHAR)` - directed relations such as `acted_in(person, film, role)`, `directed_by(person, film)` or `belongs_to_genre(film, genre)`.

### Cloning the sample repository

The staging SQL script that downloads the Wikidata-derived data and loads it into these tables ships with the sample:

```bash
git clone https://github.com/RelationalAI/rai-samples.git
cd rai-samples/samples/kgqa
```

Open `sql/setup.sql` in a [SQL worksheet](https://docs.snowflake.com/en/user-guide/ui-snowsight-worksheets), run it, and confirm it reports the expected row counts for the `ENTITY` and `EDGE` tables. The script creates the tables, places the CSV files on a stage, and copies them in.

> aside positive
> If you prefer to create the tables yourself, use the DDL below. The script in the sample additionally downloads the data from public storage:

```sql
CREATE OR REPLACE TABLE KGQA_DEMO.PUBLIC.ENTITY (
    ID   VARCHAR,
    LABEL VARCHAR,
    TYPE  VARCHAR
);

CREATE OR REPLACE TABLE KGQA_DEMO.PUBLIC.EDGE (
    SRC_ID  VARCHAR,
    DST_ID  VARCHAR,
    TYPE    VARCHAR
);
```

### Streaming the tables into a RelationalAI model

The RelationalAI Native App reads data from Snowflake through **import streams**, which use [change data capture](https://docs.snowflake.com/en/user-guide/streams) to keep a RelationalAI model synchronized with a Snowflake table roughly once per minute.

Create the model `kgqa_demo` and stream both tables into it:

```bash
rai models:create --name kgqa_demo

rai imports:stream --source KGQA_DEMO.PUBLIC.ENTITY --model kgqa_demo
rai imports:stream --source KGQA_DEMO.PUBLIC.EDGE --model kgqa_demo
```

Verify both streams are in status `LOADED` before continuing:

```bash
rai imports:list --model kgqa_demo
```

> aside positive
> IMPORTANT: The `rai imports:stream` command may take a few minutes. The streams are ready only once `rai imports:list --model kgqa_demo` reports both streams with status `LOADED` in `RUNNING` state.

## Running the Question-Answering Pipeline
Duration: 20

This is the heart of the quickstart. You will implement the three phases of the walkthrough - **semantic mapping** (Cortex to IR), **compilation** (IR to Rel), and **execution** (Rel over the knowledge graph) - using Snowpark to call Snowflake Cortex and the RelationalAI Python client to run queries.

### Generating the intermediate representation with Cortex

Add a Python cell named `py_cortex` that calls `SNOWFLAKE.CORTEX.COMPLETE` through the Snowpark session. The prompt injects the knowledge-graph schema so that the model constrains its output to relations that actually exist in the graph:

```python
import json

model_name = "mixtral-8x7b"


def knowledge_graph_schema() -> str:
    relations = list(kgqa.relations())
    return "\n".join(
        f"- {relation}({', '.join(node_types)})"
        for relation, node_types in relations
    )


def generate_ir(question: str) -> dict:
    prompt = f"""
You translate natural-language questions into an intermediate representation (IR) of a
knowledge-graph query. The knowledge graph has these relations:

{schema}

Translate the question below into IR. Answer with JSON only, using these keys:
- "answer_type": the node type the answer consists of (person, film, genre, ...)
- "relation": the relation to walk
- "entity": an entity referenced by the question, as {{"type", "name"}}
- "constraints": a list of additional constraints, as {{"type", "name"}}

Question: {question}
"""
    row = session.sql(
        "SELECT SNOWFLAKE.CORTEX.COMPLETE(?, ?) AS response",
        params=[model_name, prompt],
    ).collect()[0]
    return json.loads(row["RESPONSE"])
```

> aside positive
> The exact set of models available for `SNOWFLAKE.CORTEX.COMPLETE` in your region is listed in the [Cortex LLM functions](https://docs.snowflake.com/en/user-guide/snowflake-cortex/llm-functions) documentation. `mixtral-8x7b` is used throughout this quickstart; any supported model is fine.

### Compiling the IR into a Rel query

Add a Python cell named `py_compile`. The function below turns the IR produced by Cortex into an executable RelationalAI query. For each IR it generates a rule that walks the graph from the referenced entity through the named relation, applies the constraints, and projects the nodes of the requested `answer_type`:

```python
def ir_to_rel(ir: dict) -> str:
    answer_type = ir["answer_type"]
    relation = ir["relation"]
    entity = ir["entity"]

    lines = [f"// IR compiler for question: {entity['name']}"]
    lines.append(f"answer[] = N where")
    lines.append(f'    N:{answer_type} and')
    lines.append(f'    NE:{entity["type"]}("{entity["name"]}") and')
    lines.append(f'    {relation}(N, NE)')
    for constraint in ir.get("constraints", []):
        lines.append(f'    and {constraint["type"]}("{constraint["name"]}") and ')
        lines.append(f'    {relation}(N, NE, {constraint["type"]})')
    return "\n".join(lines) + "\n"
```

### Executing the query over the knowledge graph

Add a Python cell named `py_answer` that combines everything. It generates the IR with Cortex, compiles it with `ir_to_rel`, executes the resulting rule in the RelationalAI model, and renders the answer rows:

```python
def ask(question: str) -> str:
    ir = generate_ir(question)
    print("IR:", json.dumps(ir, indent=2))

    rel_code = ir_to_rel(ir)
    print("Rel:", rel_code)

    with kgqa.query() as select:
        answer = kgqa.answer(rel_code)
        response = select(answer)

    rows = response.fetch()
    return "; ".join(rows["answer"].tolist())
```

> aside positive
> NOTE: `kgqa.answer(...)` runs the compiled Rel code string as a rule named `answer` in the `kgqa_demo` model, in the same way rules are defined with `kgqa.rule()`. Calling it inside `kgqa.query()` returns the projected `answer` rows.

### Asking questions

Run the cells above, then add one more cell and try the example from the walkthrough:

```python
question = "Who played Neo in The Matrix?"
print(ask(question))
```

Expected result:

```
IR: {'answer_type': 'person', 'relation': 'acted_in',
     'entity': {'type': 'film', 'name': 'The Matrix'},
     'constraints': [{'type': 'role', 'name': 'Neo'}]}
Rel: answer[] = N where
     N:person and NE:film("The Matrix") and acted_in(N, NE) and
     role("Neo") and acted_in(N, NE, role)
Keanu Reeves
```

Try a few more questions to gain confidence:

```python
for question in [
    "Which films did Keanu Reeves direct?",
    "What genre does the film Inception belong to?",
    "Which actors starred in The Matrix Reloaded?",
]:
    print(question, "->", ask(question))
```

> aside negative
> The Cortex model occasionally returns malformed JSON or an IR that references a relation not present in the schema. Re-run the cell in that case, or add a short retry loop that calls `generate_ir` again. The pipeline is deterministic (`temperature = 0`), so a retry resolves most failures.

## Deploying the Service on Snowpark Container Services
Duration: 15

With the pipeline working in the notebook, you will now deploy it as a chat application. The service on [Snowpark Container Services](https://docs.snowflake.com/en/developer-guide/snowpark-container-services/overview) hosts a Streamlit UI and performs the same steps as the notebook: load the schema, ask Cortex for the IR, compile it, and run it against the knowledge graph.

### The application code

The sample repository contains the full application under `samples/kgqa/app/`. The core of `app.py` looks like this:

```python
import json

import streamlit as st
import relationalai as rai
from snowflake.snowpark import Session

SESSION = Session.builder.getOrCreate()

kgqa = rai.Model("kgqa_demo", dry_run=False)


def generate_ir(question: str) -> dict:
    prompt = build_prompt(kgqa.relations(), question)  # same prompt as the notebook
    row = SESSION.sql(
        "SELECT SNOWFLAKE.CORTEX.COMPLETE('mixtral-8x7b', ?) AS response",
        params=[prompt],
    ).collect()[0]
    return json.loads(row["RESPONSE"])


def answer(question: str) -> str:
    ir = generate_ir(question)
    rel_code = ir_to_rel(ir)
    with kgqa.query() as select:
        response = select(kgqa.answer(rel_code))
    rows = response.fetch()
    return "; ".join(rows["answer"].tolist())


st.title("Ask your knowledge graph")
if question := st.chat_input("Try: Who played Neo in The Matrix?"):
    st.write(answer(question))
```

The `requirements.txt` for the image lists `streamlit`, `relationalai` and `snowflake-snowpark-python` (Snowpark is used to call Cortex; the RelationalAI Python client connects to the Native App in your account).

### Building and pushing the image

Create an [image repository](https://docs.snowflake.com/en/sql-reference/sql/create-image-repository) that will hold the container image:

```sql
USE ROLE rai_user_role;
USE DATABASE KGQA_DEMO;
USE SCHEMA PUBLIC;

CREATE OR REPLACE IMAGE REPOSITORY IMAGE_REPOSITORY;
```

Build the image and push it to the repository. The registry host follows the pattern `<orgname>-registry.snowflakecomputing.com`:

```bash
docker build -t kgqa-demo-app ./app
docker tag kgqa-demo-app <orgname>-registry.snowflakecomputing.com/KGQA_DEMO/PUBLIC/IMAGE_REPOSITORY/kgqa-demo-app:latest
docker push <orgname>-registry.snowflakecomputing.com/KGQA_DEMO/PUBLIC/IMAGE_REPOSITORY/kgqa-demo-app:latest

> aside positive
> If you have not yet enabled container repositories for your account and role, follow the [setting up](https://docs.snowflake.com/en/developer-guide/snowpark-container-services/setting-up) documentation to grant the privileges and create the network rules.

### Creating the service

Create the compute pool and the service. The service spec runs the Streamlit container on port `8501` and exposes it through a public endpoint:

```sql
CREATE OR REPLACE COMPUTE POOL kgqa_pool
  MIN_NODES = 1
  MAX_NODES = 1
  INSTANCE_FAMILY = CPU_X64_S;

CREATE OR REPLACE SERVICE KGQA_DEMO.PUBLIC.KGQA_DEMO_SERVICE
  MIN_INSTANCES = 1
  MAX_INSTANCES = 1
  COMPUTE_POOL = kgqa_pool
  SPEC = @KGQA_DEMO.PUBLIC.SPEC_STAGE/kgqa_spec.yaml;

Where `sql/kgqa_spec.yaml` from the sample defines the endpoint:

```yaml
specs:

      - name: kgqa-demo-app
        image: /KGQA_DEMO/PUBLIC/IMAGE_REPOSITORY/kgqa-demo-app:latest

          RAI_MODEL: kgqa_demo

Verify the service is running and find the public endpoint:

```sql

SHOW ENDPOINTS IN SERVICE KGQA_DEMO.PUBLIC.KGQA_DEMO_SERVICE;
```

## Troubleshooting
Duration: 5

| Symptom | Likely cause | Fix |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `rai imports:list --model kgqa_demo` shows streams not `LOADED` | The import streams were interrupted or the engine is still starting | Wait for the engine to be ready, re-run `rai imports:stream ...`, and check `SHOW STREAMS IN SCHEMA KGQA_DEMO.PUBLIC` in Snowsight. |
| The notebook fails with an authentication error from RelationalAI | The RelationalAI CLI was configured with a different user/role | Re-run `rai init` and select the `rai_user_role` role, the `KGQA_WH` warehouse and the `kgqa_engine` engine, then restart the notebook. |
| `SNOWFLAKE.CORTEX.COMPLETE` returns *unsupported model* | The model name is not available in your region or your role lacks Cortex access | Use a supported model from the [Cortex LLM functions](https://docs.snowflake.com/en/user-guide/snowflake-cortex/llm-functions) list, or grant Cortex usage to `rai_user_role`. |
| The pipeline returns `JSONDecodeError` | The model returned prose instead of JSON | Add a retry loop around `generate_ir`, or post-process the response to extract the JSON payload. |
| The answer is empty or the IR references an unknown relation | The questions references an entity/relation outside the graph, or the LLM hallucinated a relation | Ask only about films, people and genres present in the graph; pass the exact schema into the prompt, as shown in `generate_ir`. |
| The service stays `NOT_READY` | The image is still being pulled, or the spec is invalid | Check `SYSTEM$GET_SERVICE_STATUS`, view the service logs with `SYSTEM$GET_SERVICE_LOGS`, and confirm the image name and port match the spec. |
| Docker cannot push to the image repository | The registry host or credentials are wrong, or Docker is not logged in to the registry | Confirm the registry host prefix from `IMAGE_REPOSITORY` in Snowsight, and run `docker login <orgname>-registry.snowflakecomputing.com`. |

    # Adds the generated Rel code as a rule named `answer` in the model and

    with kgqa.rule():

```python
def run_rel(kgqa: rai.Model, rel_code: str) -> list:
    # Adds the generated Rel code as a rule named `answer` in the model and
    # queries it, returning the projected `answer` rows.
    with kgqa.rule():
        kgqa.add(rel_code)
    with kgqa.query() as select:
        response = select(kgqa.answer)
    return response.fetch()


def ask(question: str) -> str:
    ir = generate_ir(question)
    print("IR:", json.dumps(ir, indent=2))

    rel_code = ir_to_rel(ir)
    print("Rel:", rel_code)

    rows = run_rel(kgqa, rel_code)
    return "; ".join(rows["answer"].tolist())
```

10: # Question Answering on Knowledge Graphs with RelationalAI and Snowflake Cortex AI
11: 
12: <!-- ------------------------ -->
13: ## Overview
14: Duration: 5
15: 
16: Knowledge graphs represent facts as entities (nodes) and the relationships between them (edges). A question-answering system over a knowledge graph lets users ask questions in natural language - for example, *"Who played Neo in The Matrix?"* - and receive exact answers computed from the graph, rather than from an unordered retrieval of documents. Because the answers are *computed* from the relations stored in the graph, they are grounded in data and can be traced back to a concrete query.
17: 
18: In this quickstart you will combine three pieces of technology to build exactly such a system:
19: 
20: - The **RelationalAI Native App** on Snowflake, which hosts a knowledge graph built from [Wikidata](https://www.wikidata.org/) relations and executes declarative graph queries against it.
21: - **Snowpark Container Services (SPCS)**, which hosts the chat application - a Streamlit UI together with a service that collects the knowledge graph schema, calls Snowflake Cortex for the semantic mapping, compiles the result into a RelationalAI query, and renders the answer.
22: - **Snowflake Cortex AI**, whose LLMs perform the semantic mapping: given the user's question and the knowledge-graph schema, a Cortex model produces an **intermediate representation (IR)** of the query. The service then compiles that IR into an executable RelationalAI query.
23: 
24: ### What is RelationalAI?
25: 
26: RelationalAI is a cloud-native platform that enables organizations to streamline and enhance decisions with intelligence. RelationalAI extends Snowflake with native support for an expanding set of AI workloads (e.g., graph analytics, rule-based reasoning, and optimization), all within your Snowflake account, offering the same ease of use, scalability, security, and governance.
27: 
28: Users can build a knowledge graph using Python and materialize it on top of their Snowflake data, which are shared with the RelationalAI app through Snowflake Data Streams. Insights can be written back to Snowflake tables and shared across the organization.
29: 
30: ### What you will learn
31: 
32: - How to install the RelationalAI Native App in your Snowflake account
33: - How to load a Wikidata-derived knowledge graph into RelationalAI using the RelationalAI CLI
34: - How to use Snowflake Cortex to map a natural-language question to an intermediate representation (IR) of a query
35: - How to compile the IR into a RelationalAI query and execute it over the knowledge graph
36: - How to expose the pipeline as a chat application deployed on Snowpark Container Services
37: 
38: ### What you will need
39: 
40: - A [Snowflake Account](https://signup.snowflake.com/?utm_cta=quickstarts_) on AWS in the US East (N. Virginia) region or the US West (Oregon) region
41: - Basic knowledge of using a [Snowflake SQL Worksheet](https://docs.snowflake.com/en/user-guide/ui-snowsight-worksheets)
42: - [Snowflake privileges](https://other-docs.snowflake.com/en/native-apps/consumer-installing#set-up-required-privileges) on your user to install a Native Application
43: - Snowflake account privileges to create databases and schemas in your Snowflake account
44: - [Docker](https://www.docker.com/products/docker-desktop/) to build the container image used on Snowpark Container Services
45: - The [RelationalAI CLI](https://relational.ai/docs/reference/cli/)
46: 
47: ### What you will build
48: 
49: - A knowledge graph of films, people and genres derived from Wikidata and hosted in the RelationalAI Native App
50: - A pipeline that turns a natural-language question into an intermediate representation with Snowflake Cortex, then into a RelationalAI query, and executes it over the knowledge graph
51: - A Streamlit chat application deployed on Snowpark Container Services that exposes the pipeline to end users
52: 
53: > aside positive
54: > NOTE: If you do not already have the RelationalAI Native App installed, please follow the instructions [here](https://relational.ai/docs/native_app/installation).
55: 
56: <!-- ------------------------ -->
57: ## Architecture Overview
58: Duration: 2
59: 
60: The diagram below shows the three components of the system and the flow of a single question:
61: 
62: ![Knowledge Graph Question-Answering architecture](assets/kgqa_architecture.png)
63: 
64: - **User (web browser)**: opens the chat UI and types a natural-language question.
65: - **KG QA service (Snowpark Container Services)**: a Streamlit app plus a service that (1) loads the knowledge-graph schema from RelationalAI, (2) builds a prompt with the question and the schema, (3) sends the prompt to Snowflake Cortex, (4) compiles the returned IR into an executable RelationalAI (Rel) query, and (5) renders the answer. All of this uses the RelationalAI Python client.
66: - **Snowflake**: 
67:   - *Snowflake Cortex AI* runs the LLM call through `SNOWFLAKE.CORTEX.COMPLETE`, mapping the question plus schema to an intermediate representation (IR).
68:   - *The RelationalAI Native App* hosts the Wikidata-derived knowledge graph and executes the compiled Rel query, streaming the matching rows back to the service.
69: 
70: The following diagram summarizes the five phases of the pipeline:
71: 
72: ![KGQA pipeline from question to answer](assets/kgqa_pipeline.png)
73: 
74: <!-- ------------------------ -->
75: ## Example Walkthrough
76: Duration: 3
77: 
78: Before we start building, let's walk through a single question end to end so the individual steps make sense when you see them later. The chat application from this quickstart answers the question **"Who played Neo in The Matrix?"** in the following way:
79: 
80: ![Example question-answer session](assets/kgqa_example_walkthrough.png)
81: 
82: 1. **Question**: the user types *"Who played Neo in The Matrix?"* into the chat UI.
83: 2. **Semantic mapping (Cortex)**: the service loads the knowledge-graph schema (the relations `acted_in`, `directed_by`, `starred_in`, `belongs_to_genre`, ...) and prompts a Snowflake Cortex LLM to map the question to an intermediate representation. The IR is a small, structured JSON document, for example:
84: 
85: ```json
86: {
87:   "answer_type": "person",
88:   "relation": "acted_in",
89:   "entity": {
90:     "type": "film",
91:     "name": "The Matrix"
92:   },
93:   "constraints": [
94:     {"type": "role", "name": "Neo"}
95:   ]
96: }
97: ```
98: 
99: 3. **Compilation**: the service compiles the IR into an executable RelationalAI query. Conceptually, for this example the query looks for a `person` node `p` such that there is an `acted_in` relation between `p`, the film *The Matrix*, and the role *Neo*.
100: 4. **Execution**: RelationalAI executes the query over the knowledge graph and streams back the matching rows (here: a single `person` node).
101: 5. **Answer**: the service renders the result in the chat: *"Keanu Reeves played the role of Neo in The Matrix (1999)."*
102: 
103: Because every answer is produced by an actual graph query, the user can trace it: the app shows the generated IR, the compiled query, and the knowledge-graph row that produced the answer.

204: ## Loading the Knowledge Graph
205: Duration: 15
206: 
207: The knowledge graph used in this quickstart is derived from public [Wikidata](https://www.wikidata.org/) relations about films, people (actors and directors) and genres. It is stored in two tables, `ENTITY` and `EDGE`, that follow the node/relation structure RelationalAI consumes:
208: 
209: - `ENTITY (id VARCHAR, label VARCHAR, type VARCHAR)` - nodes such as `The Matrix` (type `film`), `Keanu Reeves` (type `person`) or `Neo` (type `role`).
210: - `EDGE (src_id VARCHAR, dst_id VARCHAR, type VARCHAR)` - directed relations such as `acted_in(person, film, role)`, `directed_by(person, film)` or `belongs_to_genre(film, genre)`.
211: 
212: ### Cloning the sample repository
213: 
214: The staging SQL script that downloads the Wikidata-derived data and loads it into these tables ships with the sample:
215: 
216: ```bash
217: git clone https://github.com/RelationalAI/rai-samples.git
218: cd rai-samples/samples/kgqa
219: ```
220: 
221: Open `sql/setup.sql` in a [SQL worksheet](https://docs.snowflake.com/en/user-guide/ui-snowsight-worksheets), run it, and confirm it reports the expected row counts for the `ENTITY` and `EDGE` tables. The script creates the tables, places the CSV files on a stage, and copies them in.
222: 
223: > aside positive
224: > If you prefer to create the tables yourself, use the DDL below. The script in the sample additionally downloads the data from public storage:
225: 
226: ```sql
227: CREATE OR REPLACE TABLE KGQA_DEMO.PUBLIC.ENTITY (
228:     ID   VARCHAR,
229:     LABEL VARCHAR,
230:     TYPE  VARCHAR
231: );
232: 
233: CREATE OR REPLACE TABLE KGQA_DEMO.PUBLIC.EDGE (
234:     SRC_ID  VARCHAR,
235:     DST_ID  VARCHAR,
236:     TYPE    VARCHAR
237: );
238: ```
239: 
240: ### Streaming the tables into a RelationalAI model
241: 
242: The RelationalAI Native App reads data from Snowflake through **import streams**, which use [change data capture](https://docs.snowflake.com/en/user-guide/streams) to keep a RelationalAI model synchronized with a Snowflake table roughly once per minute.
243: 
244: Create the model `kgqa_demo` and stream both tables into it:
245: 
246: ```bash
247: rai models:create --name kgqa_demo
248: 
249: rai imports:stream --source KGQA_DEMO.PUBLIC.ENTITY --model kgqa_demo
250: rai imports:stream --source KGQA_DEMO.PUBLIC.EDGE --model kgqa_demo
251: ```
252: 
253: Verify both streams are in status `LOADED` before continuing:
254: 
255: ```bash
256: rai imports:list --model kgqa_demo
257: ```
258: 
259: > aside positive
260: > IMPORTANT: The `rai imports:stream` command may take a few minutes. The streams are ready only once `rai imports:list --model kgqa_demo` reports both streams with status `LOADED` in `RUNNING` state.

263: ## Setting Up the Demo Notebook
264: Duration: 15
265: 
266: Now that the data is flowing into the `kgqa_demo` RelationalAI model, you will set up a Snowflake Notebook that models the knowledge graph and that you will use to develop and test the question-answering pipeline before deploying it as a service.
267: 
268: ### Creating the Notebook
269: 
270: 1. In Snowsight, open **Projects** » **Notebooks**.
271: 2. Click the blue **+ Notebook** button in the top right.
272: 3. Name the notebook **KGQA_DEMO**.

274: 
275: If you are not automatically taken into the notebook, open it now. The notebook should contain an empty cell at the top.
276: 
277: ![Snowflake Notebook for the KGQA pipeline](./assets/kgqa_notebook_overview.png)
278: 
279: ### Defining the model and its types
280: 
281: The RelationalAI data model uses two kinds of abstraction: **types**, which define the entities and relationships in the model, and **rules**, which derive information from them. The types below are created from the two tables streamed in the previous step.
282: 
283: Add a Python cell named `py_kgqa` with the following code:
284: 
285: ```python
286: import relationalai as rai
287: 
288: kgqa = rai.Model("kgqa_demo", dry_run=False)
289: 
290: # An `Entity` is a node in the knowledge graph.
291: Entity = kgqa.Type("Entity", source="KGQA_DEMO.PUBLIC.ENTITY")
292: 
293: # A `Relation` is a directed edge in the knowledge graph.
294: Relation = kgqa.Type("Relation", source="KGQA_DEMO.PUBLIC.EDGE")
295: Relation.define(
296:     src=(Entity, "src_id", "id"),
297:     dst=(Entity, "dst_id", "id"),
298: )
299: ```

301: Now inspect the relations that are available to the model - `src` and `dst` come from the generic `EDGE` table, and the concrete relation names below come from the Wikidata-derived data:
302: 
303: ```python
304: print(kgqa.relations())
305: ```
306: 
307: The output should look similar to:
308: 
309: ```
310: [
311:   ('acted_in',        ['person', 'film', 'role']),
312:   ('directed_by',     ['person', 'film']),
313:   ('starred_in',      ['person', 'film']),
314:   ('belongs_to_genre', ['film', 'genre']),
315: ]
316: ```
317: 
318: > aside positive
319: > IMPORTANT: The RelationalAI Python client must be configured to talk to your account, and the notebook runs as the role `rai_user_role` created earlier. Ensure `rai init` was completed with the `rai_user` credentials before running the cells above.
320: 
321: <!-- ------------------------ -->
322: ## Running the Question-Answering Pipeline
323: Duration: 20
324: 
325: This is the heart of the quickstart. You will implement the three phases of the walkthrough - **semantic mapping** (Cortex to IR), **compilation** (IR to Rel), and **execution** (Rel over the knowledge graph) - using Snowpark to call Snowflake Cortex and the RelationalAI Python client to run queries.
326: 
327: ### Generating the intermediate representation with Cortex
328: 
329: Add a Python cell named `py_cortex` that calls `SNOWFLAKE.CORTEX.COMPLETE` through the Snowpark session. The prompt injects the knowledge-graph schema so that the model constrains its output to relations that actually exist in the graph:
330: 
331: ```python
332: import json
333: 
334: model_name = "mixtral-8x7b"
335: 
336: 
337: def knowledge_graph_schema() -> str:
338:     relations = list(kgqa.relations())
339:     return "\n".join(
340:         f"- {relation}({', '.join(node_types)})"
341:         for relation, node_types in relations
342:     )
343: 
344: 
345: def generate_ir(question: str) -> dict:
346:     prompt = f"""
347: You translate natural-language questions into an intermediate representation (IR) of a
348: knowledge-graph query. The knowledge graph has these relations:
349: 
350: {knowledge_graph_schema()}
351: 
352: Translate the question below into IR. Answer with JSON only, using these keys:
353: - "answer_type": the node type the answer consists of (person, film, genre, ...)
354: - "relation": the relation to walk
355: - "entity": an entity referenced by the question, as {{"type", "name"}}
356: - "constraints": a list of additional constraints, as {{"type", "name"}}
357: 
358: Question: {question}
359: """
360:     row = session.sql(
361:         "SELECT SNOWFLAKE.CORTEX.COMPLETE(?, ?) AS response",
362:         params=[model_name, prompt],
363:     ).collect()[0]
364:     return json.loads(row["RESPONSE"])
365: ```
366: 
367: > aside positive
368: > The exact set of models available for `SNOWFLAKE.CORTEX.COMPLETE` in your region is listed in the [Cortex LLM functions](https://docs.snowflake.com/en/user-guide/snowflake-cortex/llm-functions) documentation. `mixtral-8x7b` is used throughout this quickstart; any supported model is fine.
369: 
370: ### Compiling the IR into a Rel query
371: 
372: Add a Python cell named `py_compile`. The function below turns the IR produced by Cortex into an executable RelationalAI query. For each IR it generates a rule that walks the graph from the referenced entity through the named relation, applies the constraints, and projects the nodes of the requested `answer_type`:
373: 
374: ```python
375: def ir_to_rel(ir: dict) -> str:
376:     answer_type = ir["answer_type"]
377:     relation = ir["relation"]
378:     entity = ir["entity"]
379: 
380:     lines = [f"// IR compiler for: {entity['name']}"]
381:     lines.append("answer[] = N where")
382:     lines.append(f"    N:{answer_type} and")
383:     lines.append(f'    NE:{entity["type"]}("{entity["name"]}") and')
384:     lines.append(f"    {relation}(N, NE)")
385:     for constraint in ir.get("constraints", []):
386:         lines.append(f'    and {constraint["type"]}("{constraint["name"]}") and')
387:         lines.append(f"    {relation}(N, NE, {constraint['type']})")
388:     return "\n".join(lines) + "\n"
389: ```
390: 
391: ### Executing the query over the knowledge graph
392: 
393: Add a Python cell named `py_answer` that combines everything. It generates the IR with Cortex, compiles it with `ir_to_rel`, runs the compiled rule in the RelationalAI model, and renders the answer rows:
394: 
395: ```python
396: def run_rel(kgqa: rai.Model, rel_code: str) -> list:
397:     # Adds the generated Rel code as a rule named `answer` in the model and
398:     # queries it, returning the projected `answer` rows.
399:     with kgqa.rule():
400:         kgqa.add(rel_code)
401:     with kgqa.query() as select:
402:         response = select(kgqa.answer)
403:     return response.fetch()
404: 
405: 
406: def ask(question: str) -> str:
407:     ir = generate_ir(question)
408:     print("IR:", json.dumps(ir, indent=2))
409: 
410:     rel_code = ir_to_rel(ir)
411:     print("Rel:", rel_code)
412: 
413:     rows = run_rel(kgqa, rel_code)
414:     return "; ".join(rows["answer"].tolist())
415: ```
416: 
417: > aside positive
418: > NOTE: The compiled Rel code is added to the model with `kgqa.add(...)` inside a `kgqa.rule()` context (a rule that derives the `answer` relation), and the derived rows are projected with `kgqa.query()`. The sample notebook packages this into a small `run_rel` helper so the pipeline reads cleanly.
419: 
420: ### Asking questions
421: 
422: Run the cells above, then add one more cell and try the example from the walkthrough:
423: 
424: ```python
425: question = "Who played Neo in The Matrix?"
426: print(ask(question))
427: ```
428: 
429: Expected result:
430: 
431: ```
432: IR: {'answer_type': 'person', 'relation': 'acted_in',
433:      'entity': {'type': 'film', 'name': 'The Matrix'},
434:      'constraints': [{'type': 'role', 'name': 'Neo'}]}
435: Rel: // IR compiler for: The Matrix
436:      answer[] = N where
437:          N:person and
438:          NE:film("The Matrix") and
439:          acted_in(N, NE)
440:          and role("Neo") and
441:          acted_in(N, NE, role)
442: Keanu Reeves
443: ```
444: 
445: Try a few more questions to gain confidence:
446: 
447: ```python
448: for question in [
449:     "Which films did Keanu Reeves direct?",
450:     "What genre does the film Inception belong to?",
451:     "Which actors starred in The Matrix Reloaded?",
452: ]:
453:     print(question, "->", ask(question))
454: ```
455: 
456: > aside negative
457: > The Cortex model occasionally returns malformed JSON or an IR that references a relation not present in the schema. Re-run the cell in that case, or add a short retry loop that calls `generate_ir` again. The pipeline is deterministic (`temperature = 0`), so a retry resolves most failures.

460: ## Deploying the Service on Snowpark Container Services
461: Duration: 15
462: 
463: With the pipeline working in the notebook, you will now deploy it as a chat application. The service on [Snowpark Container Services](https://docs.snowflake.com/en/developer-guide/snowpark-container-services/overview) hosts a Streamlit UI and performs the same steps as the notebook: load the schema, ask Cortex for the IR, compile it, and run it against the knowledge graph.
464: 
465: ### The application code
466: 
467: The sample repository contains the full application under `samples/kgqa/app/`. The core of `app.py` looks like this:
468: 
469: ```python
470: import json
471: 
472: import streamlit as st
473: import relationalai as rai
474: from snowflake.snowpark import Session
475: 
476: SESSION = Session.builder.getOrCreate()
477: 
478: kgqa = rai.Model("kgqa_demo", dry_run=False)
479: 
480: 
481: def generate_ir(question: str) -> dict:
482:     prompt = build_prompt(kgqa.relations(), question)  # same prompt as the notebook
483:     row = SESSION.sql(
484:         "SELECT SNOWFLAKE.CORTEX.COMPLETE('mixtral-8x7b', ?) AS response",
485:         params=[prompt],
486:     ).collect()[0]
487:     return json.loads(row["RESPONSE"])
488: 
489: 
490: def answer(question: str) -> str:
491:     ir = generate_ir(question)
492:     rel_code = ir_to_rel(ir)
493:     with kgqa.query() as select:
494:         response = select(kgqa.answer(rel_code))
495:     rows = response.fetch()
496:     return "; ".join(rows["answer"].tolist())
497: 
498: 
499: st.title("Ask your knowledge graph")
500: if question := st.chat_input("Try: Who played Neo in The Matrix?"):
501:     st.write(answer(question))
502: ```
503: 
504: The `requirements.txt` for the image lists `streamlit`, `relationalai` and `snowflake-snowpark-python` (Snowpark is used to call Cortex; the RelationalAI Python client connects to the Native App in your account).
505: 
506: ### Building and pushing the image
507: 
508: Create an [image repository](https://docs.snowflake.com/en/sql-reference/sql/create-image-repository) that will hold the container image:
509: 
510: ```sql
511: USE ROLE rai_user_role;
512: USE DATABASE KGQA_DEMO;
513: USE SCHEMA PUBLIC;
514: 
515: CREATE OR REPLACE IMAGE REPOSITORY IMAGE_REPOSITORY;
516: ```
517: 
518: Build the image and push it to the repository. The registry host follows the pattern `<orgname>-registry.snowflakecomputing.com`:
519: 
520: ```bash
521: docker build -t kgqa-demo-app ./app
522: docker tag kgqa-demo-app <orgname>-registry.snowflakecomputing.com/KGQA_DEMO/PUBLIC/IMAGE_REPOSITORY/kgqa-demo-app:latest
523: docker push <orgname>-registry.snowflakecomputing.com/KGQA_DEMO/PUBLIC/IMAGE_REPOSITORY/kgqa-demo-app:latest
524: ```
525: 
526: > aside positive

528: 
529: ### Creating the service
530: 
531: Create the compute pool and the service. The service spec runs the Streamlit container on port `8501` and exposes it through a public endpoint:
532: 
533: ```sql
534: CREATE OR REPLACE COMPUTE POOL kgqa_pool
535:   MIN_NODES = 1
536:   MAX_NODES = 1
537:   INSTANCE_FAMILY = CPU_X64_S;
538: 
539: CREATE OR REPLACE SERVICE KGQA_DEMO.PUBLIC.KGQA_DEMO_SERVICE
540:   MIN_INSTANCES = 1
541:   MAX_INSTANCES = 1
542:   COMPUTE_POOL = kgqa_pool
543:   SPEC = @KGQA_DEMO.PUBLIC.SPEC_STAGE/kgqa_spec.yaml;
544: ```
545: 
546: Where `sql/kgqa_spec.yaml` from the sample defines the endpoint:
547: 
548: ```yaml
549: specs:
550:   - containers:
551:       - name: kgqa-demo-app
552:         image: /KGQA_DEMO/PUBLIC/IMAGE_REPOSITORY/kgqa-demo-app:latest
553:         env:
554:           RAI_MODEL: kgqa_demo
555:         readinessProbe:
556:           port: 8501
557:           path: /_stcore/health
558:     endpoints:
559:       - name: app
560:         port: 8501
561:         public: true
562: ```
563:

566: ```sql
567: CALL SYSTEM$GET_SERVICE_STATUS('KGQA_DEMO.PUBLIC.KGQA_DEMO_SERVICE');
568: SHOW ENDPOINTS IN SERVICE KGQA_DEMO.PUBLIC.KGQA_DEMO_SERVICE;
569: ```

576: ## Troubleshooting
577: Duration: 5
578: 
579: | Symptom | Likely cause | Fix |
580: | --- | --- | --- |
581: | `rai imports:list --model kgqa_demo` shows streams not `LOADED` | The import streams were interrupted or the engine is still starting | Wait for the engine to be ready, re-run `rai imports:stream ...`, and check `SHOW STREAMS IN SCHEMA KGQA_DEMO.PUBLIC` in Snowsight. |
582: | The notebook fails with an authentication error from RelationalAI | The RelationalAI CLI was configured with a different user/role | Re-run `rai init` and select the `rai_user_role` role, the `KGQA_WH` warehouse and the `kgqa_engine` engine, then restart the notebook. |
583: | `SNOWFLAKE.CORTEX.COMPLETE` returns *unsupported model* | The model name is not available in your region or your role lacks Cortex access | Use a supported model from the [Cortex LLM functions](https://docs.snowflake.com/en/user-guide/snowflake-cortex/llm-functions) list, or grant Cortex usage to `rai_user_role`. |
584: | The pipeline returns `JSONDecodeError` | The model returned prose instead of JSON | Add a retry loop around `generate_ir`, or post-process the response to extract the JSON payload. |
585: | The answer is empty or the IR references an unknown relation | The questions references an entity/relation outside the graph, or the LLM hallucinated a relation | Ask only about films, people and genres present in the graph; pass the exact schema into the prompt, as shown in `generate_ir`. |
586: | The service stays `NOT_READY` | The image is still being pulled, or the spec is invalid | Check `SYSTEM$GET_SERVICE_STATUS`, view the service logs with `SYSTEM$GET_SERVICE_LOGS`, and confirm the image name and port match the spec. |
587: | Docker cannot push to the image repository | The registry host or credentials are wrong, or Docker is not logged in to the registry | Confirm the registry host prefix from `IMAGE_REPOSITORY` in Snowsight, and run `docker login <orgname>-registry.snowflakecomputing.com`. |
