1: # Codelab Formatting Guide
2: 
3: Bug or feature request? File it [here](https://github.com/googlecodelabs/tools/issues).
4: 
5: ## Getting Started
6: 
7: Copy [this template doc](https://docs.google.com/document/d/1E6XMcdTexh5O8JwGy42SY3Ehzi8gOfUGiqTiUX6N04o/edit) as a starting point and then iteratively mutate the metadata and contents to your liking, following the formatting rules described below.
8: 
9: To preview a codelab:
10: 
11: -  (optional one-time setup) Install the [Preview Codelab Chrome extension](https://chrome.google.com/webstore/detail/preview-codelab/lhojjnijnkiglhkggagbapfonpdlinji) in your browser.
12: 
13: - Click the Chrome extension's button while you're in your codelab Google Doc tab, or
14: - Navigate manually to **https://codelabs-preview.appspot.com/?file_id=[google-doc-id]**.
15: 
16: ## Formatting Reference
17: 
18: 1. Table of Contents
19: 
20:     Every codelab document must use the **Heading 1** paragraph style to delineate the steps of the codelab. In turn, these headings will be used to automatically create a Table of Contents which shows the student exactly where they are in the codelab and lets them jump to any step.
21: 
22:     The table of contents disappears for smaller browsers but is still available from the hamburger menu.
23: 
24: 1. Codelab Metadata (Google Docs)
25: 
26:     There is some additional metadata that is required in order to properly publish a codelab. This metadata should be added as a **two-column table** anywhere before the first step of the codelab. For example:
27: 
28: 
29: 
30:     You are free to add your own metadata here if you'd like but certain key/value pairs are reserved for specific codelab publishing features. The current list of reserved metadata terms are:
31: 
32:     * **Summary:** A short summary of the codelab that will be shown in the codelab browser UI.
33:     * **URL:** The URL suffix where this codelab will be published, i.e. the path after the root URL to a collection of codelabs. For example, the Google Codelabs site uses codelabs.developers.google.com/codelabs/ as root and this value is appended to that base to form the unique URL for a given codelab.
34:     * **Category:** A single, top-level category that will be used to group codelabs by platform. Categories are normally curated by an organization (e.g. we have a set we use for the Google Codelabs site) but each publisher is free to use this value at their discretion.
35:     * **Environment**: A tag that allows use to output some codelabs for a specific environment. All codelabs default to the "Web" environment but given some hardware constraints we might only want to generate them for a "Kiosk" environment where we know people will have the right hardware. \
36: You can also use this to target specific events, for instance:  \
37: "Web, polymer-summit" (without quotes)
38:     * **Status:** One or more of (Draft, Published, Deprecated, Hidden) to indicate the progress and whether the codelab is ready to be published. 'Hidden' implies the codelab is for restricted use, should be available only by direct URL, and should not appear on the main index page.
39:     * **Feedback Link:** The URL that the student should be sent to when they click on the feedback link to report a bug in the codelab.
40:     * **Analytics Account:** This allows you to specify a custom Google Analytics ID for your codelab. If no ID is specified, it defaults to a global codelabs analytics account.
41: 
42: 1. Codelab Metadata (Markdown)
43: 
44:     You are free to add your own metadata here if you'd like but certain key/value pairs are reserved for specific codelab publishing features. The current list of reserved metadata terms are:
45: 
46:     * **summary:** A short summary of the codelab that will be shown in the codelab browser UI.
47:     * **id:** The name of the folder that will be generated once you export the markdown file via claat.
48:     * **categories:** A single, top-level category that will be used to group codelabs by platform. Categories are normally curated by an organization (e.g. we have a set we use for the Google Codelabs site) but each publisher is free to use this value at their discretion.
49:     * **environments**: A tag that allows use to output some codelabs for a specific environment. All codelabs default to the "Web" environment but given some hardware constraints we might only want to generate them for a "Kiosk" environment where we know people will have the right hardware. \
50: You can also use this to target specific events, for instance:  \
51: "Web, polymer-summit" (without quotes)
52:     * **status:** One or more of (Draft, Published, Deprecated, Hidden) to indicate the progress and whether the codelab is ready to be published. 'Hidden' implies the codelab is for restricted use, should be available only by direct URL, and should not appear on the main index page.
53:     * **feedback link:** The URL that the student should be sent to when they click on the feedback link to report a bug in the codelab.
54:     * **analytics account:** This allows you to specify a custom Google Analytics ID for your codelab. If no ID is specified, it defaults to a global codelabs analytics account.
55:     * **tags:** Add relevant tags to make your codelab easily found.
56:     * **authors:** Indicate the author(s) of this specific codelab.
57: 
58: 1. Headers
59: 
60:     Within the steps of your codelab you should use the **Heading 2**, **Heading 3** and **Heading 4** paragraph styles to organize your content. These will get translated to `<h2>`, `<h3>` and `<h4>` tags in the codelab markup.
61: 
62:     Also, if you wish to include some additional administrative information at the beginning of your codelab you can freely use the **Heading 2**, **Heading 3** and **Heading 4** paragraph styles and they will not show up in the codelab as long as they appear before the first **Heading 1**.
63: 
64: 1. Text Styles
65: 
66:     For the most part, it doesn't matter which fonts you use in your Google Doc draft; everything will be formatted using Roboto in the final codelab.
67: 
68:     There are some simple ways that you can add emphasis to certain parts of the text. Bolded and italicized text will be passed through to the codelab markup as `<strong>` and `<em>` tags respectively. Also, passages of text formatted with the `Courier New` font will be passed through as an inline `<code>` tag in the markup.
69: 
70: 1. Responsive Images
71: 
72:     Inline images in your codelab should just work seamlessly. You can re-size them in your codelab document and that width will be applied as a **max-width** on the image in the codelab markup so that images are the same size relative to the text but also scale down appropriately for smaller browsers.
73: 
74: 1. Youtube Videos
75: 
76:     Youtube Videos can be embedded by doing:
77:      - Add an image in the document. The image can be a screenshot of the video for instance but it doesn't really matter since it won't be displayed but replaced by the embedded video.
78:      - Add an "Alt Text" to the image by doing **Cmd+Opt+Y** or **Right click > "Alt Text..."**
79:      - Put a Youtube video link in the **Description** field of the Alt Text. in the format `https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=[video_ID]`
80:     > Specifying a start time is not supported at this time.
81: 
82: 1. Embedded Iframes
83: 
84:     Iframes can be embedded by doing:
85:      - Add an image in the document. The image can be a screenshot of the iframe for instance but it doesn't really matter since it won't be displayed but replaced by the embedded iframe.
86:      - Add an "Alt Text" to the image by doing **Cmd+Opt+Y** or **Right click > "Alt Text..."**
87:      - Put a full URL in the **Description** field of the Alt Text. in the format `https://www.domain.com/watch?foo=bar`. Note that for security reasons, iframe embbedding is limited to an enumerated set of allowable iframe source URLs. Feel free to submit a PR if you'd like to augment that list or tweak your own version of the claat command.
88: 
89: 1. Info Boxes
90: 
91:     For additional information that you would like to specially call-out in your codelab, there are two styles of info boxes:
92: 
93:     1. Positive information like best practices and time saving tips should be formatted as a **single-cell table** with a **light green 3** background.
94: 
95:     2. Negative information like warnings and API usage restrictions should be formatted as a **single-cell table** with a **light orange 3** background.
96: 
97:     It is recommended that you keep your infoboxes clean, concise and focused on a single topic. If you have information which may be useful to know but is not a critical part of the codelab instructions, then you should link to that information from the FAQ section rather than including it as an infobox.
98: 
99: 1. Command-line Snippets
100: 
101:     It's often the case that you will have command-line instructions or log messages which are formatted with a monospaced font and have pre-defined whitespace. You can add these sections to your codelab by creating a **single-cell table** and making sure that all the text is formatted using the **Consolas font**.
102: 
103: 1. Code Snippets
104: 
105:     Code snippets with syntax highlighting can be added by creating a **single-cell table** and making sure that all the text is formatted using the **`Courier New`** font.
106: 
107:     Any additional styles applied to the code will be overridden by the syntax highlighting. This means that you're free to use code highlighting Add-ons in your codelab doc but it will have no effect on how the code is highlighted in the final codelab.
108: 
109:     It is also strongly recommended that you provide a **Heading 3** header directly above your code snippet with the file name. This helps students keep track of where the code is coming from. The codelab framework also uses the file extension of the prior header as a clue for how to highlight the code.
110: 
111:     It is also strongly recommended that you make your **Heading 3** header a hyperlink to the actual file if it is available on GitHub. A GitHub icon will automatically be added to the heading in such cases.
112: 
113: 1. Frequently Asked Questions
114: 
115:     As the author of the codelab, you have developed and tested your code. You've probably run into all sorts of common issues or misconceptions. By linking to frequently asked questions, after each step where they often occur, you will reassure the students that they have everything they need to complete the codelab and avoid having to explain everything inline in your codelab.
116:     FAQs are easy to add. All the author needs to do is provide an unordered list of hyperlinks and preface it with a **Heading 3** header with the exact text: **Frequently Asked Questions**.
117: 
118:     Link icons will be added automatically for stackoverflow.com, developers.google.com, developers.android.com and support.google.com. All links will be configured to open in a new tab.
119: 
120: 1. Download Buttons
121: 
122:     You can make it really easy to get started by including direct download buttons inline in your codelab. In order to add a button to your codelab, simply add a hyperlink and make sure that it is highlighted with a **dark green 1** background.
123: 
124:     Additionally, if the link text begins with the word "Download", a file download icon will be added to the button.
125: 
126: 1. Per-step Time Estimates
127: 
128:     Many participants are not fully committed to completing a codelab when they start it. One of the ways that we can keep them in our codelab is by giving them accurate estimates about how much additional effort is required to complete the codelab at each step.
129: 
130:     In order to add this feature to your codelab, simply annotate each step in your codelab doc with a Duration: which uses **dark grey 1** text.
131: 
132:     That's it. The codelab framework will do everything else for you. If you forget to annotate a step with a duration, the default is 1:00. Also, if the last step of your codelab is just a congratulations page, you should set the duration of that step to **0**.
133: 
134: 1. Conditional Steps
135: 
136:     Sometimes it's useful to have different versions of a codelab for different environments. For example, you might have some steps that only apply to students who take the codelab in a classroom setting while other steps only apply to people who are following the instructions at their own pace online.
137: 
138:     The format is similar to the duration metadata. You simply specify one or more environments with an Environment: which uses **dark grey 1** text. The Duration and/or Environment fields, when present, should be followed by a blank line and should be set in normal text (not in Heading 1, lest they be considered part of the step title).
139: 
140:     If no environment metadata is specified, the default environment is "Web, Kiosk".
141: 
142:     When previewing your codelab, you can change environments using the &env=web or &env=kiosk parameters.
143: 
144: 1. Fragment imports
145: 
146:     It is possible for a codelab to import another doc as a step fragment. For instance, it could be a set of setup instructions shared among multiple codelabs:
147: 
148:     [[**import** [funny dog](https://docs.google.com/document/d/1VkJopEKiqitwFgqFOEU6rpB1VE-R-uYWq4erNHP2TQ4/edit)]]
149: 
150:     The contents of the funny dog document will be inserted in the codelab, replacing import instruction.
151: 
152:     The instruction syntax is:
153: 
154:     *   start with [[ (two square brackets)
155:     *   followed by **import** keyword in bold
156:     *   followed by a link to a doc
157:     *   end with ]] (two square brackets)
158: 
159:     Caveat: The imported doc is limited to content within a step (hence the term "fragment"). Including multiple steps, or even the step title/heading, within the imported doc is not supported.
160: 
161: 1. Resumable Codelabs
162: 
163:     When a user returns to a codelab, they may be returning via a bookmark or a short-link posted online, it usually takes them to the first page of the codelab. In that case, the codelab remembers where they left off and asks them if they wish to resume where they left off. This makes it easier for the user to jump back in and gives us more accurate analytics about how long users spend on each step.
164: 
165:     This is simply part of the framework. There is nothing that you need to do as a codelab author to enable this feature.
166: 
167: 1. Feedback Links
168: 
169:     At the bottom of every step of the codelab there is a link for reporting bugs. This link can be configured using the **Feedback Link** setting in your metadata table.
170: 
171: 1. Inline Surveys
172: 
173:     **NOTE: Surveys cannot be used to collect data that can individually, or in conjunction with other information from this site, help locate and identify a particular user or reveal their sensitive demographics information. Any data collected should be sufficiently anonymized and aggregated. Also, consider that the surveys can possibly send a numerical ID of the selections instead of the actual value itself. Apart from helping on the localization front, this can also help prevent from injecting obvious PII values into GA.**
174: 
175:     As we've seen in previous years, participants consume our codelabs for a wide range of reasons. In order to give us some more insight into how different people consume codelabs, we can ask them some quick multiple choice questions in the early stages of our codelab.
176: 
177:     You can configure these short survey questions to ask whatever you think is relevant to your codelab. In order to include a survey question in your codelab, add a single-cell table with a **light blue 3** background. Format your question with the **Heading 4** paragraph style and provide an **unordered list** of choices.
178: 
179:     The participants' answers will automatically be added as custom variables in Google Analytics which can help you understand things like:
180: 
181:     *   _What is the difference in completion rate between novices and experts?_
182:     *   _What is the average time spent for people who wanted to write code vs. people who just wanted to read?_
183:     *   _Is the bounce rate affected by the students' preference in IDE?_
184: 
185:     Of course, we need to be mindful of our participants' time and concentration and only ask a few key questions. It is _not_ recommended to have a survey after each step.
186: 
187: 1. What you'll learn
188: 
189:     Having a header 2 of "What you'll learn" followed by a bullet point list creates a list of check marks.
190: 
191:     A title of "What we've covered" has the same effect.
192:     
193: 1. YouTube Video Embeds
194: 
195:     Use a video tag like so `<video id="DWAinkJ54AP8"></video>` to embed a video uploaded to YouTube with the URL https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=DWAinkJ54AP8
196: 
197: ## Things to avoid
198: 
199: - **Footers:** Any characters included in the footer (beyond the default page number) result in parsing bugs. For this reason, page footers are not recommended.

10: # Build a Custom API in Python and Flask
11: <!-- ------------------------ -->
12: ## Overview 
13: Duration: 5
14: 
15: Many builders want to share some of the data stored in Snowflake over an http API. Modern mobile and web applications often want to retrieve that data through http APIs. This tutorial will go through how to build, deploy, and host a custom API Powered by Snowflake.
16: 
17: This API consists of reporting endpoints from data stored in Snowflake. After completing this guide, you will have built a custom API built with [Python Flask](https://flask.palletsprojects.com/). 
18: 
19: The dataset is the [TPC-H](https://docs.snowflake.com/en/user-guide/sample-data-tpch) data set included in your Snowflake account.
20: 
21: 
22: ### Prerequisites
23: - Privileges necessary to create a user, database, warehouse, compute pool, repository, network network rule, external access integration, and service in Snowflake
24: - Privileges necessary to access the tables in the `SNOWFLAKE_SAMPLE_DATA.TPCH_SF10` database and schema
25: - Access to run SQL in the Snowflake console or SnowSQL
26: - Basic experience using git, GitHub, and Codespaces
27: - Intermediate knowledge of Python
28: 
29: ### What You’ll Learn 
30: - How to configure and build a custom API Powered by Snowflake
31: - How to build, publish, and deploy a container with the API in Snowflake
32: 
33: ### What You’ll Need 
34: - [Snowflake](https://snowflake.com) Account in an AWS commercial region
35: - [GitHub](https://github.com/) Account with credits for Codespaces
36: - [ngrok](https://ngrok.com) Account (Optional, needed for Step 10)
37: 
38: ### What You’ll Build 
39: - API Powered by Snowflake

41: <!-- ------------------------ -->
42: ## Setting up a Warehouse
43: Duration: 1
44: 
45: The API needs a warehouse to query the data to return to the caller. To create the database and warehouse, connect to Snowflake and run the following commands in the Snowflake console or using SnowSQL:
46: 
47: ```sql
48: USE ROLE ACCOUNTADMIN;
49: CREATE WAREHOUSE DATA_API_WH WITH WAREHOUSE_SIZE='xsmall';
50: ```
51: 
52: ### Create the Application Role in Snowflake
53: Duration: 1
54: 
55: The application will run as a new role with minimal priviledges. To create the role, connect to Snowflake and run the following SQL statements to create the role and grant it access to the data needed for the application.
56: 
57: ```SQL
58: USE ROLE ACCOUNTADMIN;
59: CREATE ROLE DATA_API_ROLE;
60: 
61: GRANT USAGE ON WAREHOUSE DATA_API_WH TO ROLE DATA_API_ROLE;
62: GRANT IMPORTED PRIVILEGES ON DATABASE SNOWFLAKE_SAMPLE_DATA TO ROLE DATA_API_ROLE;
63: 
64: GRANT ROLE DATA_API_ROLE TO ROLE ACCOUNTADMIN;
65: ```
66: 
67: <!-- ------------------------ -->
68: ## Setting up your Development Environment
69: Duration: 3
70: 
71: The code used in this guide is hosted in github. You will need a new Codespace from the GitHub [repository]](https://github.com/sfc-gh-bculberson/lab_data_api_python).
72: 
73: To create a new codespace, browse to the GitHub [repository](https://github.com/sfc-gh-bculberson/lab_data_api_python) in a browser. You will need to login to GitHub if you are not already logged in to access Codespaces. After logging in, click on the green "<> Code" button and "create codespace on main" button.
74: 
75: You will then be redirected into Codespaces where your development environment will load and all code from GitHub will be loaded in the project.
76: 
77: ### Endpoints
78: The API creates two sets of endpoints, one for using the Snowflake connector:
79: 1. `https://host/connector/customers/top10`
80:   * Which takes the following optional query parameters:
81:     1. `start_range` - the start date of the range in `YYYY-MM-DD` format. Defaults to `1995-01-01`.
82:     1. `end_range` - the end date of the range in `YYYY-MM-DD` format. Defaults to `1995-03-31`.
83: 2. `https://host/connector/clerk/<CLERKID>/yearly_sales/<YEAR>`
84:   * Which takes 2 required path parameters:
85:     1. `CLERKID` - the clerk ID. Use just the numbers, such as `000000001`.
86:     2. `YEAR` - the year to use, such as `1995`.
87: 
88: And the same ones using Snowpark:
89: 1. `https://host/snowpark/customers/top10`
90:   * Which takes the following optional query parameters:
91:     1. `start_range` - the start date of the range in `YYYY-MM-DD` format. Defaults to `1995-01-01`.
92:     1. `end_range` - the end date of the range in `YYYY-MM-DD` format. Defaults to `1995-03-31`.
93: 2. `https://host/snowpark/clerk/<CLERKID>/yearly_sales/<YEAR>`
94:   * Which takes 2 required path parameters:
95:     1. `CLERKID` - the clerk ID. Use just the numbers, such as `000000001`.
96:     2. `YEAR` - the year to use, such as `1995`.
97: 
98: ### Code
99: The `src/` directory has all the source code for the API. The `connector.py` file contains all the entrypoints for the API endpoints using the Snowflake Connector for Python. The `customers_top10()` function is one of the API endpoints we needed for this API which finds the top 10 customers by sales in a date range. Review the code and the SQL needed to retrieve the data from Snowflake and serialize it to JSON for the response. This endpoint also takes 2 optional query string parameters start_range and end_range.
100: 
101: ```python
102: @connector.route('/customers/top10')
103: def customers_top10():
104:     # Validate arguments
105:     sdt_str = request.args.get('start_range') or '1995-01-01'
106:     edt_str = request.args.get('end_range') or '1995-03-31'
107:     try:
108:         sdt = datetime.datetime.strptime(sdt_str, dateformat)
109:         edt = datetime.datetime.strptime(edt_str, dateformat)
110:     except:
111:         abort(400, "Invalid start and/or end dates.")
112:     sql_string = '''
113:         SELECT
114:             o_custkey
115:           , SUM(o_totalprice) AS sum_totalprice
116:         FROM snowflake_sample_data.tpch_sf10.orders
117:         WHERE o_orderdate >= '{sdt}'
118:           AND o_orderdate <= '{edt}'
119:         GROUP BY o_custkey
120:         ORDER BY sum_totalprice DESC
121:         LIMIT 10
122:     '''
123:     sql = sql_string.format(sdt=sdt, edt=edt)
124:     try:
125:         res = conn.cursor(DictCursor).execute(sql)
126:         return make_response(jsonify(res.fetchall()))
127:     except:
128:         abort(500, "Error reading from Snowflake. Check the logs for details.")
129: ```
130: 
131: You can also review the other endpoints in [connector.py](https://github.com/sfc-gh-bculberson/lab_data_api_python/blob/main/src/connector.py) to see how simple it is to host multiple endpoints.
132: 
133: If you would also like to see how to build endpoints using the Snowflake Snowpark API, review [snowpark.py](https://github.com/sfc-gh-bculberson/lab_data_api_python/blob/main/src/snowpark.py).

136: ## Building the Application Container
137: Duration: 1
138: 
139: To create the application container, we will leverage docker. The Dockerfile is based on python 3.8 and installs the required libraries needed for the application as well as the code. To create the docker container, run this command in the terminal provided by Codespaces:
140: ```bash
141: docker build -t dataapi .
142: ```
143: 
144: <!-- ------------------------ -->
145: ## Creating the Image Registry
146: Duration: 1
147: 
148:  To create the image registry and the database which contains it, connect to Snowflake and run the following commands in the Snowflake console or using SnowSQL:
149: 
150: ```sql
151: 
152: USE ROLE ACCOUNTADMIN;
153: CREATE DATABASE API;
154: 
155: GRANT ALL ON DATABASE API TO ROLE DATA_API_ROLE;
156: GRANT ALL ON SCHEMA API.PUBLIC TO ROLE DATA_API_ROLE;
157: 
158: USE DATABASE API;
159: CREATE OR REPLACE IMAGE REPOSITORY API;
160: 
161: GRANT READ ON IMAGE REPOSITORY API TO ROLE DATA_API_ROLE;
162: 
163: SHOW IMAGE REPOSITORIES;
164: ```
165: 
166: Note the `repository_url` in the response as that will be needed in the next step.
167: 
168: <!-- ------------------------ -->
169: ## Pushing the Container to the Repository
170: Duration: 1
171: 
172: Run the following command in the terminal, replacing the `<repository_url>` with your repository in the previous step, in Codespaces to login to the container repository. You will be prompted for your Snowflake username and password to login to your repository.
173: 
174: ```bash
175: docker login <repository_url>
176: docker build -t <repository_url>/dataapi .
177: docker push <repository_url>/dataapi
178: ```
179: 
180: <!-- ------------------------ -->
181: ## Creating the Compute Pool
182: Duration: 1
183: 
184:  To create the compute pool to run the application, connect to Snowflake and run the following command in the Snowflake console or using SnowSQL:
185: 
186: ```sql
187: 
188: USE ROLE ACCOUNTADMIN;
189: 
190: CREATE COMPUTE POOL API
191:   MIN_NODES = 1
192:   MAX_NODES = 5
193:   INSTANCE_FAMILY = CPU_X64_XS;
194: 
195: GRANT USAGE ON COMPUTE POOL API TO ROLE DATA_API_ROLE;
196: GRANT MONITOR ON COMPUTE POOL API TO ROLE DATA_API_ROLE;
197: 
198: ```
199: 
200: <!-- ------------------------ -->
201: ## Creating the Application Service
202: Duration: 1
203: 
204: To create the service to host the application, connect to Snowflake and run the following command in the Snowflake console or using SnowSQL.
205: 
206: ```sql
207: 
208: USE ROLE ACCOUNTADMIN;
209: GRANT BIND SERVICE ENDPOINT ON ACCOUNT TO ROLE DATA_API_ROLE;
210: 
211: CREATE SECURITY INTEGRATION IF NOT EXISTS SNOWSERVICES_INGRESS_OAUTH 
212: TYPE=oauth
213: OAUTH_CLIENT=snowservices_ingress
214: ENABLED=true;
215: 
216: USE ROLE DATA_API_ROLE;
217: CREATE SERVICE API.PUBLIC.API
218:  IN COMPUTE POOL API
219:  FROM SPECIFICATION  
220: $$
221: spec:
222:   container:
223:   - name: api
224:     image: /api/public/api/dataapi:latest
225:     resources:                          
226:       requests:
227:         cpu: 0.5
228:         memory: 128M
229:       limits:
230:         cpu: 1
231:         memory: 256M
232:   endpoint:
233:   - name: api
234:     port: 8001
235:     public: true
236: $$
237: QUERY_WAREHOUSE = DATA_API_WH;
238: 
239: ```
240: 
241: It will take a few minutes for your service to initialize, you can check status with these commands:
242: 
243: ```sql
244: CALL SYSTEM$GET_SERVICE_STATUS('api');
245: CALL SYSTEM$GET_SERVICE_LOGS('api.public.api', 0, 'api');
246: 
247: ```
248: 
249: After your service has started, you can get the endpoints with this command:
250: 
251: ```sql
252: SHOW ENDPOINTS IN SERVICE API;
253: ```
254: 
255: Make note of the ingress_url as that will be need to test the application. This service will start the API, running at https://<INGRESS_URL>.
256: 
257: 
258: <!-- ------------------------ -->
259: ## Testing the API
260: Duration: 1
261: 
262: To verify the API is online, go to the https://<INGRESS_URL> in your browser. You will be asked to authenticate to Snowflake and be given the root content: 
263: 
264: ```json
265: {"result":"Nothing to see here"}
266: ```
267: 
268: ### Testing using a webpage
269: This project comes with a simple webpage that allows you to test the API. To get to it, open https://<INGRESS_URL>/test in a web browser.
270: 
271: At the top you can choose if you want to exercise the Snowflake Connector for Python or the Snowflake Snowpark API endpoints.
272: 
273: There are 2 forms below that. The first one allows you to enter parameters to test the "Top 10 Customers" endpoint. The second one allows you to enter parameters to test the "Montly Clerk Sales" endpoint.
274: 
275: When you hit the `Submit` button, the API endpoint is called and the data is returned to the web page.
276: 
277: <!-- ------------------------ -->
278: ## Making the API Public
279: Duration: 3
280: 
281: For the next steps you will need a ngrok token. To get a token, go to [ngrok](https://ngrok.com) and Sign up for a free account. After registration you can get your authtoken in the UI under Getting Stared.
282: 
283: The service created will need network access to ngrok to create the tunnel. To do this, you'll need a new network rule, an external access integration and to use that integration in the service.
284: 
285: In order for the container to get your ngrok token, you'll also need to add it to the service environment. Make sure to replace <YOUR_NGROK_AUTHTOKEN> with your token.
286: 
287: Run the following commands in the Snowflake console or using SnowSQL.
288: 
289: ```sql
290: USE ROLE ACCOUNTADMIN;
291: CREATE OR REPLACE NETWORK RULE NGROK_OUT TYPE=HOST_PORT MODE = EGRESS VALUE_LIST=('connect.ngrok-agent.com:443');
292: 
293: CREATE OR REPLACE EXTERNAL ACCESS INTEGRATION NGROK
294: ALLOWED_NETWORK_RULES = (NGROK_OUT) ENABLED = TRUE;
295: 
296: GRANT USAGE ON INTEGRATION NGROK TO ROLE DATA_API_ROLE;
297: DROP SERVICE API.PUBLIC.API;
298: 
299: USE ROLE DATA_API_ROLE;
300: CREATE SERVICE API.PUBLIC.API
301: IN COMPUTE POOL API
302: FROM SPECIFICATION 
303: $$
304: spec:
305:   container:
306:   - name: api
307:     image: /api/public/api/dataapi:latest
308:     env:
309:       NGROK_AUTHTOKEN: <YOUR_NGROK_AUTHTOKEN>
310:     resources:                          
311:       requests:
312:         cpu: 0.5
313:         memory: 128M
314:       limits:
315:         cpu: 1
316:         memory: 256M
317:   endpoint:
318:   - name: api
319:     port: 8001
320:     public: true
321: $$
322: QUERY_WAREHOUSE = DATA_API_WH
323: EXTERNAL_ACCESS_INTEGRATIONS = (NGROK);
324: 
325: CALL SYSTEM$GET_SERVICE_STATUS('api');
326: ```
327: 
328: This will deploy a new service which will have public network access and your ngrok key. 
329: 
330: The url of the public service will be in logs after startup.
331: 
332: ```sql
333: CALL SYSTEM$GET_SERVICE_LOGS('api.public.api', 0, 'api');
334: ```
335: 
336: ### Testing using cURL
337: The API can be tested using the cURL command-line tool. Make sure to replace the <YOUR_NGROK_URL> in the commands with the url found in the previous step.
338: 
339: #### Top 10 Customers
340: To retrieve the top 10 customers in the date range of `1995-02-01` to `1995-02-14` using the Snowflake Connector for Python, run:
341: 
342: ```bash
343: curl -X GET "https://<YOUR_NGROK_URL>/connector/customers/top10?start_range=1995-02-01&end_range=1995-02-14"
344: ```
345: 
346: To retrieve the top 10 customers in the date range of `1995-02-01` to `1995-02-14` using the Snowflake Snowpark API, run:
347: ```bash
348: curl -X GET "https://<YOUR_NGROK_URL>/snowpark/customers/top10?start_range=1995-02-01&end_range=1995-02-14"
349: ```
350: 
351: If you call the endpoint without specifying the `start_range` then `1995-01-01` will be used. If you call the endpoint without specifying the `end_range` then `1995-03-31` will be used.
352: 
353: #### Monthly sales for a given year for a sales clerk
354: To retrieve the monthly sales for clerk `000000002` for the year `1995` using the Snowflake Connector for Python, run:
355: ```bash
356: curl -X GET "https://<YOUR_NGROK_URL>/connector/clerk/000000002/yearly_sales/1995"
357: ```
358: 
359: To retrieve the monthly sales for clerk `000000002` for the year `1995` using the Snowflake Snowpark API, run:
360: ```bash
361: curl -X GET "https://<YOUR_NGROK_URL>/snowpark/clerk/000000002/yearly_sales/1995"
362: ```
363: 
364: <!-- ------------------------ -->
365: ## Stopping the API
366: Duration: 1
367: 
368: To stop the API, you can suspend the service. From the Snowflake console or SnowSQL, run:
369: 
370: ```sql
371: USE ROLE DATA_API_ROLE;
372: ALTER SERVICE API.PUBLIC.API SUSPEND;
373: ```
374: 
375: <!-- ------------------------ -->
376: ## Cleanup
377: Duration: 2
378: 
379: To fully remove everything you did today you only need to drop some objects in your Snowflake account. From the Snowflake console or SnowSQL, as `ACCOUNTADMIN` run:
380: ```SQL
381: USE ROLE ACCOUNTADMIN;
382: 
383: DROP DATABASE IF EXISTS API;
384: DROP ROLE IF EXISTS DATA_API_ROLE;
385: DROP COMPUTE POOL IF EXISTS API;
386: DROP WAREHOUSE IF EXISTS DATA_API_WH;
387: DROP INTEGRATION IF EXISTS NGROK;
388: DROP NETWORK RULE IF EXISTS NGROK_OUT;
389: ```

391: <!-- ------------------------ -->
392: ## Conclusion
393: Duration: 1
394: 
395: You've successfully built a custom API in Python Powered by Snowflake. 
396: 
397: When you go to put a data API into production you should protect the API with some level of authentication and authorization. You can do this with ngrok, but you will need to change the configuration used as this example had it publicly accessible.

399: Another consideration is enabling a frontend website to access the endpoint, the test site worked in this example because it's hosted on the same domain as the api. If you need to access the api from another website, you will need to do additional configuration.

10: # Question Answering on Knowledge Graphs with RelationalAI and Snowflake Cortex AI
11: 
12: <!-- ------------------------ -->
13: ## Overview
14: Duration: 5
15: 
16: Knowledge graphs represent facts as entities (nodes) and the relationships between them (edges). A question-answering system over a knowledge graph lets users ask questions in natural language - for example, *"Who played Neo in The Matrix?"* - and receive exact answers computed from the graph, rather than from an unordered retrieval of documents. Because the answers are *computed* from the relations stored in the graph, they are grounded in data and can be traced back to a concrete query.
17: 
18: In this quickstart you will combine three pieces of technology to build exactly such a system:
19: 
20: - The **RelationalAI Native App** on Snowflake, which hosts a knowledge graph built from [Wikidata](https://www.wikidata.org/) relations and executes declarative graph queries against it.
21: - **Snowpark Container Services (SPCS)**, which hosts the chat application - a Streamlit UI together with a service that collects the knowledge graph schema, calls Snowflake Cortex for the semantic mapping, compiles the result into a RelationalAI query, and renders the answer.
22: - **Snowflake Cortex AI**, whose LLMs perform the semantic mapping: given the user's question and the knowledge-graph schema, a Cortex model produces an **intermediate representation (IR)** of the query. The service then compiles that IR into an executable RelationalAI query.
23: 
24: ### What is RelationalAI?
25: 
26: RelationalAI is a cloud-native platform that enables organizations to streamline and enhance decisions with intelligence. RelationalAI extends Snowflake with native support for an expanding set of AI workloads (e.g., graph analytics, rule-based reasoning, and optimization), all within your Snowflake account, offering the same ease of use, scalability, security, and governance.
27: 
28: Users can build a knowledge graph using Python and materialize it on top of their Snowflake data, which are shared with the RelationalAI app through Snowflake Data Streams. Insights can be written back to Snowflake tables and shared across the organization.
29: 
30: ### What you will learn
31: 
32: - How to install the RelationalAI Native App in your Snowflake account
33: - How to load a Wikidata-derived knowledge graph into RelationalAI using the RelationalAI CLI
34: - How to use Snowflake Cortex to map a natural-language question to an intermediate representation (IR) of a query
35: - How to compile the IR into a RelationalAI query and execute it over the knowledge graph
36: - How to expose the pipeline as a chat application deployed on Snowpark Container Services
37: 
38: ### What you will need
39: 
40: - A [Snowflake Account](https://signup.snowflake.com/?utm_cta=quickstarts_) on AWS in the US East (N. Virginia) region or the US West (Oregon) region
41: - Basic knowledge of using a [Snowflake SQL Worksheet](https://docs.snowflake.com/en/user-guide/ui-snowsight-worksheets)
42: - [Snowflake privileges](https://other-docs.snowflake.com/en/native-apps/consumer-installing#set-up-required-privileges) on your user to install a Native Application
43: - Snowflake account privileges to create databases and schemas in your Snowflake account
44: - [Docker](https://www.docker.com/products/docker-desktop/) to build the container image used on Snowpark Container Services
45: - The [RelationalAI CLI](https://relational.ai/docs/reference/cli/)
46: 
47: ### What you will build
48: 
49: - A knowledge graph of films, people and genres derived from Wikidata and hosted in the RelationalAI Native App
50: - A pipeline that turns a natural-language question into an intermediate representation with Snowflake Cortex, then into a RelationalAI query, and executes it over the knowledge graph
51: - A Streamlit chat application deployed on Snowpark Container Services that exposes the pipeline to end users
52: 
53: > aside positive
54: > NOTE: If you do not already have the RelationalAI Native App installed, please follow the instructions [here](https://relational.ai/docs/native_app/installation).
55: 
56: <!-- ------------------------ -->
57: ## Architecture Overview
58: Duration: 2
59: 
60: The diagram below shows the three components of the system and the flow of a single question:
61: 
62: ![Knowledge Graph Question-Answering architecture](./assets/kgqa_architecture.png)
63: 
64: - **User (web browser)**: opens the chat UI and types a natural-language question.
65: - **KG QA service (Snowpark Container Services)**: a Streamlit app plus a service that (1) loads the knowledge-graph schema from RelationalAI, (2) builds a prompt with the question and the schema, (3) sends the prompt to Snowflake Cortex, (4) compiles the returned IR into an executable RelationalAI (Rel) query, and (5) renders the answer. All of this uses the RelationalAI Python client.
66: - **Snowflake**: 
67:   - *Snowflake Cortex AI* runs the LLM call through `SNOWFLAKE.CORTEX.COMPLETE`, mapping the question plus schema to an intermediate representation (IR).
68:   - *The RelationalAI Native App* hosts the Wikidata-derived knowledge graph and executes the compiled Rel query, streaming the matching rows back to the service.
69: 
70: The following diagram summarizes the five phases of the pipeline:
71: 
72: ![KGQA pipeline from question to answer](./assets/kgqa_pipeline.png)
73:

11: # Getting Started with Traces
12: <!-- ------------------------ -->
13: ## Overview
14: Duration: 5
15: 
16: Observability is the ability to understand what is happening inside your data pipelines, why it is happening, and how long it takes. Snowflake provides first-class observability for the Python and SQL code you run with logging, **tracing**, and metrics support:
17: 
18: * **Logs** are timestamped, free-form messages emitted by your code, such as `logger.info("job started")`. They are great for triaging problems after the fact.
19: * **Traces** are structured records of a single execution. A trace is made up of **spans** (units of work with a duration) that carry **attributes** (key/value pairs) and **span events** (named, timestamped events with their own attributes). Because spans and events are structured, you can aggregate and analyze them with SQL.
20: * **Metrics** are aggregated measurements of a resource or behavior over time, for example memory or CPU consumption.
21: 
22: When you run a Python UDF, a stored procedure, or a Notebook, Snowflake's [logging and tracing](https://docs.snowflake.com/en/developer-guide/logging-tracing/logging-tracing-overview) automatically creates a trace for the execution, and additionally captures any log records, span attributes, and span events your code emits. All of this is written to an **event table**, which you can query like any other table, and the most recent executions are visualized in the **Trace** page of Snowsight.
23: 
24: In this quickstart you will build a Snowflake Notebook that pulls live weather data from the [OpenWeather](https://openweathermap.org/) REST API and stores it as the **bronze** layer of a [Medallion Architecture](https://www.snowflake.com/en/blog/medallion-architecture/) pipeline. Along the way you will:
25: 
26: * Create a **Python UDF** that calls an external REST API, with custom span attributes and span events that record the API call and the runtime memory/CPU used by the function.
27: * Create a **stored procedure** that ingests the API response into a bronze-level table, instrumented with its own span events.
28: * **Enable tracing** at the database and schema level, and **view the resulting traces** in Snowsight - filtering by query ID or executable name - and analyze them with SQL.
29: 
30: ### Prerequisites
31: 
32: - A [Snowflake](https://signup.snowflake.com/?utm_cta=quickstarts_) account. Sign up for a [30-day free trial](https://signup.snowflake.com/?utm_cta=quickstarts_) account, if required.
33: - Familiarity with [Snowflake](https://quickstarts.snowflake.com/guide/getting_started_with_snowflake/index.html#0) and the Python programming language.
34: - Some familiarity with [Snowflake Notebooks](https://docs.snowflake.com/en/user-guide/ui-snowsight/notebooks) and the [Snowpark Python API](https://docs.snowflake.com/en/developer-guide/snowpark/python/index).
35: 
36: ### What You'll Need
37: 
38: - A Snowflake account and a role with the privileges necessary to create a database, schema, warehouse, secret, network rule, and external access integration. For simplicity this quickstart uses the `ACCOUNTADMIN` role.
39: - An **OpenWeather API key**. Visit [OpenWeather's current weather data API](https://openweathermap.org/current) and click **Sign up** to create a free account, then copy the API key from the **API keys** tab of your dashboard. The free plan includes hundreds of requests per day, which is more than enough for this quickstart.
40: 
41: > aside positive
42: >  **What is a Medallion Architecture?** The medallion architecture organizes data into progressively more refined layers: **bronze** (raw, uncurated data as it arrives), **silver** (cleaned, conformed, deduplicated data), and **gold** (rich, business-ready analytics models and aggregates). In this quickstart we focus on the bronze layer: raw payloads from the OpenWeather API stored verbatim, ready for later cleaning into silver and gold layers.
43: 
44: ### What You'll Build
45: 
46: - A Snowflake **Notebook** (`WEATHER_TRACES_NOTEBOOK`) with a mix of **Python** and **SQL** cells.
47: - A **Python UDF** (`GET_WEATHER_DATA`) that calls the OpenWeather REST API, using Snowflake's **external network access** and a **secret** to store the API key, and that emits custom span events capturing runtime **memory/CPU** information.
48: - A **stored procedure** (`POPULATE_BRONZE_WEATHER`) that calls the UDF and inserts raw payloads into the bronze table `BRONZE_WEATHER_RAW`.
49: - **Traces** of those executions to view in Snowsight and to analyze with SQL.
50:

# Codelabs command line tool

The program takes an input in form of a resource location,
which can either be a Google Doc ID, local file path or an arbitrary URL.
It then converts the input into a codelab format, HTML by default.

For more info run `claat help`.

## Install

The easiest way is to download pre-compiled binary.
The binaries, as well as their checksums are available at the
[Releases page](https://github.com/googlecodelabs/tools/releases/latest).

Alternatively, if you have [Go installed](https://golang.org/doc/install):

    go get github.com/googlecodelabs/tools/claat

If none of the above works, compile the tool from source following Dev workflow
instructions below.

## Dev workflow

**Prerequisites**

1. Install [Go](https://golang.org/dl/) if you don't have it.
2. Make sure this directory is placed under
   `$GOPATH/src/github.com/googlecodelabs/tools`.
3. Install package dependencies with `go get ./...` from this directory.

To build the binary, run `make`.

Testing is done with `make test` or `go test ./...` if preferred.

Don't forget to run `make lint` or `golint ./...` before creating a new CL.

To create cross-compiled versions for all supported OS/Arch, run `make release`.
It will place the output in `bin/claat-<os>-<arch>`.

arguments.content:
author: Ockam
id: build_a_private_custom_api_in_python
summary: Build, deploy, and host a private custom API powered by Snowflake, Python/Flask, and Ockam. Keep the API endpoint completely private inside Snowflake and reach it securely from your enterprise VPC through encrypted Ockam Portals.
categories: getting-started,app-development,architecture-patterns,solution-examples
environments: web
status: Published
feedback link: https://github.com/Snowflake-Labs/sfguides/issues
tags: Getting Started, Data Applications, API, Snowpark Container Services, Ockam, Private Connectivity, Python, Flask

# Build a Private Custom API in Python

<!-- ------------------------ -->
## Overview
Duration: 5

Many builders want to share the data stored in Snowflake with other applications through an http API. The [Build a Custom API in Python and Flask](https://quickstarts.snowflake.com/guide/build_a_custom_api_in_python/index.html#0) quickstart shows how to build, deploy, and host such an API with a **public** endpoint. In production, however, you often do not want your data API to be reachable from the Internet at all. Instead you want it to be reachable only from systems inside your own enterprise private environment, such as applications running in your company VPC.

This quickstart builds the same custom API Powered by Snowflake, but keeps it **private**. Instead of creating a public endpoint, you will use [Ockam](https://ockam.io) [Portals](https://docs.ockam.io) to create an encrypted tunnel between your enterprise private environment and the private API service running inside Snowflake. Traffic flowing through the tunnel is authenticated, authorized, and end-to-end encrypted. Your private API never gets a public address, and is not exposed to the Internet.

The API consists of reporting endpoints over the [TPC-H](https://docs.snowflake.com/en/user-guide/sample-data-tpch) sample dataset included in your Snowflake account, built with [Python Flask](https://flask.palletsprojects.com/).

The diagram below shows the architecture you will build:

![Private custom API architecture](./assets/private_custom_api_architecture.png)

- Your **enterprise application** (or developer laptop) connects to a local port exposed by the **Ockam TCP Inlet** running in your VPC.
- The **Ockam Orchestrator** authenticates both sides and relays encrypted data along an end-to-end encrypted Ockam channel.
- Inside your **Snowflake Account**, an **Ockam TCP Outlet** service connects to the **Private API service** and forwards requests to it over Snowflake's internal network.
- The **Private API service** queries the TPC-H sample data using the Snowpark Container Services and Snowflake's Python connector.

No `public: true` endpoint is ever created for the API, so it cannot be reached from the Internet. Only systems that are granted access via Ockam can use the API.

### Prerequisites
- Privileges necessary to create a user, database, warehouse, compute pool, repository, network rule, external access integration, and service in Snowflake (this quickstart uses `ACCOUNTADMIN`)
- Privileges necessary to access the tables in the `SNOWFLAKE_SAMPLE_DATA.TPCH_SF10` database and schema
- Access to run SQL in the Snowflake console or SnowSQL
- Basic experience using git, GitHub, and Codespaces
- Intermediate knowledge of Python

### What You’ll Learn
- How to configure and build a private custom API Powered by Snowflake
- How to build, publish, and deploy a container with the API in Snowflake without exposing a public endpoint
- How to securely connect your enterprise private environment to the private API with Ockam Portals

### What You’ll Need
- A [Snowflake](https://snowflake.com) account on an AWS commercial region
- A [GitHub](https://github.com/) account with credits for Codespaces
- An [Ockam](https://ockam.io) Orchestrator account (free tier is enough; you will create one in this guide)
- Basic familiarity with the [Snowpark Container Services](https://docs.snowflake.com/en/developer-guide/snowpark-container-services/overview)

### What You’ll Build
- A private API Powered by Snowflake, deployed with Snowpark Container Services and reachable only through an encrypted Ockam tunnel from your enterprise private environment

<!-- ------------------------ -->
## Setting up a Warehouse
Duration: 1

The API needs a warehouse to query the data to return to the caller. To create the database and warehouse, connect to Snowflake and run the following commands in the Snowflake console or using SnowSQL:

```sql
USE ROLE ACCOUNTADMIN;
CREATE WAREHOUSE DATA_API_WH WITH WAREHOUSE_SIZE='xsmall';
```

### Create the Application Role in Snowflake
Duration: 1

The application will run as a new role with minimal privileges. To create the role, connect to Snowflake and run the following SQL statements to create the role and grant it access to the data needed for the application:

```SQL
USE ROLE ACCOUNTADMIN;
CREATE ROLE DATA_API_ROLE;

GRANT USAGE ON WAREHOUSE DATA_API_WH TO ROLE DATA_API_ROLE;
GRANT IMPORTED PRIVILEGES ON DATABASE SNOWFLAKE_SAMPLE_DATA TO ROLE DATA_API_ROLE;

GRANT ROLE DATA_API_ROLE TO ROLE ACCOUNTADMIN;
```

<!-- ------------------------ -->
## Setting up your Development Environment
Duration: 3

The code used in this guide is hosted in GitHub. You will need a new Codespace from the GitHub [repository](https://github.com/sfc-gh-bculberson/lab_data_api_python).

To create a new Codespace, browse to the GitHub [repository](https://github.com/sfc-gh-bculberson/lab_data_api_python) in a browser. You will need to log in to GitHub if you are not already logged in to access Codespaces. After logging in, click on the green "<> Code" button and "create codespace on main" button.

You will then be redirected into Codespaces where your development environment will load and all code from GitHub will be loaded in the project.

> aside positive
> The Ockam TCP Inlet in this quickstart runs on this Codespace, which plays the role of a system inside your enterprise private environment. A Codespace is used for convenience - in production you would run the same commands on a machine inside your company VPC.

<!-- ------------------------ -->
## Reviewing the API Endpoints
Duration: 3

The API creates two sets of endpoints, one for using the Snowflake connector:
1. `https://host/connector/customers/top10`
  * Which takes the following optional query parameters:
    1. `start_range` - the start date of the range in `YYYY-MM-DD` format. Defaults to `1995-01-01`.
    1. `end_range` - the end date of the range in `YYYY-MM-DD` format. Defaults to `1995-03-31`.
2. `https://host/connector/clerk/<CLERKID>/yearly_sales/<YEAR>`
  * Which takes 2 required path parameters:
    1. `CLERKID` - the clerk ID. Use just the numbers, such as `000000001`.
    2. `YEAR` - the year to use, such as `1995`.

And the same ones using Snowpark:
1. `https://host/snowpark/customers/top10`
  * Which takes the following optional query parameters:
    1. `start_range` - the start date of the range in `YYYY-MM-DD` format. Defaults to `1995-01-01`.
    1. `end_range` - the end date of the range in `YYYY-MM-DD` format. Defaults to `1995-03-31`.
2. `https://host/snowpark/clerk/<CLERKID>/yearly_sales/<YEAR>`
  * Which takes 2 required path parameters:
    1. `CLERKID` - the clerk ID. Use just the numbers, such as `000000001`.
    2. `YEAR` - the year to use, such as `1995`.

The `src/` directory has all the source code for the API. The `connector.py` file contains all the entrypoints for the API endpoints using the Snowflake Connector for Python. The `customers_top10()` function is one of the API endpoints we need for this API, which finds the top 10 customers by sales in a date range. Review the code and the SQL needed to retrieve the data from Snowflake and serialize it to JSON for the response. This endpoint also takes 2 optional query string parameters `start_range` and `end_range`.

```python
@connector.route('/customers/top10')
def customers_top10():
    # Validate arguments
    sdt_str = request.args.get('start_range') or '1995-01-01'
    edt_str = request.args.get('end_range') or '1995-03-31'
    try:
        sdt = datetime.datetime.strptime(sdt_str, dateformat)
        edt = datetime.datetime.strptime(edt_str, dateformat)
    except:
        abort(400, "Invalid start and/or end dates.")
    sql_string = '''
        SELECT
            o_custkey
          , SUM(o_totalprice) AS sum_totalprice
        FROM snowflake_sample_data.tpch_sf10.orders
        WHERE o_orderdate >= '{sdt}'
          AND o_orderdate <= '{edt}'
        GROUP BY o_custkey
        ORDER BY sum_totalprice DESC
        LIMIT 10
    '''
    sql = sql_string.format(sdt=sdt, edt=edt)
    try:
        res = conn.cursor(DictCursor).execute(sql)
        return make_response(jsonify(res.fetchall()))
    except:
        abort(500, "Error reading from Snowflake. Check the logs for details.")
```

You can also review the other endpoints in [connector.py](https://github.com/sfc-gh-bculberson/lab_data_api_python/blob/main/src/connector.py) to see how simple it is to host multiple endpoints.

If you would also like to see how to build endpoints using the Snowflake Snowpark API, review [snowpark.py](https://github.com/sfc-gh-bculberson/lab_data_api_python/blob/main/src/snowpark.py).

GRANT ALL ON DATABASE API TO ROLE DATA_API_ROLE;
GRANT ALL ON SCHEMA API.PUBLIC TO ROLE DATA_API_ROLE;

USE DATABASE API;
CREATE OR REPLACE IMAGE REPOSITORY API;

GRANT READ ON IMAGE REPOSITORY API TO ROLE DATA_API_ROLE;

SHOW IMAGE REPOSITORIES;
```

Note the `repository_url` in the response as that will be needed in the next step.

Duration: 1

docker push <repository_url>/dataapi
```

Duration: 1

USE ROLE ACCOUNTADMIN;

  MIN_NODES = 1
  MAX_NODES = 5
  INSTANCE_FAMILY = CPU_X64_XS;

GRANT USAGE ON COMPUTE POOL API TO ROLE DATA_API_ROLE;

## Deploying the Private API Service
Duration: 3

To create a service to host the application **without exposing a public endpoint**, connect to Snowflake and run the following commands in the Snowflake console or using SnowSQL. Note that, unlike the public API quickstart, the endpoint in the specification below has **no `public: true` property**. The service will still be reachable from inside your Snowflake account, but Snowflake will not assign it a public address.

```sql

USE ROLE ACCOUNTADMIN;
GRANT BIND SERVICE ENDPOINT ON ACCOUNT TO ROLE DATA_API_ROLE;

CREATE SECURITY INTEGRATION IF NOT EXISTS SNOWSERVICES_INGRESS_OAUTH
TYPE=oauth
OAUTH_CLIENT=snowservices_ingress
ENABLED=true;

USE ROLE DATA_API_ROLE;
CREATE SERVICE API.PUBLIC.API
 IN COMPUTE POOL API
 FROM SPECIFICATION
$$
spec:
  container:
  - name: api
    image: /api/public/api/dataapi:latest
    resources:
      requests:
        cpu: 0.5
        memory: 128M
      limits:
        cpu: 1
        memory: 256M
  endpoint:
  - name: api
    port: 8001
$$
QUERY_WAREHOUSE = DATA_API_WH;

```

It will take a few minutes for your service to initialize. You can check its status with these commands:

```sql
CALL SYSTEM$GET_SERVICE_STATUS('api');
CALL SYSTEM$GET_SERVICE_LOGS('api.public.api', 0, 'api');
```

Once the service is ready, retrieve its private connectivity details:

```sql
SHOW ENDPOINTS IN SERVICE API;
```

Because the endpoint is private, the `ingress_url` column is empty and the `host` column shows the private (internal) DNS name that resolves only inside Snowflake, for example `...snowflakecomputing.internal`. Make note of that hostname, combined with port `8001`, as `<PRIVATE_API_URL>` - the Ockam outlet service will use it to reach the API over Snowflake's internal network. See the Snowflake documentation on [private connectivity](https://docs.snowflake.com/en/user-guide/admin-security-privatelink) for more details.

> aside positive
> Because no public endpoint exists, you cannot open this API in a browser. That is the point - the API is only reachable from inside Snowflake, and we will now securely bridge your enterprise private environment to it with Ockam.

<!-- ------------------------ -->
## Exposing the API with Ockam Portals
Duration: 15

Now we will make the private API reachable from your enterprise private environment, without ever exposing a public endpoint. [Ockam](https://ockam.io) creates authenticated, end-to-end encrypted tunnels - called **Portals** - between two private environments.

In our architecture:

- The **Ockam TCP Outlet** runs inside Snowflake as a Snowpark Container Services workload next to the private API service. It forwards traffic destined for the API into the service over Snowflake's internal network.
- The **Ockam Orchestrator** (the Ockam cloud) verifies the identity of both sides and relays the encrypted traffic between them.
- The **Ockam TCP Inlet** runs in your enterprise private environment (here, your Codespace) and exposes the API on a local port, for example `localhost:9000`.
- Your existing application just connects to `localhost:9000` - it does not need to know anything about Ockam.

### Download the Ockam CLI

Open a terminal in your Codespace and install the Ockam CLI. The exact install command is always published in the [Ockam docs](https://docs.ockam.io/install/):

```bash
curl --proto '=https' --tlsv1.2 -sSfL https://install.command.ockam.io | sh
export PATH="$HOME/.ockam/bin:$PATH"
ockam --version
```

### Create an Ockam project and login

If this is your first time using Ockam, enroll a new Ockam Orchestrator account. This creates a space and a default project and connects your local machine to it:

```bash
ockam enroll
```

To enroll a machine into an **existing** project - for example when the Codespace is recreated - use the project's enrollment token instead:

```bash
ockam project enroll <YOUR_PROJECT_ENROLLMENT_TOKEN>
```

Your Ockam project is used by both the inlet (in your VPC) and the outlet (in Snowflake) so that they can authenticate each other and negotiate an encrypted channel. Make a note of your project name (shown when you run `ockam enroll` or visit the Ockam console).

Create a dedicated node on this machine and use it for all the inlet commands below:

```bash
ockam node create enterprise_app
```

### Create the forwarder on the Ockam Orchestrator

A **forwarder** publishes the address of the outlet (in Snowflake) on the Ockam Orchestrator so that the inlet (in your VPC) can discover it, even though the snowflake outlet is not directly reachable from your VPC:

```bash
ockam forwarder create --at private_api_relay
```

### Give Snowflake permission to reach the Ockam Orchestrator

The Ockam outlet service running in Snowflake needs outbound (egress) network access to the Ockam Orchestrator. In Snowflake, create a network rule and an external access integration. The value list below allows egress to Ockam's relay endpoints; if your project uses a specific relay host, use that host instead:

```sql
USE ROLE ACCOUNTADMIN;
CREATE OR REPLACE NETWORK RULE OCKAM_EGRESS_NETWORK_RULE
  TYPE = HOST_PORT
  MODE = EGRESS
  VALUE_LIST = ('relay.ockam.network:443');

CREATE OR REPLACE EXTERNAL ACCESS INTEGRATION OCKAM_EGRESS
  ALLOWED_NETWORK_RULES = (OCKAM_EGRESS_NETWORK_RULE)
  ENABLED = TRUE;

GRANT USAGE ON INTEGRATION OCKAM_EGRESS TO ROLE DATA_API_ROLE;
```

### Build the Ockam outlet container

In your Codespace, create a small container image that runs the Ockam CLI and creates the TCP outlet pointing at the private API service. First add the two files below to the project.

### Dockerfile.ockam

```dockerfile
FROM python:3.11-slim

RUN apt-get update \
    && apt-get install -y --no-install-recommends ca-certificates curl \
    && rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/*

RUN curl --proto '=https' --tlsv1.2 -sSfL https://install.command.ockam.io | sh

COPY entrypoint.sh /entrypoint.sh
RUN chmod +x /entrypoint.sh

ENTRYPOINT ["/entrypoint.sh"]
```

### entrypoint.sh

```bash
#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail

IDENTITY_NAME="${OCKAM_IDENTITY_NAME:-snowflake_outlet}"

# Create an identity and enroll this node into your Ockam project.
ockam identity create "$IDENTITY_NAME" 2>/dev/null || true
ockam project enroll "$OCKAM_ENROLLMENT_TOKEN" --identity "$IDENTITY_NAME"

# Create the outlet node and open a TCP outlet at the private API service.
// This forwards any requests it receives through the Ockam channel
// to the private API endpoint inside Snowflake.
ockam node create "$IDENTITY_NAME" 2>/dev/null || true
ockam tcp-outlet create --from /service/outlet --to "$PRIVATE_API_URL" --node "$IDENTITY_NAME"

# Keep the container alive so the Ockam node and outlet keep running.
sleep infinity
```

### Push the Ockam outlet container to Snowflake

```bash
docker build -f Dockerfile.ockam -t <repository_url>/ockam_box .
docker push <repository_url>/ockam_box
```

### Deploy the Ockam outlet service in Snowflake

Connect to Snowflake and create a service that runs the Ockam outlet. It connects to `PRIVATE_API_URL` (the private DNS name from the [Deploying the Private API Service](#) step, including the `http://` scheme and port `8001`), and reaches the Ockam Orchestrator through the `OCKAM_EGRESS` integration:

```sql
USE ROLE ACCOUNTADMIN;
GRANT USAGE ON COMPUTE POOL API TO ROLE DATA_API_ROLE;

CREATE OR REPLACE NETWORK RULE OCKAM_EGRESS_NETWORK_RULE
  TYPE = HOST_PORT
  MODE = EGRESS
  VALUE_LIST = ('relay.ockam.network:443');

CREATE OR REPLACE EXTERNAL ACCESS INTEGRATION OCKAM_EGRESS
  ALLOWED_NETWORK_RULES = (OCKAM_EGRESS_NETWORK_RULE)
  ENABLED = TRUE;

GRANT USAGE ON INTEGRATION OCKAM_EGRESS TO ROLE DATA_API_ROLE;

USE ROLE DATA_API_ROLE;
CREATE SERVICE API.PUBLIC.OCKAM_OUTLET
 IN COMPUTE POOL API
 FROM SPECIFICATION
$$
spec:
  container:
  - name: ockam
    image: /api/public/api/ockam_box:latest
    env:
      OCKAM_ENROLLMENT_TOKEN: <YOUR_PROJECT_ENROLLMENT_TOKEN>
      OCKAM_IDENTITY_NAME: snowflake_outlet
      PRIVATE_API_URL: http://<PRIVATE_INGRESS_DNS>:8001
    resources:
      requests:
        cpu: 0.5
        memory: 128M
      limits:
        cpu: 1
        memory: 500M
$$
QUERY_WAREHOUSE = DATA_API_WH
EXTERNAL_ACCESS_INTEGRATIONS = (OCKAM_EGRESS);

```

Check that the outlet service starts successfully:

```sql
CALL SYSTEM$GET_SERVICE_STATUS('api.public.ockam_outlet');
CALL SYSTEM$GET_SERVICE_LOGS('api.public.ockam_outlet', 0, 'ockam');
```

The logs should show the outlet node enrolling into your Ockam project and creating the TCP outlet to the private API service.

### Create the TCP inlet in your enterprise environment

Back in the Codespace terminal, open the TCP inlet that exposes the private API on `localhost:9000`. The address routes through your Ockam project, the forwarder, and an encrypted channel to the `/service/outlet` endpoint inside Snowflake:

```bash
ockam tcp-inlet create --from 9000 \
  --to /project/<YOUR_PROJECT>/forward/private_api_relay/secure_channel/service/outlet \
  --node enterprise_app
```

> aside negative
> Ockam's CLI is updated frequently. If any command above has changed in your installed version, follow the exact current syntax in the [Ockam Portals guide](https://docs.ockam.io) - the concepts and the architecture are the same, and every command is documented with copy-paste examples.

<!-- ------------------------ -->
## Testing the Private API
Duration: 3

With the inlet running on `localhost:9000`, your enterprise application (and curl) can use the API as if it were running locally - even though the API service itself has no public endpoint and is sitting inside Snowflake.

To verify the tunnel works, call the root endpoint:

```bash
curl http://localhost:9000/
```

You should get the JSON response:

```json
{"result":"Nothing to see here"}
```

### Top 10 Customers

To retrieve the top 10 customers in the date range of `1995-02-01` to `1995-02-14` using the Snowflake Connector for Python, run:

```bash
curl -X GET "http://localhost:9000/connector/customers/top10?start_range=1995-02-01&end_range=1995-02-14"
```

To retrieve the top 10 customers in the date range of `1995-02-01` to `1995-02-14` using the Snowflake Snowpark API, run:

```bash
curl -X GET "http://localhost:9000/snowpark/customers/top10?start_range=1995-02-01&end_range=1995-02-14"
```

If you call the endpoint without specifying the `start_range` then `1995-01-01` will be used. If you call the endpoint without specifying the `end_range` then `1995-03-31` will be used.

### Monthly sales for a given year for a sales clerk

To retrieve the monthly sales for clerk `000000002` for the year `1995` using the Snowflake Connector for Python, run:

```bash
curl -X GET "http://localhost:9000/connector/clerk/000000002/yearly_sales/1995"
```

To retrieve the monthly sales for clerk `000000002` for the year `1995` using the Snowflake Snowpark API, run:

```bash
curl -X GET "http://localhost:9000/snowpark/clerk/000000002/yearly_sales/1995"
```

Every request is authenticated by the Ockam Orchestrator and travels end-to-end encrypted from the inlet in your VPC to the outlet service inside Snowflake, and from there over Snowflake's internal network to the private API service.

> aside positive
> If a request fails, check the status of both services with `CALL SYSTEM$GET_SERVICE_STATUS('api.public.api');` and `CALL SYSTEM$GET_SERVICE_STATUS('api.public.ockam_outlet');`. The Ockam [troubleshooting guide](https://docs.ockam.io) is also a good resource when the tunnel itself is the problem.

<!-- ------------------------ -->
## Cleanup
Duration: 2

To fully remove everything you did today, stop the portal and drop the Snowflake objects you created. From the Snowflake console or SnowSQL, as `ACCOUNTADMIN` run:

```SQL
USE ROLE ACCOUNTADMIN;

DROP SERVICE IF EXISTS API.PUBLIC.API;
DROP SERVICE IF EXISTS API.PUBLIC.OCKAM_OUTLET;
DROP COMPUTE POOL IF EXISTS API;
DROP DATABASE IF EXISTS API;
DROP ROLE IF EXISTS DATA_API_ROLE;
DROP WAREHOUSE IF EXISTS DATA_API_WH;
DROP INTEGRATION IF EXISTS OCKAM_EGRESS;
DROP NETWORK RULE IF EXISTS OCKAM_EGRESS_NETWORK_RULE;
```

To delete the Ockam forwarder and the local inlet node from the Codespace terminal, run:

```bash
ockam tcp-inlet delete --from 9000 --node enterprise_app
ockam forwarder delete --at private_api_relay
ockam node delete enterprise_app
```

<!-- ------------------------ -->
## Conclusion and Resources
Duration: 2

You've successfully built a **private** custom API in Python Powered by Snowflake and made it securely reachable from your enterprise private environment with Ockam Portals. Because the API service never had a `public: true` endpoint, it is not reachable from the Internet. Only the Ockam TCP Inlet you created - running in your VPC - can reach it, and every request travels through an authenticated, end-to-end encrypted Ockam channel.

The same pattern works for any service: run an Ockam **outlet** next to any private workload (a database, an API, a message broker), publish a forwarder on the Ockam Orchestrator, and let applications in your private environment reach it through an Ockam **inlet** on a local port. Ockam handles authentication, authorization, and encryption for you.

### What we've covered
- How to configure and build a private custom API Powered by Snowflake
- How to publish and deploy a container with the API in Snowflake without a public endpoint
- How to securely connect an application in your enterprise private environment to the private API with Ockam Portals

### Related Resources
- [Build a Custom API in Python and Flask](https://quickstarts.snowflake.com/guide/build_a_custom_api_in_python/index.html#0) - the companion quickstart that exposes the same API publicly

- [Snowpark Container Services: working with image registries](https://docs.snowflake.com/en/developer-guide/snowpark-container-services/working-with-container-registries-and-repositories)
- [Snowpark Container Services: working with compute pools](https://docs.snowflake.com/en/developer-guide/snowpark-container-services/working-with-compute-pool)
- [External network access in Snowflake](https://docs.snowflake.com/en/developer-guide/external-network-access/external-network-access-overview)

10: # Build a Private Custom API in Python
11: 
12: <!-- ------------------------ -->
13: ## Overview
14: Duration: 5
15: 
16: Many builders want to share the data stored in Snowflake with other applications through an http API. The [Build a Custom API in Python and Flask](https://quickstarts.snowflake.com/guide/build_a_custom_api_in_python/index.html#0) quickstart shows how to build, deploy, and host such an API with a **public** endpoint. In production, however, you often do not want your data API to be reachable from the Internet at all. Instead you want it to be reachable only from systems inside your own enterprise private environment, such as applications running in your company VPC.
17: 
18: This quickstart builds the same custom API Powered by Snowflake, but keeps it **private**. Instead of creating a public endpoint, you will use [Ockam](https://ockam.io) [Portals](https://docs.ockam.io) to create an encrypted tunnel between your enterprise private environment and the private API service running inside Snowflake. Traffic flowing through the tunnel is authenticated, authorized, and end-to-end encrypted. Your private API never gets a public address, and is not exposed to the Internet.
19: 
20: The API consists of reporting endpoints over the [TPC-H](https://docs.snowflake.com/en/user-guide/sample-data-tpch) sample dataset included in your Snowflake account, built with [Python Flask](https://flask.palletsprojects.com/).
21: 
22: The diagram below shows the architecture you will build:
23: 
24: ![Private custom API architecture](./assets/private_custom_api_architecture.png)
25: 
26: - Your **enterprise application** (or developer laptop) connects to a local port exposed by the **Ockam TCP Inlet** running in your VPC.
27: - The **Ockam Orchestrator** authenticates both sides and relays encrypted data along an end-to-end encrypted Ockam channel.
28: - Inside your **Snowflake Account**, an **Ockam TCP Outlet** service connects to the **Private API service** and forwards requests to it over Snowflake's internal network.
29: - The **Private API service** queries the TPC-H sample data using the Snowpark Container Services and Snowflake's Python connector.
30: 
31: No `public: true` endpoint is ever created for the API, so it cannot be reached from the Internet. Only systems that are granted access via Ockam can use the API.
32: 
33: ### Prerequisites
34: - Privileges necessary to create a user, database, warehouse, compute pool, repository, network rule, external access integration, and service in Snowflake (this quickstart uses `ACCOUNTADMIN`)
35: - Privileges necessary to access the tables in the `SNOWFLAKE_SAMPLE_DATA.TPCH_SF10` database and schema
36: - Access to run SQL in the Snowflake console or SnowSQL
37: - Basic experience using git, GitHub, and Codespaces
38: - Intermediate knowledge of Python
39: 
40: ### What You’ll Learn
41: - How to configure and build a private custom API Powered by Snowflake
42: - How to build, publish, and deploy a container with the API in Snowflake without exposing a public endpoint
43: - How to securely connect your enterprise private environment to the private API with Ockam Portals
44: 
45: ### What You’ll Need
46: - A [Snowflake](https://snowflake.com) account on an AWS commercial region
47: - A [GitHub](https://github.com/) account with credits for Codespaces
48: - An [Ockam](https://ockam.io) Orchestrator account (free tier is enough; you will create one in this guide)
49: - Basic familiarity with the [Snowpark Container Services](https://docs.snowflake.com/en/developer-guide/snowpark-container-services/overview)
50: 
51: ### What You’ll Build
52: - A private API Powered by Snowflake, deployed with Snowpark Container Services and reachable only through an encrypted Ockam tunnel from your enterprise private environment
53:

55: ## Setting up a Warehouse
56: Duration: 1
57: 
58: The API needs a warehouse to query the data to return to the caller. To create the database and warehouse, connect to Snowflake and run the following commands in the Snowflake console or using SnowSQL:
59: 
60: ```sql
61: USE ROLE ACCOUNTADMIN;
62: CREATE WAREHOUSE DATA_API_WH WITH WAREHOUSE_SIZE='xsmall';
63: ```
64: 
65: ### Create the Application Role in Snowflake
66: Duration: 1
67: 
68: The application will run as a new role with minimal privileges. To create the role, connect to Snowflake and run the following SQL statements to create the role and grant it access to the data needed for the application:
69: 
70: ```SQL
71: USE ROLE ACCOUNTADMIN;
72: CREATE ROLE DATA_API_ROLE;
73: 
74: GRANT USAGE ON WAREHOUSE DATA_API_WH TO ROLE DATA_API_ROLE;
75: GRANT IMPORTED PRIVILEGES ON DATABASE SNOWFLAKE_SAMPLE_DATA TO ROLE DATA_API_ROLE;
76: 
77: GRANT ROLE DATA_API_ROLE TO ROLE ACCOUNTADMIN;
78: ```
79: 
80: <!-- ------------------------ -->
81: ## Setting up your Development Environment
82: Duration: 3
83: 
84: The code used in this guide is hosted in GitHub. You will need a new Codespace from the GitHub [repository](https://github.com/sfc-gh-bculberson/lab_data_api_python).
85: 
86: To create a new Codespace, browse to the GitHub [repository](https://github.com/sfc-gh-bculberson/lab_data_api_python) in a browser. You will need to log in to GitHub if you are not already logged in to access Codespaces. After logging in, click on the green "<> Code" button and "create codespace on main" button.
87: 
88: You will then be redirected into Codespaces where your development environment will load and all code from GitHub will be loaded in the project.

91: > The Ockam TCP Inlet in this quickstart runs on this Codespace, which plays the role of a system inside your enterprise private environment. A Codespace is used for convenience - in production you would run the same commands on a machine inside your company VPC.
92:

94: ## Reviewing the API Endpoints
95: Duration: 3
96: 
97: The API creates two sets of endpoints, one for using the Snowflake connector:
98: 1. `https://host/connector/customers/top10`
99:   * Which takes the following optional query parameters:
100:     1. `start_range` - the start date of the range in `YYYY-MM-DD` format. Defaults to `1995-01-01`.
101:     1. `end_range` - the end date of the range in `YYYY-MM-DD` format. Defaults to `1995-03-31`.
102: 2. `https://host/connector/clerk/<CLERKID>/yearly_sales/<YEAR>`
103:   * Which takes 2 required path parameters:
104:     1. `CLERKID` - the clerk ID. Use just the numbers, such as `000000001`.
105:     2. `YEAR` - the year to use, such as `1995`.
106: 
107: And the same ones using Snowpark:
108: 1. `https://host/snowpark/customers/top10`
109:   * Which takes the following optional query parameters:
110:     1. `start_range` - the start date of the range in `YYYY-MM-DD` format. Defaults to `1995-01-01`.
111:     1. `end_range` - the end date of the range in `YYYY-MM-DD` format. Defaults to `1995-03-31`.
112: 2. `https://host/snowpark/clerk/<CLERKID>/yearly_sales/<YEAR>`
113:   * Which takes 2 required path parameters:
114:     1. `CLERKID` - the clerk ID. Use just the numbers, such as `000000001`.
115:     2. `YEAR` - the year to use, such as `1995`.
116: 
117: The `src/` directory has all the source code for the API. The `connector.py` file contains all the entrypoints for the API endpoints using the Snowflake Connector for Python. The `customers_top10()` function is one of the API endpoints we need for this API, which finds the top 10 customers by sales in a date range. Review the code and the SQL needed to retrieve the data from Snowflake and serialize it to JSON for the response. This endpoint also takes 2 optional query string parameters `start_range` and `end_range`.
118: 
119: ```python
120: @connector.route('/customers/top10')
121: def customers_top10():
122:     # Validate arguments
123:     sdt_str = request.args.get('start_range') or '1995-01-01'
124:     edt_str = request.args.get('end_range') or '1995-03-31'
125:     try:
126:         sdt = datetime.datetime.strptime(sdt_str, dateformat)
127:         edt = datetime.datetime.strptime(edt_str, dateformat)
128:     except:
129:         abort(400, "Invalid start and/or end dates.")
130:     sql_string = '''
131:         SELECT
132:             o_custkey
133:           , SUM(o_totalprice) AS sum_totalprice
134:         FROM snowflake_sample_data.tpch_sf10.orders
135:         WHERE o_orderdate >= '{sdt}'
136:           AND o_orderdate <= '{edt}'
137:         GROUP BY o_custkey
138:         ORDER BY sum_totalprice DESC
139:         LIMIT 10
140:     '''
141:     sql = sql_string.format(sdt=sdt, edt=edt)
142:     try:
143:         res = conn.cursor(DictCursor).execute(sql)
144:         return make_response(jsonify(res.fetchall()))
145:     except:
146:         abort(500, "Error reading from Snowflake. Check the logs for details.")
147: ```
148: 
149: You can also review the other endpoints in [connector.py](https://github.com/sfc-gh-bculberson/lab_data_api_python/blob/main/src/connector.py) to see how simple it is to host multiple endpoints.
150: 
151: If you would also like to see how to build endpoints using the Snowflake Snowpark API, review [snowpark.py](https://github.com/sfc-gh-bculberson/lab_data_api_python/blob/main/src/snowpark.py).
152:

154: ## Building the Application Container
155: Duration: 1
156: 
157: To create the application container, we will leverage Docker. The Dockerfile is based on Python 3.8 and installs the required libraries needed for the application as well as the code. To create the Docker container, run this command in the terminal provided by Codespaces:

160: docker build -t dataapi .
161: ```
