164: ## Creating the Image Registry
165: Duration: 1
166: 
167: To create the image registry and the database which contains it, connect to Snowflake and run the following commands in the Snowflake console or using SnowSQL:
168: 
169: ```sql
170: 
171: USE ROLE ACCOUNTADMIN;
172: CREATE DATABASE API;
173: 
174: GRANT ALL ON DATABASE API TO ROLE DATA_API_ROLE;
175: GRANT ALL ON SCHEMA API.PUBLIC TO ROLE DATA_API_ROLE;
176: 
177: USE DATABASE API;
178: CREATE OR REPLACE IMAGE REPOSITORY API;
179: 
180: GRANT READ ON IMAGE REPOSITORY API TO ROLE DATA_API_ROLE;
181: 
182: SHOW IMAGE REPOSITORIES;
183: ```
184: 
185: Note the `repository_url` in the response as that will be needed in the next step.
186: 
187: <!-- ------------------------ -->
188: ## Pushing the Container to the Repository
189: Duration: 1
190: 
191: Run the following commands in the terminal in Codespaces, replacing the `<repository_url>` with your repository from the previous step, to log in to the container repository. You will be prompted for your Snowflake username and password to log in to your repository.
192: 
193: ```bash
194: docker login <repository_url>
195: docker build -t <repository_url>/dataapi .
196: docker push <repository_url>/dataapi
197: ```
198: 
199: <!-- ------------------------ -->
200: ## Creating the Compute Pool
201: Duration: 1
202: 
203: To create the compute pool to run the application, connect to Snowflake and run the following commands in the Snowflake console or using SnowSQL:
204: 
205: ```sql
206: 
207: USE ROLE ACCOUNTADMIN;
208: 
209: CREATE COMPUTE POOL API
210:   MIN_NODES = 1
211:   MAX_NODES = 5
212:   INSTANCE_FAMILY = CPU_X64_XS;
213: 
214: GRANT USAGE ON COMPUTE POOL API TO ROLE DATA_API_ROLE;
215: GRANT MONITOR ON COMPUTE POOL API TO ROLE DATA_API_ROLE;
216: 
217: ```
218: 
219: <!-- ------------------------ -->
220: ## Deploying the Private API Service
221: Duration: 3
222: 
223: To create a service to host the application **without exposing a public endpoint**, connect to Snowflake and run the following commands in the Snowflake console or using SnowSQL. Note that, unlike the public API quickstart, the endpoint in the specification below has **no `public: true` property**. The service will still be reachable from inside your Snowflake account, but Snowflake will not assign it a public address.
224: 
225: ```sql
226: 
227: USE ROLE ACCOUNTADMIN;
228: GRANT BIND SERVICE ENDPOINT ON ACCOUNT TO ROLE DATA_API_ROLE;
229: 
230: CREATE SECURITY INTEGRATION IF NOT EXISTS SNOWSERVICES_INGRESS_OAUTH
231: TYPE=oauth
232: OAUTH_CLIENT=snowservices_ingress
233: ENABLED=true;
234: 
235: USE ROLE DATA_API_ROLE;
236: CREATE SERVICE API.PUBLIC.API
237:  IN COMPUTE POOL API
238:  FROM SPECIFICATION
239: $$
240: spec:
241:   container:
242:   - name: api
243:     image: /api/public/api/dataapi:latest
244:     resources:
245:       requests:
246:         cpu: 0.5
247:         memory: 128M
248:       limits:
249:         cpu: 1
250:         memory: 256M
251:   endpoint:
252:   - name: api
253:     port: 8001
254: $$
255: QUERY_WAREHOUSE = DATA_API_WH;
256: 
257: ```
258: 
259: It will take a few minutes for your service to initialize. You can check its status with these commands:
260: 
261: ```sql
262: CALL SYSTEM$GET_SERVICE_STATUS('api');
263: CALL SYSTEM$GET_SERVICE_LOGS('api.public.api', 0, 'api');
264: ```
265: 
266: Once the service is ready, retrieve its private connectivity details:
267: 
268: ```sql
269: SHOW ENDPOINTS IN SERVICE API;
270: ```
271: 
272: Because the endpoint is private, the `ingress_url` column is empty and the `host` column shows the private (internal) DNS name that resolves only inside Snowflake, for example `...snowflakecomputing.internal`. Make note of that hostname, combined with port `8001`, as `<PRIVATE_API_URL>` - the Ockam outlet service will use it to reach the API over Snowflake's internal network. See the Snowflake documentation on [private connectivity](https://docs.snowflake.com/en/user-guide/admin-security-privatelink) for more details.
273: 
274: > aside positive
275: > Because no public endpoint exists, you cannot open this API in a browser. That is the point - the API is only reachable from inside Snowflake, and we will now securely bridge your enterprise private environment to it with Ockam.
276: 
277: <!-- ------------------------ -->
278: ## Exposing the API with Ockam Portals
279: Duration: 15
280: 
281: Now we will make the private API reachable from your enterprise private environment, without ever exposing a public endpoint. [Ockam](https://ockam.io) creates authenticated, end-to-end encrypted tunnels - called **Portals** - between two private environments.
282: 
283: In our architecture:
284: 
285: - The **Ockam TCP Outlet** runs inside Snowflake as a Snowpark Container Services workload next to the private API service. It forwards traffic destined for the API into the service over Snowflake's internal network.
286: - The **Ockam Orchestrator** (the Ockam cloud) verifies the identity of both sides and relays the encrypted traffic between them.
287: - The **Ockam TCP Inlet** runs in your enterprise private environment (here, your Codespace) and exposes the API on a local port, for example `localhost:9000`.
288: - Your existing application just connects to `localhost:9000` - it does not need to know anything about Ockam.
289: 
290: ### Download the Ockam CLI
291: 
292: Open a terminal in your Codespace and install the Ockam CLI. The exact install command is always published in the [Ockam docs](https://docs.ockam.io/install/):
293: 
294: ```bash
295: curl --proto '=https' --tlsv1.2 -sSfL https://install.command.ockam.io | sh
296: export PATH="$HOME/.ockam/bin:$PATH"
297: ockam --version
298: ```
299: 
300: ### Create an Ockam project and login
301: 
302: If this is your first time using Ockam, enroll a new Ockam Orchestrator account. This creates a space and a default project and connects your local machine to it:
303: 
304: ```bash
305: ockam enroll
306: ```
307: 
308: To enroll a machine into an **existing** project - for example when the Codespace is recreated - use the project's enrollment token instead:
309: 
310: ```bash
311: ockam project enroll <YOUR_PROJECT_ENROLLMENT_TOKEN>
312: ```
313: 
314: Your Ockam project is used by both the inlet (in your VPC) and the outlet (in Snowflake) so that they can authenticate each other and negotiate an encrypted channel. Make a note of your project name (shown when you run `ockam enroll` or visit the Ockam console).
315: 
316: Create a dedicated node on this machine and use it for all the inlet commands below:
317: 
318: ```bash
319: ockam node create enterprise_app
320: ```
321: 
322: ### Create the forwarder on the Ockam Orchestrator
323: 
324: A **forwarder** publishes the address of the outlet (in Snowflake) on the Ockam Orchestrator so that the inlet (in your VPC) can discover it, even though the snowflake outlet is not directly reachable from your VPC:
325: 
326: ```bash
327: ockam forwarder create --at private_api_relay
328: ```
329: 
330: ### Give Snowflake permission to reach the Ockam Orchestrator
331: 
332: The Ockam outlet service running in Snowflake needs outbound (egress) network access to the Ockam Orchestrator. In Snowflake, create a network rule and an external access integration. The value list below allows egress to Ockam's relay endpoints; if your project uses a specific relay host, use that host instead:
333: 
334: ```sql
335: USE ROLE ACCOUNTADMIN;
336: CREATE OR REPLACE NETWORK RULE OCKAM_EGRESS_NETWORK_RULE
337:   TYPE = HOST_PORT
338:   MODE = EGRESS
339:   VALUE_LIST = ('relay.ockam.network:443');
340: 
341: CREATE OR REPLACE EXTERNAL ACCESS INTEGRATION OCKAM_EGRESS
342:   ALLOWED_NETWORK_RULES = (OCKAM_EGRESS_NETWORK_RULE)
343:   ENABLED = TRUE;
344: 
345: GRANT USAGE ON INTEGRATION OCKAM_EGRESS TO ROLE DATA_API_ROLE;
346: ```
347: 
348: ### Build the Ockam outlet container
349: 
350: In your Codespace, create a small container image that runs the Ockam CLI and creates the TCP outlet pointing at the private API service. First add the two files below to the project.
351: 
352: ### Dockerfile.ockam
353: 
354: ```dockerfile
355: FROM python:3.11-slim
356: 
357: RUN apt-get update \
358:     && apt-get install -y --no-install-recommends ca-certificates curl \
359:     && rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/*
360: 
361: RUN curl --proto '=https' --tlsv1.2 -sSfL https://install.command.ockam.io | sh
362: 
363: COPY entrypoint.sh /entrypoint.sh
364: RUN chmod +x /entrypoint.sh
365: 
366: ENTRYPOINT ["/entrypoint.sh"]
367: ```
368: 
369: ### entrypoint.sh
370: 
371: ```bash
372: #!/usr/bin/env bash
373: set -euo pipefail
374: 
375: IDENTITY_NAME="${OCKAM_IDENTITY_NAME:-snowflake_outlet}"
376: 
377: # Create an identity and enroll this node into your Ockam project.
378: ockam identity create "$IDENTITY_NAME" 2>/dev/null || true
379: ockam project enroll "$OCKAM_ENROLLMENT_TOKEN" --identity "$IDENTITY_NAME"
380: 
381: # Create the outlet node and open a TCP outlet at the private API service.
382: # This forwards any requests it receives through the Ockam channel
383: # to the private API endpoint inside Snowflake.
384: ockam node create "$IDENTITY_NAME" 2>/dev/null || true
385: ockam tcp-outlet create --from /service/outlet --to "$PRIVATE_API_URL" --node "$IDENTITY_NAME"
386: 
387: # Keep the container alive so the Ockam node and outlet keep running.
388: sleep infinity
389: ```
390: 
391: ### Push the Ockam outlet container to Snowflake
392: 
393: ```bash
394: docker build -f Dockerfile.ockam -t <repository_url>/ockam_box .
395: docker push <repository_url>/ockam_box
396: ```
397: 
398: ### Deploy the Ockam outlet service in Snowflake
399: 
400: Connect to Snowflake and create a service that runs the Ockam outlet. It connects to `PRIVATE_API_URL` (the private DNS name from the Deploying the Private API Service step, with the `http://` scheme and port `8001`), and reaches the Ockam Orchestrator through the `OCKAM_EGRESS` integration created in the previous subsection:
401: 
402: ```sql
403: USE ROLE DATA_API_ROLE;
404: CREATE SERVICE API.PUBLIC.OCKAM_OUTLET
405:  IN COMPUTE POOL API
406:  FROM SPECIFICATION
407: $$
408: spec:
409:   container:
410:   - name: ockam
411:     image: /api/public/api/ockam_box:latest
412:     env:
413:       OCKAM_ENROLLMENT_TOKEN: <YOUR_PROJECT_ENROLLMENT_TOKEN>
414:       OCKAM_IDENTITY_NAME: snowflake_outlet
415:       PRIVATE_API_URL: http://<PRIVATE_INGRESS_DNS>:8001
416:     resources:
417:       requests:
418:         cpu: 0.5
419:         memory: 128M
420:       limits:
421:         cpu: 1
422:         memory: 500M
423: $$
424: QUERY_WAREHOUSE = DATA_API_WH
425: EXTERNAL_ACCESS_INTEGRATIONS = (OCKAM_EGRESS);
426: 
427: ```
428: 
429: Check that the outlet service starts successfully:
430: 
431: ```sql
432: CALL SYSTEM$GET_SERVICE_STATUS('api.public.ockam_outlet');
433: CALL SYSTEM$GET_SERVICE_LOGS('api.public.ockam_outlet', 0, 'ockam');
434: ```
435: 
436: The logs should show the outlet node enrolling into your Ockam project and creating the TCP outlet to the private API service.
437: 
438: ### Create the TCP inlet in your enterprise environment
439: 
440: Back in the Codespace terminal, open the TCP inlet that exposes the private API on `localhost:9000`. The address routes through your Ockam project, the forwarder, and an encrypted channel to the `/service/outlet` endpoint inside Snowflake:
441: 
442: ```bash
443: ockam tcp-inlet create --from 9000 \
444:   --to /project/<YOUR_PROJECT>/forward/private_api_relay/secure_channel/service/outlet \
445:   --node enterprise_app
446: ```
447: 
448: > aside negative
449: > Ockam's CLI is updated frequently. If any command above has changed in your installed version, follow the exact current syntax in the [Ockam Portals guide](https://docs.ockam.io) - the concepts and the architecture are the same, and every command is documented with copy-paste examples.
450: 
451: <!-- ------------------------ -->
452: ## Testing the Private API
453: Duration: 3
454: 
455: With the inlet running on `localhost:9000`, your enterprise application (and curl) can use the API as if it were running locally - even though the API service itself has no public endpoint and is sitting inside Snowflake.
456: 
457: To verify the tunnel works, call the root endpoint:
458: 
459: ```bash
460: curl http://localhost:9000/
461: ```
462: 
463: You should get the JSON response:
464: 
465: ```json
466: {"result":"Nothing to see here"}
467: ```
468: 
469: ### Top 10 Customers
470: 
471: To retrieve the top 10 customers in the date range of `1995-02-01` to `1995-02-14` using the Snowflake Connector for Python, run:
472: 
473: ```bash
474: curl -X GET "http://localhost:9000/connector/customers/top10?start_range=1995-02-01&end_range=1995-02-14"
475: ```
476: 
477: To retrieve the top 10 customers in the date range of `1995-02-01` to `1995-02-14` using the Snowflake Snowpark API, run:
478: 
479: ```bash
480: curl -X GET "http://localhost:9000/snowpark/customers/top10?start_range=1995-02-01&end_range=1995-02-14"
481: ```
482: 
483: If you call the endpoint without specifying the `start_range` then `1995-01-01` will be used. If you call the endpoint without specifying the `end_range` then `1995-03-31` will be used.
484: 
485: ### Monthly sales for a given year for a sales clerk
486: 
487: To retrieve the monthly sales for clerk `000000002` for the year `1995` using the Snowflake Connector for Python, run:
488: 
489: ```bash
490: curl -X GET "http://localhost:9000/connector/clerk/000000002/yearly_sales/1995"
491: ```
492: 
493: To retrieve the monthly sales for clerk `000000002` for the year `1995` using the Snowflake Snowpark API, run:
494: 
495: ```bash
496: curl -X GET "http://localhost:9000/snowpark/clerk/000000002/yearly_sales/1995"
497: ```
498: 
499: Every request is authenticated by the Ockam Orchestrator and travels end-to-end encrypted from the inlet in your VPC to the outlet service inside Snowflake, and from there over Snowflake's internal network to the private API service.
500: 
501: > aside positive
502: > If a request fails, check the status of both services with `CALL SYSTEM$GET_SERVICE_STATUS('api.public.api');` and `CALL SYSTEM$GET_SERVICE_STATUS('api.public.ockam_outlet');`. The Ockam [troubleshooting guide](https://docs.ockam.io) is also a good resource when the tunnel itself is the problem.
503: 
504: <!-- ------------------------ -->
505: ## Cleanup
506: Duration: 2
507: 
508: To fully remove everything you did today, stop the portal and drop the Snowflake objects you created. From the Snowflake console or SnowSQL, as `ACCOUNTADMIN` run:
509: 
510: ```SQL
511: USE ROLE ACCOUNTADMIN;
512: 
513: DROP SERVICE IF EXISTS API.PUBLIC.API;
514: DROP SERVICE IF EXISTS API.PUBLIC.OCKAM_OUTLET;
515: DROP COMPUTE POOL IF EXISTS API;
516: DROP DATABASE IF EXISTS API;
517: DROP ROLE IF EXISTS DATA_API_ROLE;
518: DROP WAREHOUSE IF EXISTS DATA_API_WH;
519: DROP INTEGRATION IF EXISTS OCKAM_EGRESS;
520: DROP NETWORK RULE IF EXISTS OCKAM_EGRESS_NETWORK_RULE;
521: ```
522: 
523: To delete the Ockam forwarder and the local inlet node from the Codespace terminal, run:
524: 
525: ```bash
526: ockam tcp-inlet delete --from 9000 --node enterprise_app
527: ockam forwarder delete --at private_api_relay
528: ockam node delete enterprise_app
529: ```
530: 
531: <!-- ------------------------ -->
532: ## Conclusion and Resources
533: Duration: 2
534: 
535: You've successfully built a **private** custom API in Python Powered by Snowflake and made it securely reachable from your enterprise private environment with Ockam Portals. Because the API service never had a `public: true` endpoint, it is not reachable from the Internet. Only the Ockam TCP Inlet you created - running in your VPC - can reach it, and every request travels through an authenticated, end-to-end encrypted Ockam channel.
536: 
537: The same pattern works for any service: run an Ockam **outlet** next to any private workload (a database, an API, a message broker), publish a forwarder on the Ockam Orchestrator, and let applications in your private environment reach it through an Ockam **inlet** on a local port. Ockam handles authentication, authorization, and encryption for you.
538: 
539: ### What we've covered
540: - How to configure and build a private custom API Powered by Snowflake
541: - How to publish and deploy a container with the API in Snowflake without a public endpoint
542: - How to securely connect an application in your enterprise private environment to the private API with Ockam Portals
543: 
544: ### Related Resources
545: - [Build a Custom API in Python and Flask](https://quickstarts.snowflake.com/guide/build_a_custom_api_in_python/index.html#0) - the companion quickstart that exposes the same API publicly
546: - [Ockam](https://ockam.io) - secure communication for modern distributed apps
547: - [Ockam Documentation](https://docs.ockam.io) - install, Node, and Portal guides
548: - [Ockam on GitHub](https://github.com/ockam-network/ockam) - source code and examples
549: - [Snowpark Container Services](https://docs.snowflake.com/en/developer-guide/snowpark-container-services/overview)
550: - [Snowpark Container Services: working with services](https://docs.snowflake.com/en/developer-guide/snowpark-container-services/working-with-services)
551: - [Snowpark Container Services: working with image registries](https://docs.snowflake.com/en/developer-guide/snowpark-container-services/working-with-container-registries-and-repositories)
552: - [Snowpark Container Services: working with compute pools](https://docs.snowflake.com/en/developer-guide/snowpark-container-services/working-with-compute-pool)
553: - [External network access in Snowflake](https://docs.snowflake.com/en/developer-guide/external-network-access/external-network-access-overview)
554: - [Snowflake private connectivity](https://docs.snowflake.com/en/user-guide/admin-security-privatelink)

5: ## Getting Started
6: 
7: Copy [this template doc](https://docs.google.com/document/d/1E6XMcdTexh5O8JwGy42SY3Ehzi8gOfUGiqTiUX6N04o/edit) as a starting point and then iteratively mutate the metadata and contents to your liking, following the formatting rules described below.
8: 
9: To preview a codelab:
10: 
11: -  (optional one-time setup) Install the [Preview Codelab Chrome extension](https://chrome.google.com/webstore/detail/preview-codelab/lhojjnijnkiglhkggagbapfonpdlinji) in your browser.
12: 
13: - Click the Chrome extension's button while you're in your codelab Google Doc tab, or
14: - Navigate manually to **https://codelabs-preview.appspot.com/?file_id=[google-doc-id]**.
15: 
16: ## Formatting Reference
17: 
18: 1. Table of Contents
19: 
20:     Every codelab document must use the **Heading 1** paragraph style to delineate the steps of the codelab. In turn, these headings will be used to automatically create a Table of Contents which shows the student exactly where they are in the codelab and lets them jump to any step.
21: 
22:     The table of contents disappears for smaller browsers but is still available from the hamburger menu.
23: 
24: 1. Codelab Metadata (Google Docs)
25: 
26:     There is some additional metadata that is required in order to properly publish a codelab. This metadata should be added as a **two-column table** anywhere before the first step of the codelab. For example:
27: 
28: 
29: 
30:     You are free to add your own metadata here if you'd like but certain key/value pairs are reserved for specific codelab publishing features. The current list of reserved metadata terms are:
31: 
32:     * **Summary:** A short summary of the codelab that will be shown in the codelab browser UI.
33:     * **URL:** The URL suffix where this codelab will be published, i.e. the path after the root URL to a collection of codelabs. For example, the Google Codelabs site uses codelabs.developers.google.com/codelabs/ as root and this value is appended to that base to form the unique URL for a given codelab.
34:     * **Category:** A single, top-level category that will be used to group codelabs by platform. Categories are normally curated by an organization (e.g. we have a set we use for the Google Codelabs site) but each publisher is free to use this value at their discretion.
35:     * **Environment**: A tag that allows use to output some codelabs for a specific environment. All codelabs default to the "Web" environment but given some hardware constraints we might only want to generate them for a "Kiosk" environment where we know people will have the right hardware. \
36: You can also use this to target specific events, for instance:  \
37: "Web, polymer-summit" (without quotes)
38:     * **Status:** One or more of (Draft, Published, Deprecated, Hidden) to indicate the progress and whether the codelab is ready to be published. 'Hidden' implies the codelab is for restricted use, should be available only by direct URL, and should not appear on the main index page.
39:     * **Feedback Link:** The URL that the student should be sent to when they click on the feedback link to report a bug in the codelab.
40:     * **Analytics Account:** This allows you to specify a custom Google Analytics ID for your codelab. If no ID is specified, it defaults to a global codelabs analytics account.
41: 
42: 1. Codelab Metadata (Markdown)
43: 
44:     You are free to add your own metadata here if you'd like but certain key/value pairs are reserved for specific codelab publishing features. The current list of reserved metadata terms are:
45: 
46:     * **summary:** A short summary of the codelab that will be shown in the codelab browser UI.
47:     * **id:** The name of the folder that will be generated once you export the markdown file via claat.
48:     * **categories:** A single, top-level category that will be used to group codelabs by platform. Categories are normally curated by an organization (e.g. we have a set we use for the Google Codelabs site) but each publisher is free to use this value at their discretion.
49:     * **environments**: A tag that allows use to output some codelabs for a specific environment. All codelabs default to the "Web" environment but given some hardware constraints we might only want to generate them for a "Kiosk" environment where we know people will have the right hardware. \
50: You can also use this to target specific events, for instance:  \
51: "Web, polymer-summit" (without quotes)
52:     * **status:** One or more of (Draft, Published, Deprecated, Hidden) to indicate the progress and whether the codelab is ready to be published. 'Hidden' implies the codelab is for restricted use, should be available only by direct URL, and should not appear on the main index page.
53:     * **feedback link:** The URL that the student should be sent to when they click on the feedback link to report a bug in the codelab.
54:     * **analytics account:** This allows you to specify a custom Google Analytics ID for your codelab. If no ID is specified, it defaults to a global codelabs analytics account.
55:     * **tags:** Add relevant tags to make your codelab easily found.
56:     * **authors:** Indicate the author(s) of this specific codelab.
57: 
58: 1. Headers
59: 
60:     Within the steps of your codelab you should use the **Heading 2**, **Heading 3** and **Heading 4** paragraph styles to organize your content. These will get translated to `<h2>`, `<h3>` and `<h4>` tags in the codelab markup.
61: 
62:     Also, if you wish to include some additional administrative information at the beginning of your codelab you can freely use the **Heading 2**, **Heading 3** and **Heading 4** paragraph styles and they will not show up in the codelab as long as they appear before the first **Heading 1**.
63: 
64: 1. Text Styles
65: 
66:     For the most part, it doesn't matter which fonts you use in your Google Doc draft; everything will be formatted using Roboto in the final codelab.
67: 
68:     There are some simple ways that you can add emphasis to certain parts of the text. Bolded and italicized text will be passed through to the codelab markup as `<strong>` and `<em>` tags respectively. Also, passages of text formatted with the `Courier New` font will be passed through as an inline `<code>` tag in the markup.
69: 
70: 1. Responsive Images
71: 
72:     Inline images in your codelab should just work seamlessly. You can re-size them in your codelab document and that width will be applied as a **max-width** on the image in the codelab markup so that images are the same size relative to the text but also scale down appropriately for smaller browsers.
73: 
74: 1. Youtube Videos
75: 
76:     Youtube Videos can be embedded by doing:
77:      - Add an image in the document. The image can be a screenshot of the video for instance but it doesn't really matter since it won't be displayed but replaced by the embedded video.
78:      - Add an "Alt Text" to the image by doing **Cmd+Opt+Y** or **Right click > "Alt Text..."**
79:      - Put a Youtube video link in the **Description** field of the Alt Text. in the format `https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=[video_ID]`
80:     > Specifying a start time is not supported at this time.
81: 
82: 1. Embedded Iframes
83: 
84:     Iframes can be embedded by doing:
85:      - Add an image in the document. The image can be a screenshot of the iframe for instance but it doesn't really matter since it won't be displayed but replaced by the embedded iframe.
86:      - Add an "Alt Text" to the image by doing **Cmd+Opt+Y** or **Right click > "Alt Text..."**
87:      - Put a full URL in the **Description** field of the Alt Text. in the format `https://www.domain.com/watch?foo=bar`. Note that for security reasons, iframe embbedding is limited to an enumerated set of allowable iframe source URLs. Feel free to submit a PR if you'd like to augment that list or tweak your own version of the claat command.
88: 
89: 1. Info Boxes
90: 
91:     For additional information that you would like to specially call-out in your codelab, there are two styles of info boxes:
92: 
93:     1. Positive information like best practices and time saving tips should be formatted as a **single-cell table** with a **light green 3** background.
94: 
95:     2. Negative information like warnings and API usage restrictions should be formatted as a **single-cell table** with a **light orange 3** background.
96: 
97:     It is recommended that you keep your infoboxes clean, concise and focused on a single topic. If you have information which may be useful to know but is not a critical part of the codelab instructions, then you should link to that information from the FAQ section rather than including it as an infobox.
98: 
99: 1. Command-line Snippets
100: 
101:     It's often the case that you will have command-line instructions or log messages which are formatted with a monospaced font and have pre-defined whitespace. You can add these sections to your codelab by creating a **single-cell table** and making sure that all the text is formatted using the **Consolas font**.
102: 
103: 1. Code Snippets
104: 
105:     Code snippets with syntax highlighting can be added by creating a **single-cell table** and making sure that all the text is formatted using the **`Courier New`** font.
106: 
107:     Any additional styles applied to the code will be overridden by the syntax highlighting. This means that you're free to use code highlighting Add-ons in your codelab doc but it will have no effect on how the code is highlighted in the final codelab.
108: 
109:     It is also strongly recommended that you provide a **Heading 3** header directly above your code snippet with the file name. This helps students keep track of where the code is coming from. The codelab framework also uses the file extension of the prior header as a clue for how to highlight the code.
110: 
111:     It is also strongly recommended that you make your **Heading 3** header a hyperlink to the actual file if it is available on GitHub. A GitHub icon will automatically be added to the heading in such cases.
112: 
113: 1. Frequently Asked Questions
114: 
115:     As the author of the codelab, you have developed and tested your code. You've probably run into all sorts of common issues or misconceptions. By linking to frequently asked questions, after each step where they often occur, you will reassure the students that they have everything they need to complete the codelab and avoid having to explain everything inline in your codelab.
116:     FAQs are easy to add. All the author needs to do is provide an unordered list of hyperlinks and preface it with a **Heading 3** header with the exact text: **Frequently Asked Questions**.
117: 
118:     Link icons will be added automatically for stackoverflow.com, developers.google.com, developers.android.com and support.google.com. All links will be configured to open in a new tab.
119: 
120: 1. Download Buttons
121: 
122:     You can make it really easy to get started by including direct download buttons inline in your codelab. In order to add a button to your codelab, simply add a hyperlink and make sure that it is highlighted with a **dark green 1** background.
123: 
124:     Additionally, if the link text begins with the word "Download", a file download icon will be added to the button.
125: 
126: 1. Per-step Time Estimates
127: 
128:     Many participants are not fully committed to completing a codelab when they start it. One of the ways that we can keep them in our codelab is by giving them accurate estimates about how much additional effort is required to complete the codelab at each step.
129: 
130:     In order to add this feature to your codelab, simply annotate each step in your codelab doc with a Duration: which uses **dark grey 1** text.
131: 
132:     That's it. The codelab framework will do everything else for you. If you forget to annotate a step with a duration, the default is 1:00. Also, if the last step of your codelab is just a congratulations page, you should set the duration of that step to **0**.
133: 
134: 1. Conditional Steps
135: 
136:     Sometimes it's useful to have different versions of a codelab for different environments. For example, you might have some steps that only apply to students who take the codelab in a classroom setting while other steps only apply to people who are following the instructions at their own pace online.
137: 
138:     The format is similar to the duration metadata. You simply specify one or more environments with an Environment: which uses **dark grey 1** text. The Duration and/or Environment fields, when present, should be followed by a blank line and should be set in normal text (not in Heading 1, lest they be considered part of the step title).
139: 
140:     If no environment metadata is specified, the default environment is "Web, Kiosk".
141: 
142:     When previewing your codelab, you can change environments using the &env=web or &env=kiosk parameters.
143: 
144: 1. Fragment imports
145: 
146:     It is possible for a codelab to import another doc as a step fragment. For instance, it could be a set of setup instructions shared among multiple codelabs:
147: 
148:     [[**import** [funny dog](https://docs.google.com/document/d/1VkJopEKiqitwFgqFOEU6rpB1VE-R-uYWq4erNHP2TQ4/edit)]]
149: 
150:     The contents of the funny dog document will be inserted in the codelab, replacing import instruction.
151: 
152:     The instruction syntax is:
153: 
154:     *   start with [[ (two square brackets)
155:     *   followed by **import** keyword in bold
156:     *   followed by a link to a doc
157:     *   end with ]] (two square brackets)
158: 
159:     Caveat: The imported doc is limited to content within a step (hence the term "fragment"). Including multiple steps, or even the step title/heading, within the imported doc is not supported.
160: 
161: 1. Resumable Codelabs
162: 
163:     When a user returns to a codelab, they may be returning via a bookmark or a short-link posted online, it usually takes them to the first page of the codelab. In that case, the codelab remembers where they left off and asks them if they wish to resume where they left off. This makes it easier for the user to jump back in and gives us more accurate analytics about how long users spend on each step.
164: 
165:     This is simply part of the framework. There is nothing that you need to do as a codelab author to enable this feature.
166: 
167: 1. Feedback Links
168: 
169:     At the bottom of every step of the codelab there is a link for reporting bugs. This link can be configured using the **Feedback Link** setting in your metadata table.
170: 
171: 1. Inline Surveys
172: 
173:     **NOTE: Surveys cannot be used to collect data that can individually, or in conjunction with other information from this site, help locate and identify a particular user or reveal their sensitive demographics information. Any data collected should be sufficiently anonymized and aggregated. Also, consider that the surveys can possibly send a numerical ID of the selections instead of the actual value itself. Apart from helping on the localization front, this can also help prevent from injecting obvious PII values into GA.**
174: 
175:     As we've seen in previous years, participants consume our codelabs for a wide range of reasons. In order to give us some more insight into how different people consume codelabs, we can ask them some quick multiple choice questions in the early stages of our codelab.
176: 
177:     You can configure these short survey questions to ask whatever you think is relevant to your codelab. In order to include a survey question in your codelab, add a single-cell table with a **light blue 3** background. Format your question with the **Heading 4** paragraph style and provide an **unordered list** of choices.
178: 
179:     The participants' answers will automatically be added as custom variables in Google Analytics which can help you understand things like:
180: 
181:     *   _What is the difference in completion rate between novices and experts?_
182:     *   _What is the average time spent for people who wanted to write code vs. people who just wanted to read?_
183:     *   _Is the bounce rate affected by the students' preference in IDE?_
184: 
185:     Of course, we need to be mindful of our participants' time and concentration and only ask a few key questions. It is _not_ recommended to have a survey after each step.
186: 
187: 1. What you'll learn
188: 
189:     Having a header 2 of "What you'll learn" followed by a bullet point list creates a list of check marks.
190: 
191:     A title of "What we've covered" has the same effect.
192:     
193: 1. YouTube Video Embeds
194: 
195:     Use a video tag like so `<video id="DWAinkJ54AP8"></video>` to embed a video uploaded to YouTube with the URL https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=DWAinkJ54AP8
196: 
197: ## Things to avoid
198: 
199: - **Footers:** Any characters included in the footer (beyond the default page number) result in parsing bugs. For this reason, page footers are not recommended.

(End of file - total 199 lines)
</content>

10: # Build a Private Custom API in Python
11: 
12: <!-- ------------------------ -->
13: ## Overview
14: Duration: 5
15: 
16: Many builders want to share the data stored in Snowflake with other applications through an http API. The [Build a Custom API in Python and Flask](https://quickstarts.snowflake.com/guide/build_a_custom_api_in_python/index.html#0) quickstart shows how to build, deploy, and host such an API with a **public** endpoint. In production, however, you often do not want your data API to be reachable from the Internet at all. Instead you want it to be reachable only from systems inside your own enterprise private environment, such as applications running in your company VPC.
17: 
18: This quickstart builds the same custom API Powered by Snowflake, but keeps it **private**. Instead of creating a public endpoint, you will use [Ockam](https://ockam.io) [Portals](https://docs.ockam.io) to create an encrypted tunnel between your enterprise private environment and the private API service running inside Snowflake. Traffic flowing through the tunnel is authenticated, authorized, and end-to-end encrypted. Your private API never gets a public address, and is not exposed to the Internet.
19: 
20: The API consists of reporting endpoints over the [TPC-H](https://docs.snowflake.com/en/user-guide/sample-data-tpch) sample dataset included in your Snowflake account, built with [Python Flask](https://flask.palletsprojects.com/).
21: 
22: The diagram below shows the architecture you will build:
23: 
24: ![Private custom API architecture](./assets/private_custom_api_architecture.png)
25: 
26: - Your **enterprise application** (or developer laptop) connects to a local port exposed by the **Ockam TCP Inlet** running in your VPC.
27: - The **Ockam Orchestrator** authenticates both sides and relays encrypted data along an end-to-end encrypted Ockam channel.
28: - Inside your **Snowflake Account**, an **Ockam TCP Outlet** service connects to the **Private API service** and forwards requests to it over Snowflake's internal network.
29: - The **Private API service** queries the TPC-H sample data using the Snowpark Container Services and Snowflake's Python connector.
30: 
31: No `public: true` endpoint is ever created for the API, so it cannot be reached from the Internet. Only systems that are granted access via Ockam can use the API.
32: 
33: ### Prerequisites
34: - Privileges necessary to create a user, database, warehouse, compute pool, repository, network rule, external access integration, and service in Snowflake (this quickstart uses `ACCOUNTADMIN`)
35: - Privileges necessary to access the tables in the `SNOWFLAKE_SAMPLE_DATA.TPCH_SF10` database and schema
36: - Access to run SQL in the Snowflake console or SnowSQL
37: - Basic experience using git, GitHub, and Codespaces
38: - Intermediate knowledge of Python
39: 
40: ### What You’ll Learn
41: - How to configure and build a private custom API Powered by Snowflake
42: - How to build, publish, and deploy a container with the API in Snowflake without exposing a public endpoint
43: - How to securely connect your enterprise private environment to the private API with Ockam Portals
44: 
45: ### What You’ll Need
46: - A [Snowflake](https://snowflake.com) account on an AWS commercial region
47: - A [GitHub](https://github.com/) account with credits for Codespaces
48: - An [Ockam](https://ockam.io) Orchestrator account (free tier is enough; you will create one in this guide)
49: - Basic familiarity with the [Snowpark Container Services](https://docs.snowflake.com/en/developer-guide/snowpark-container-services/overview)
50: 
51: ### What You’ll Build
52: - A private API Powered by Snowflake, deployed with Snowpark Container Services and reachable only through an encrypted Ockam tunnel from your enterprise private environment
53: 
54: <!-- ------------------------ -->
55: ## Setting up a Warehouse
56: Duration: 1
57: 
58: The API needs a warehouse to query the data to return to the caller. To create the database and warehouse, connect to Snowflake and run the following commands in the Snowflake console or using SnowSQL:
59: 
60: ```sql
61: USE ROLE ACCOUNTADMIN;
62: CREATE WAREHOUSE DATA_API_WH WITH WAREHOUSE_SIZE='xsmall';
63: ```
64: 
65: ### Create the Application Role in Snowflake
66: Duration: 1
67: 
68: The application will run as a new role with minimal privileges. To create the role, connect to Snowflake and run the following SQL statements to create the role and grant it access to the data needed for the application:
69: 
70: ```SQL
71: USE ROLE ACCOUNTADMIN;
72: CREATE ROLE DATA_API_ROLE;
73: 
74: GRANT USAGE ON WAREHOUSE DATA_API_WH TO ROLE DATA_API_ROLE;
75: GRANT IMPORTED PRIVILEGES ON DATABASE SNOWFLAKE_SAMPLE_DATA TO ROLE DATA_API_ROLE;
76: 
77: GRANT ROLE DATA_API_ROLE TO ROLE ACCOUNTADMIN;
78: ```
79: 
80: <!-- ------------------------ -->
81: ## Setting up your Development Environment
82: Duration: 3
83: 
84: The code used in this guide is hosted in GitHub. You will need a new Codespace from the GitHub [repository](https://github.com/sfc-gh-bculberson/lab_data_api_python).
85: 
86: To create a new Codespace, browse to the GitHub [repository](https://github.com/sfc-gh-bculberson/lab_data_api_python) in a browser. You will need to log in to GitHub if you are not already logged in to access Codespaces. After logging in, click on the green "<> Code" button and "create codespace on main" button.
87: 
88: You will then be redirected into Codespaces where your development environment will load and all code from GitHub will be loaded in the project.
89: 
90: > aside positive
91: > The Ockam TCP Inlet in this quickstart runs on this Codespace, which plays the role of a system inside your enterprise private environment. A Codespace is used for convenience - in production you would run the same commands on a machine inside your company VPC.
92:

1: # Codelabs Site
2: 
3: A site for hosting codelabs content.
4: 
5: 
6: ## Prerequisites
7: 
8: The project requires the following major dependencies:
9: 
10: - [Go](https://golang.org/dl/) language
11: - [Node.js](https://nodejs.org/en/download/) v10+ and [npm](https://www.npmjs.com/get-npm)
12: - [gsutil](https://cloud.google.com/storage/docs/gsutil_install)
13: - [claat](https://github.com/googlecodelabs/tools/tree/master/claat#install)
14: 
15: With Node installed, run `npm install` in the root of the `site` (this folder):
16: 
17: ```text
18: $ npm install
19: ```
20: 
21: (Optional) npm installs binstubs at `./node_modules/.bin/`. When running tasks
22: like `gulp`, you may want to add `./node_modules/.bin/` to your `$PATH` for convenience:
23: 
24: ```text
25: $ export PATH="./node_modules/.bin/:$PATH"
26: ```
27: 
28: This does pose a mild security risk, so please do so at your own risk.
29: 
30: 
31: ## Development
32: 
33: ### Serve
34: 
35: To serve the site in dev mode, run `gulp serve`, passing a path to a directory
36: with the codelabs content as an argument. This will compile all the views and
37: codelabs into the `build/` directory and start a web server to serve that
38: content.
39: 
40: ```text
41: $ gulp serve
42: ```
43: 
44: The output will include the address where the server is running
45: (http://localhost:8000 by default).
46: 
47: You can also serve the completely compiled and minified (prod) version with the
48: `serve:dist` command. Always run this before publishing, as it will show you an
49: replica of what will appear on staging/production.
50: 
51: ```text
52: $ gulp serve:dist
53: ```
54: 
55: ### Views
56: 
57: Views are themed/styled collections of codelabs, served from the same url.
58: Codelab tags are used for selecting codelabs into views. View definitions are
59: stored in `/app/views` directory. Views commonly correspond to events (e.g. NEXT
60: 2018) or abstract themes (e.g. Windows), but we refer to them generically as
61: "views" internally.
62: 
63: #### Add a new view
64: 
65: To add a new view (e.g. to serve codelabs for a particular event):
66: 
67: 1. Create a new folder in `app/views`, which will be the "view id". As the view
68: id will appear in the URL, the name should be sluggified, meaning all lowercase
69: with special characters replaced with dashes.
70: 
71:     ```text
72:     // General example
73:     My Codelab -> my-codelab
74:

171: ## Deployment
172: 
173: Once you build, serve, and verify your labs, you're on your own for publishing the artifacts. There are many ways to publish a static web site and we won't try to cover them all, however, we have included support for deploying your landing pages and codelabs to Google Cloud Storage (GCS).
174: 
175: ### Setup for GCS Support
176: 
177: #### Set  environment variables like this (use your own names):
178: 
179: ```
180: export STAGING_BUCKET=gs://mco-codelabs-staging
181: export PROD_BUCKET=gs://mco-codelabs-prod
182: ```
183: 
184: #### Create staging and production buckets like this (use your own names):
185: 
186: ```
187: 18:42:32 site$ gsutil mb is $STAGING_BUCKET
188: Creating gs://mco-codelabs-staging/...
189: 18:42:47 site$ gsutil mb $PROD_BUCKET
190: Creating gs://mco-codelabs-prod/...
191: ```
192: 
193: #### Setup permissions and web access to your buckets
194: 
195: 1. Make newly uploaded files world-readable and ensure user@ has owner
196: permissions:
197: 
198:     ```text
199:     $ gsutil defacl ch -g all:R -u you@your-domain.com:O $STAGING_BUCKET $PROD_BUCKET
200:     $ gsutil iam ch allUsers:objectViewer $STAGING_BUCKET $PROD_BUCKET
201:     ```
202: 
203:     Add as many `-u user@` as you require. This ensures the users will remain
204:     owners no matter who updates your bucket.
205: 
206: ### Deploy to staging
207: 
208: The following commands perform a "copy" operation, uploading all local files to
209: the staging bucket. The local copy of a file will overwrite the staging copy of
210: the same file. Staging files that do not exist in the local copy will be
211: untouched. To perform a complete "sync" (make staging look exactly like the
212: local copy), specify `--delete-missing` on the publish command.
213: 
214: 1. Compile and minify the build:
215: 
216:     ```text
217:     $ gulp dist
218:     ```
219: 
220: 1. Deploy views to the staging bucket:
221: 
222:     ```text
223:     $ gulp publish:staging:views --staging-bucket=$STAGING_BUCKET
224:     ```
225: 
226: 1. Deploy codelabs to the staging bucket:
227: 
228:     ```text
229:     $ gulp publish:staging:codelabs --staging-bucket=$STAGING_BUCKET
230:     ```
231: 
232: 1. Visit the [staging site](https://mco-codelabs-staging.storage.googleapis.com/index.html) (modify link to match your staging bucket name).
233: 
234: See [#options](#options) for information on how to customize the staging bucket.
235: 
236: ### Deploy to prod
237: 
238: We do not deploy from local to production. Instead, we "promote" a staging build
239: to production.
240: 
241: The following commands perform a "copy" operation, uploading all staging files
242: to the prod bucket. The staging copy of a file will overwrite the prod copy of
243: the same file. Prod files that do not exist in the staging bucket will be
244: untouched. To perform a complete "sync" (make prod look exactly like staging),
245: specify `--delete-missing` on the publish command.
246: 
247: 1. Deploy views from the staging bucket to the production bucket:
248: 
249:     ```text
250:     $ gulp publish:prod:views --staging-bucket=$STAGING_BUCKET --prod-bucket=$PROD_BUCKET
251:     ```
252: 
253: 1. Deploy codelabs from the staging bucket to the production bucket:
254: 
255:     ```text
256:     $ gulp publish:prod:codelabs --staging-bucket=$STAGING_BUCKET --prod-bucket=$PROD_BUCKET
257:     ```
258: 
259: 1. Visit the [production site](https://mco-codelabs-prod.storage.googleapis.com/index.html)  (modify link to match your production bucket name).
260: 
261: See [#options](#options) for information on how to customize the staging and
262: prod bucket.
263: 
264: ### Deploy to custom bucket
265: 
266: This section describes the steps to create and deploy to a custom bucket.
267: Replace `gs://codelabs.mycompany.com` with the name of your bucket. If you want
268: to use GCS directly for serving, the bucket name **must** be a valid domain.
269: 
270: 1. Create a new bucket:
271: 
272:     ```text
273:     $ gsutil mb gs://codelabs.mycompany.com
274:     ```
275: 
276: 1. Make newly uploaded files world-readable and ensure user@ has owner
277: permissions:
278: 
279:     ```text
280:     $ gsutil defacl ch -g all:R -u you@your-domain.com:O gs://codelabs.mycompany.com
281:     $ gsutil iam ch allUsers:objectViewer gs://codelabs.mycompany.com
282:     ```
283: 
284:     Add as many `-u user@` as you require. This ensures the users will remain
285:     owners no matter who updates your bucket.
286: 
287: 1. Set the default main page suffix and not found page:
288: 
289:     ```text
290:     $ gsutil web set -m index.html -e 404.html gs://codelabs.mycompany.com
291:     ```
292: 
293:     This option is only available on bucket names that are valid domains.
294: 
295: 
296: Follow the steps in [deploy to staging](#deploy-to-staging) with a custom
297: `--staging-bucket` parameter. See [#options](#options) for information.
298: 
299: 
300: ### Deploy single view or codelab
301: 
302: Where possible, build and publish the entire website. This will ensure all
303: assets are up-to-date.
304: 
305: To build and publish a set of views to staging:
306: 
307: ```text
308: $ gulp dist --views-filter=^my-event
309: $ gulp publish:staging:views
310: ```
311: 
312: To build and publish a set of codelabs to staging:
313: 
314: ```text
315: $ gulp dist --codelabs-filter=^my-codelab
316: $ gulp publish:staging:codelabs
317: ```
318: 
319: ## Options
320: 
321: `--base-url` - base URL for serving canonical links. This should always include
322: the protocol (http:// or https://) and NOT including a trailing slash. The
323: default value is "https://codelabs.developers.google.com".
324: 
325: `--codelabs-dir` - absolute or relative path on disk where codelabs are stored.
326: Any filters will be applied to these codelabs, and then the resulting selection
327: is symlinked into the build folder. The default value is "." (the current directory).
328: 
329: `--codelabs-filter` - regular expression by which to filter codelabs IDs for
330: inclusion. If a filter is not specified, all codelabs are included.
331: 
332: `--codelabs-namespace` - URL path where codelabs will be served in the web
333: server. The default value is "/codelabs", meaning codelabs will be served at
334: https://URL/codelabs.
335: 
336: `--dry` - Print out steps instead of actually taking them. This only applies  to
337: publish operations.
338: 
339: `--delete-missing` - Delete any files in the destination that are not present
340: at the source (rsync-style behavior).
341: 
342: `--prod-bucket` - name of the GCS bucket to use for production resources. This
343: is only used for publishing.
344: 
345: `--staging-bucket` - name of the GCS bucket to use for staging resources. This
346: is only used for publishing.
347: 
348: `--views-filter` - regular expression by which to filter included views
349: (events). If a filter is not specified, all views are included.
350: 
351: The following options are only relevant when invoking claat:
352: 
353: `--codelabs-env` - environment for which to build codelabs. The default value is
354: "web".
355: 
356: `--codelabs-format` - format in which to build the codelabs. The default value
357: is "html"
358: 
359: `--codelab-source` - Google Doc ID from which to build codelab. This can be
360: specified multiple times to build from multiple sources.
361: 
362: 
363: ## Testing
364: 
365: To run the tests manually in a browser, execute the following:
366: 
367: ```text
368: $ gulp serve
369: $ open http://localhost:8000/app/js/all_tests.html
370: ```
371: 
372: 
373: ## Help
374: 
375: For help documentation/usage of the Gulp tasks, run:
376: 
377: ```text
378: $ gulp -T
379: ```
380: 
381: If gulp startup times are really slow, try removing `node_modules/` or running
382: 
383: ```text
384: $ npm dedupe
385: ```

154: ## Building the Application Container
155: Duration: 1
156: 
157: To create the application container, we will leverage Docker. The Dockerfile is based on Python 3.8 and installs the required libraries needed for the application as well as the code. To create the Docker container, run this command in the terminal provided by Codespaces:
158: 
159: ```bash
160: docker build -t dataapi .
161: ```
162: 
163: <!-- ------------------------ -->
164: ## Creating the Image Registry
165: Duration: 1
166: 
167: To create the image registry and the database which contains it, connect to Snowflake and run the following commands in the Snowflake console or using SnowSQL:
168: 
169: ```sql
170: 
171: USE ROLE ACCOUNTADMIN;
172: CREATE DATABASE API;
173: 
174: GRANT ALL ON DATABASE API TO ROLE DATA_API_ROLE;
175: GRANT ALL ON SCHEMA API.PUBLIC TO ROLE DATA_API_ROLE;
176: 
177: USE DATABASE API;
178: CREATE OR REPLACE IMAGE REPOSITORY API;
179: 
180: GRANT READ ON IMAGE REPOSITORY API TO ROLE DATA_API_ROLE;
181: 
182: SHOW IMAGE REPOSITORIES;
183: ```
184: 
185: Note the `repository_url` in the response as that will be needed in the next step.
186: 
187: <!-- ------------------------ -->
188: ## Pushing the Container to the Repository
189: Duration: 1
190: 
191: Run the following commands in the terminal in Codespaces, replacing the `<repository_url>` with your repository from the previous step, to log in to the container repository. You will be prompted for your Snowflake username and password to log in to your repository.
192: 
193: ```bash
194: docker login <repository_url>
195: docker build -t <repository_url>/dataapi .
196: docker push <repository_url>/dataapi
197: ```
198: 
199: <!-- ------------------------ -->
200: ## Creating the Compute Pool
201: Duration: 1
202: 
203: To create the compute pool to run the application, connect to Snowflake and run the following commands in the Snowflake console or using SnowSQL:
204: 
205: ```sql
206: 
207: USE ROLE ACCOUNTADMIN;
208: 
209: CREATE COMPUTE POOL API
210:   MIN_NODES = 1
211:   MAX_NODES = 5
212:   INSTANCE_FAMILY = CPU_X64_XS;
213: 
214: GRANT USAGE ON COMPUTE POOL API TO ROLE DATA_API_ROLE;
215: GRANT MONITOR ON COMPUTE POOL API TO ROLE DATA_API_ROLE;
216: 
217: ```
218: 
219: <!-- ------------------------ -->
220: ## Deploying the Private API Service
221: Duration: 3
222: 
223: To create a service to host the application **without exposing a public endpoint**, connect to Snowflake and run the following commands in the Snowflake console or using SnowSQL. Note that, unlike the public API quickstart, the endpoint in the specification below has **no `public: true` property**. The service will still be reachable from inside your Snowflake account, but Snowflake will not assign it a public address.
224: 
225: ```sql
226: 
227: USE ROLE ACCOUNTADMIN;
228: GRANT BIND SERVICE ENDPOINT ON ACCOUNT TO ROLE DATA_API_ROLE;
229: 
230: CREATE SECURITY INTEGRATION IF NOT EXISTS SNOWSERVICES_INGRESS_OAUTH
231: TYPE=oauth
232: OAUTH_CLIENT=snowservices_ingress
233: ENABLED=true;
234: 
235: USE ROLE DATA_API_ROLE;
236: CREATE SERVICE API.PUBLIC.API
237:  IN COMPUTE POOL API
238:  FROM SPECIFICATION
239: $$
240: spec:
241:   container:
242:   - name: api
243:     image: /api/public/api/dataapi:latest
244:     resources:
245:       requests:
246:         cpu: 0.5
247:         memory: 128M
248:       limits:
249:         cpu: 1
250:         memory: 256M
251:   endpoint:
252:   - name: api
253:     port: 8001
254: $$
255: QUERY_WAREHOUSE = DATA_API_WH;
256: 
257: ```
258: 
259: It will take a few minutes for your service to initialize. You can check its status with these commands:
260: 
261: ```sql
262: CALL SYSTEM$GET_SERVICE_STATUS('api');
263: CALL SYSTEM$GET_SERVICE_LOGS('api.public.api', 0, 'api');
264: ```
265: 
266: Once the service is ready, retrieve its private connectivity details:
267: 
268: ```sql
269: SHOW ENDPOINTS IN SERVICE API;
270: ```
271: 
272: Because the endpoint is private, the `ingress_url` column is empty and the `host` column shows the private (internal) DNS name that resolves only inside Snowflake, for example `...snowflakecomputing.internal`. Make note of that hostname, combined with port `8001`, as `<PRIVATE_API_URL>` - the Ockam outlet service will use it to reach the API over Snowflake's internal network. See the Snowflake documentation on [private connectivity](https://docs.snowflake.com/en/user-guide/admin-security-privatelink) for more details.
273: 
274: > aside positive
275: > Because no public endpoint exists, you cannot open this API in a browser. That is the point - the API is only reachable from inside Snowflake, and we will now securely bridge your enterprise private environment to it with Ockam.

278: ## Exposing the API with Ockam Portals

303:

10: # Getting Started with Bedrock, Streamlit and Snowflake
11: <!-- ------------------------ -->
12: ## Overview
13: 
14: Duration: 5
15: 
16: In this quickstart we will build a Streamlit application that leverages Snowpark External Access in Snowflake with Amazon Bedrock that will generate a personalized marketing message to customers to cross-sell products.
17: 
18: In summary this is what you will do:
19: - Set up environments in both Snowflake and AWS.
20: - Create a function that leverages Snowpark External Access to make a call to Amazon Bedrock.
21: - Create a Streamlit app that leverages the above function to generate responses using data from Snowflake and prompts.
22: 
23: ### What is Generative AI?
24: Generative AI is a category of artificial intelligence techniques that enable machines to create new, original content, such as text, images, or music, by learning from existing data. These models, often based on neural networks, generate content by understanding patterns and structures in the training data and then producing novel examples that resemble what they have learned. Generative AI has applications in various fields, including natural language processing, computer vision, and creative arts.
25: 
26: ### What is Amazon Bedrock?
27: Amazon Bedrock is a fully managed service that offers a choice of high-performing foundation models via a single API, along with a broad set of capabilities to build generative AI applications. Amazon Bedrock is a managed service from Amazon Web Services designed to simplify the deployment, management, and scaling of Kubernetes clusters. It integrates with AWS's ecosystem to provide robust security, networking, and operational features, enabling users to focus more on their applications rather than on managing infrastructure. Bedrock aims to offer a seamless and efficient way to run containerized applications at scale, leveraging AWS's cloud capabilities for improved performance and reliability.	
28: 
29: ### What is Snowflake?
30: Snowflake is a cloud-based data warehousing solution that allows businesses to store and analyze large volumes of data efficiently. It separates storage and compute functionalities, enabling users to scale resources independently and pay only for what they use. Snowflake supports a wide range of data workloads, including data warehousing, data lakes, and data engineering, and offers robust data sharing capabilities across different cloud platforms.
31: 
32: ### What is Streamlit?
33: Streamlit is a Python library that makes it easy to create and share custom web apps for machine learning and data science. In just a few minutes you can build and deploy powerful data apps.
34: 
35: ### Pre-requisites
36: - Familiarity with [Snowflake](https://quickstarts.snowflake.com/guide/getting_started_with_snowflake/index.html#0) and a Snowflake account
37: with Access to [Streamlit](https://streamlit.io/) in your Snowflake account.
38: - [AWS Account](https://aws.amazon.com/premiumsupport/knowledge-center/create-and-activate-aws-account/).
39: - The AWS account should be a sandbox account with open network policies or you you should [create a VPC](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/vpc/latest/userguide/working-with-vpcs.html) in the same region as the Snowflake account.Additionally, users should have access to Bedrock models in their AWS account.
40: - In the VPC [create subnets](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/vpc/latest/userguide/VPC_Internet_Gateway.html) in a few AZs with an internet gateway to allow egress traffic to the internet by using a routing table and security group for outbound traffic
41: Note: please make sure to use a supported Amazon Bedrock region.
42: Familiarity with the Python programming language.
43: - (Optional) access to Sagemaker Canvas to fine tune a Bedrock model.
44:

1: author: Tim Buchhorn
2: id: data_collaboration_two_way
3: summary: This is a Snowflake Guide on how to use Snowflake's Data Collaboration features to share an enrich data. 
4: categories: Getting-Started
5: environments: web
6: status: Published 
7: feedback link: https://github.com/Snowflake-Labs/sfguides/issues
8: tags: Getting Started, Data Science, Data Engineering 
9: 
10: # Two Way Data Collaboration
11: <!-- ------------------------ -->
12: ## Overview 
13: Duration: 5
14: 
15: This guide will take you through Snowflake's Collaboration features, and highlight how easy it is to share data between two organisations.
16: 
17: It also highlights Snowflakes ability to perform feature engineering, host an ML model, score data from shared data, and share the enriched (scored) data back to the original provider. Hence, it is a 2-way sharing relationship, where both accounts are providers and consumers.
18: 
19: We will also build on these concepts, and introduce how we can utilise Streams and Tasks to automate this entire process.
20: 
21: ### Prerequisites
22: - [Git](https://git-scm.com/book/en/v2/Getting-Started-Installing-Git) installed
23:     **Download the git repo here: https://github.com/Snowflake-Labs/sfguide-two-way-data-collaboration**
24: - [Anaconda](https://www.anaconda.com/) installed
25: - [Python 3.10](https://www.python.org/downloads/) installed
26:     - Note that you will be creating a Python environment with 3.10 in the **Consumer Account - Create Model** step
27: - Snowflake accounts with [Anaconda Packages enabled by ORGADMIN](https://docs.snowflake.com/en/developer-guide/udf/python/udf-python-packages.html#using-third-party-packages-from-anaconda). If you do not have a Snowflake account, you can register for a [free trial account](https://signup.snowflake.com/?utm_cta=quickstarts_).
28: - Snowflake accounts with the Snowflake Marketplace T&C's accepted. This will allow you to create Listings.
29: - A Snowflake account login with a role that has the ability to create Listings, Databases, Schemas, Tables, Stages, User-Defined Functions, and Stored Procedures. If not, you will need to register for free trials or use a different role.
30: - The [Snowpark ML](https://docs.snowflake.com/developer-guide/snowpark-ml/index#installing-snowpark-ml-from-the-snowflake-conda-channel) package installed
31: 
32: ### What You’ll Learn
33: - How to become a Provider in Snowflake Marketplace (Private Listings)
34: - How to consume a shared private asset in the Snowflake Marketplace
35: - How to deploy a ML model in Snowflake
36: - How to share seamlessly between two Snowflake Accounts
37: - How to automate the process using Streams and Tasks  
38: 
39: ### What You’ll Need 
40: - Two [Snowflake](https://signup.snowflake.com/?utm_cta=quickstarts_) Accounts in the same cloud and region
41: - Complete the prerequisites above
42: 
43: ### What You’ll Build 
44: - Ingestion of Credit Card Customer Profile Data
45: - Sharing raw data seamlessly via a Private Listing
46: - Consuming shared data via a Private Listing
47: - Perform feature engineering
48: - Scoring shared data using a ML model
49: - Sharing back scored data to the original Provider account
50: - Automating the above data pipeline using Streams and Tasks
51: 
52: <!-- ------------------------ -->
53: ## Business Use Case and Context
54: Duration: 5
55: 
56: In this hands-on-lab, we are playing the role of SnowBank. The Credit Risk team has noticed a rise in credit card default rates which affects the bottom line of the business. It has enlisted the help of an external organisation (Zamboni) to score the credit card default risk of their existing customers, based on a series of attributes in categories such as spending, balance, delinquency, payment and risk. The data needs to be shared between the two parties.
57: 
58: Both companies have chosen to use Snowflake. The advantages of doing this are:
59: - Direct access and no delay data sharing between the Provider and Consumer accounts
60: - Govern access to your data offering and monitor usage
61: - Enable targeted discovery with one or many organizations
62: - Rely on a multitude of built-in data security features

def make_img(W, H):
    return [[BG for _ in range(W)] for _ in range(H)]

def pset(img, x, y, color):
    if 0 <= x < len(img[0]) and 0 <= y < len(img):
        img[y][x] = color

def rect(img, x0, y0, x1, y1, fill, border=None, bw=2, dash=False):
    H = len(img); W = len(img[0])
    if x0 < 0: x0 = 0
    if y0 < 0: y0 = 0
    if x1 > W-1: x1 = W-1
    if y1 > H-1: y1 = H-1
    for y in range(y0, y1+1):
        for x in range(x0, x1+1):
            on_edge = (x - x0) < bw or (x1 - x) < bw or (y - y0) < bw or (y1 - y) < bw
            if border is not None and on_edge:
                if dash:
                    i = (x - x0) // 12
                    if i % 2 == 0:
                        img[y][x] = border
                else:
                    img[y][x] = border
            else:
                img[y][x] = fill

def round_rect(img, x0, y0, x1, y1, r, fill, border, bw=3):
    rect(img, x0 + r, y0, x1 - r, y1, fill, border, bw)
    rect(img, x0, y0 + r, x1, y1 - r, fill, border, bw)
    for cx in (x0 + r, x1 - r):
        for cy in range(y0 + r, y1 - r + 1):
            for dx in range(-r, r + 1):
                for dy in range(-r, r + 1):
                    if dx*dx + dy*dy <= r*r:
                        x, y = cx + dx, cy + dy
                        if (abs(x - x0) < bw or abs(x1 - x) < bw or abs(y - y0) < bw or abs(y1 - y) < bw):
                            img[y][x] = border
                        else:
                            img[y][x] = fill

def line(img, x0, y0, x1, y1, color, w=3, dash=False, arrow=False, head_sz=18):
    dx = x1 - x0; dy = y1 - y0
    steps = max(abs(dx), abs(dy))
    if steps == 0:
        return
    for i in range(steps + 1):
        x = x0 + dx * i // steps
        y = y0 + dy * i // steps
        if dash and (i // 10) % 2 == 1:
            continue
        for wx in range(-w // 2, w // 2 + 1):
            for wy in range(-w // 2, w // 2 + 1):
                pset(img, x + wx, y + wy, color)
    if arrow:
        ang = 0.36
        base = math.atan2(dy, dx)
        for a in (base - math.pi + ang, base - math.pi - ang):
            ax = x1 + head_sz * math.cos(a)
            ay = y1 + head_sz * math.sin(a)
            for i in range(head_sz + 1):
                t = i / head_sz
                px = int(round(x1 + (ax - x1) * t))
                py = int(round(y1 + (ay - y1) * t))
                for wx in range(-w // 2, w // 2 + 1):
                    for wy in range(-w // 2, w // 2 + 1):
                        pset(img, px + wx, py + wy, color)

def echo(img, x, y, text, color=NAVY, scale=2):
    text = text.upper()
    for ch in text:
        glyph = FONT.get(ch, FONT['?'])
        for row in range(7):
            v = glyph[row]
            for col in range(5):
                if v & (0x80 >> col):
                    for sy in range(scale):
                        for sx in range(scale):
                            pset(img, x + col*scale + sx, y + row*scale + sy, color)
        x += 6 * scale

def textw(text, scale=2):
    return len(text) * 6 * scale

def tch(img, cx, y, text, color=NAVY, scale=2):
    w = textw(text, scale)
    echo(img, cx - w // 2, y, text, color, scale)

def text_block(img, cx, cy, lines, color=WHITE, scale=1, lh=None):
    if lh is None:
        lh = 8 * scale + 6
    total_h = len(lines) * lh
    y = cy - total_h // 2
    for ln in lines:
        tch(img, cx, y, ln, color, scale)
        y += lh

def write_png(out, img):
    H = len(img); W = len(img[0])
    raw = bytearray()
    for y in range(H):
        raw.append(0)
        for x in range(W):
            r, g, b = img[y][x]
            raw.append(r); raw.append(g); raw.append(b)
    def chunk(tag, data):
        c = tag + data
        return struct.pack(">I", len(data)) + c + struct.pack(">I", zlib.crc32(c) & 0xffffffff)
    png = b"\x89PNG\r\n\x1a\n"
    png += chunk(b"IHDR", struct.pack(">IIBBBBB", W, H, 8, 2, 0, 0, 0))
    png += chunk(b"IDAT", zlib.compress(bytes(raw), 9))
    png += chunk(b"IEND", b"")
    os.makedirs(os.path.dirname(out), exist_ok=True)
    with open(out, "wb") as fh:
        fh.write(png)
    print("wrote", out, f"{W}x{H}")
