arguments.content:
author: Cordial
id: cordial_bidirectional_data_share
summary: Learn how to set up a bidirectional data share between Cordial and Snowflake, including requesting and accepting Cordial's Secure Data Share listing in the Snowflake Marketplace and automating data intake into Cordial with Cordial Data Jobs.
categories: getting-started,data-sharing,data-engineering,solution-examples
environments: web
status: Published
feedback link: https://github.com/Snowflake-Labs/sfguides/issues
tags: Getting Started, Data Sharing, Data Engineering, Snowflake Marketplace, Cordial, Data Jobs, Marketing

# Bidirectional Data Share Between Cordial and Snowflake

<!-- ------------------------ -->
## Overview
Duration: 5

Data-driven marketers live in both Snowflake and their lifecycle marketing platform. Analytics, segmentation, and AI models run on the governed, collaborative data platform in Snowflake, while personalized campaigns are orchestrated in Cordial. Historically, keeping these two systems synchronized meant building and maintaining custom ETL jobs, moving files back and forth, or waiting for nightly extracts. This quickstart shows you how to connect them in **both directions** without moving data by hand:

- **Cordial to Snowflake (read side):** Cordial publishes the data stored in your Cordial account as a **Secure Data Share** listing in the Snowflake Marketplace. After you request and accept the share, contacts, events, and other available views appear as a live, read-only database inside your own Snowflake account - with no ETL and no copy of the data.
- **Snowflake to Cordial (write side):** Workforce data that lives in your Snowflake account is pulled into Cordial using **Cordial Data Jobs**. You configure Snowflake as a source for Cordial - a warehouse, a role, and a user with either key-pair or password authentication - and then create Data Jobs that run full and incremental refreshes to keep your Cordial profiles up to date.

The diagram below shows the architecture you will build:

![Bidirectional data share between Cordial and Snowflake](./assets/cordial_bidirectional_data_share_architecture.png)

- **Cordial's Snowflake account** holds the operational data behind your Cordial account (profiles, event streams, campaign activity).
- The **Snowflake Marketplace listing** exposes that data through a secure, governed, live share.
- **Your Snowflake account** reads the shared database with your own warehouse and query tools, and pushes data back to Cordial through **Cordial Data Jobs**.

### What is Cordial?
Cordial is a customer engagement platform for email, mobile, and other lifecycle messaging. It manages profiles, event streams, and campaign data in Snowflake and provides intelligent orchestration and automation for marketers.

### What is Snowflake Secure Data Sharing?
Snowflake's [secure data sharing](https://docs.snowflake.com/en/user-guide/data-sharing-intro) lets a data provider expose a database, schema, or table to a consumer account without moving or copying the data. The consumer queries the data live in their own account. Listing a share on the [Snowflake Marketplace](https://www.snowflake.com/en/data-cloud/marketplace/) adds discovery, terms, and access control on top of the share itself.

### What are Cordial Data Jobs?
Cordial Data Jobs are Cordial's automated ingestion feature. A Data Job connects to a source (in this guide, your Snowflake account), reads records such as contacts, and creates or updates the corresponding objects inside Cordial. You control the load strategy - **full refresh** or **incremental refresh** - and the schedule.

### Prerequisites
- A [Snowflake](https://signup.snowflake.com/) account (a free trial works) with a role that can create warehouses, users, and roles and import shares (this guide uses `ACCOUNTADMIN`)
- A Cordial account with access to the Cordial platform, including the Snowflake listing request flow and **Data Jobs**
- Access to [Snowsight](https://docs.snowflake.com/en/user-guide/ui-snowsight-gs), the web interface for running SQL worksheets (the steps below use Snowsight; the same actions work with SQL clients and SnowSQL)

### What You'll Learn
- How to request and accept a Secure Data Share from Cordial's Snowflake Marketplace listing
- How to query the shared datasets (contacts, events, and other available views) from your own Snowflake account
- How to configure Snowflake as a source for Cordial Data Jobs, including a warehouse, role, user, and key-pair or password authentication
- How to create and run Data Jobs for full and incremental refreshes

### What You'll Need
- A Snowflake account with a warehouse you can use for queries
- A Cordial account, signed in, with visibility into the Marketplace listing and Data Jobs

### What You'll Build
- A live, read-only connection from your Snowflake account to your Cordial data via the Snowflake Marketplace
- An automated ingestion pipeline that reads tables in your Snowflake account and keeps Cordial profiles in sync

<!-- ------------------------ -->
## Request the Secure Data Share
Duration: 5

The first direction of the integration is **Cordial to Snowflake**: making the data stored in your Cordial account queryable inside your own Snowflake account. Cordial publishes this data as a listing on the Snowflake Marketplace, and you request access to it.

To request the share:

1. Sign in to Snowsight and accept the Marketplace terms if you have not already done so: navigate to **Admin > Billing & Terms** and enable the **Snowflake Marketplace**.
2. In the left navigation, select **Data Products > Marketplace**.
3. Search the Marketplace for the **Cordial** listing (for example, "Cordial Secure Data Share").
4. Open the listing and review the available datasets, usage notes, and the terms of the listing.
5. Click **Request** (or **Get**, depending on how Cordial configured the listing).

For a listing that requires approval, Cordial reviews your request and approves it once your account is verified. For an open (auto-publish) listing, the share is provisioned immediately after you click **Get**. You will see a confirmation in Snowsight and the shared database will become ready in your account.

The flow below summarizes the request and accept process:

![Request and accept the secure data share](./assets/secure_data_share_flow.png)

> aside positive
> The Snowflake Marketplace listing is free to request, and accepting it does **not** copy any data. The datasets are live views over Cordial's account, so the data refreshes automatically as your Cordial data changes.

<!-- ------------------------ -->
## Accept the Secure Data Share
Duration: 5

Once Cordial has granted access, the inbound share appears in your account and you accept it to materialize the database you will query.

To accept the share:

1. In Snowsight, select **Data Products > Private Sharing** to see inbound shares from your provider accounts.
2. Find the inbound share from Cordial and select **Get** (also labeled **Create Database** in some releases). Snowflake creates the database in your account automatically.
3. In **Data > Databases**, locate the new database. Record its name and the schema it contains - you will use them when you query the data. The database name is chosen by the provider (for example, `CORDIAL_SHARE`), not by you.
4. Grant read access to the roles and users who should be able to query the data. Run the following as a role with sufficient privileges:

```sql
USE ROLE ACCOUNTADMIN;

GRANT IMPORTED PRIVILEGES ON DATABASE <CORDIAL_SHARED_DB> TO ROLE DATA_ANALYST;
```

5. Confirm the objects are visible:

```sql
SHOW DATABASES LIKE '%CORDIAL%';
SHOW TABLES IN DATABASE <CORDIAL_SHARED_DB>;
SHOW VIEWS IN DATABASE <CORDIAL_SHARED_DB>;
```

> aside negative
> A shared database is **read-only**. You cannot insert, update, or delete rows in it. Use this share for analytics, segmentation, and activation queries, and use Cordial Data Jobs (covered later in this guide) for the opposite direction.

<!-- ------------------------ -->
## Query the Shared Data
Duration: 10

With the share accepted, you can query your Cordial data with standard SQL from your own Snowflake account. Queries run on your warehouse, so first make sure you have one to use.

Create a warehouse if you do not already have one:

```sql
USE ROLE ACCOUNTADMIN;

CREATE WAREHOUSE IF NOT EXISTS ANALYTICS_WH
  WITH WAREHOUSE_SIZE = 'XSMALL'
       AUTO_SUSPEND = 60
       AUTO_RESUME = TRUE;
```

Explore what Cordial shares with you:

```sql
SHOW TABLES  IN DATABASE <CORDIAL_SHARED_DB>;
SHOW VIEWS   IN DATABASE <CORDIAL_SHARED_DB>;
```

The listing typically exposes objects such as:

- **Contacts** - the profiles Cordial stores for your audience
- **Events** - recorded activity such as email sends, opens, clicks, bounces, and opt-outs
- **Views** - pre-aggregated or joined datasets (for example, campaign delivery or unsubscribe summaries)

Query the contacts dataset:

```sql
SELECT contact_id, email, created_at, channel_status
  FROM <CORDIAL_SHARED_DB>.<CORDIAL_SHARED_SCHEMA>.contacts
  LIMIT 10;
```

Query recent events:

```sql
SELECT contact_id, event_name, event_time, campaign_id
  FROM <CORDIAL_SHARED_DB>.<CORDIAL_SHARED_SCHEMA>.events
 WHERE event_time >= DATEADD(day, -7, CURRENT_TIMESTAMP())
 ORDER BY event_time DESC
 LIMIT 100;
```

Views are queried exactly like tables:

```sql
SELECT COUNT(*) AS campaign_sends, COUNT(DISTINCT contact_id) AS recipients
  FROM <CORDIAL_SHARED_DB>.<CORDIAL_SHARED_SCHEMA>.campaign_delivery;
```

> aside positive
> Because the datasets are shared live rather than copied, queries you run now will reflect activity that happened in Cordial seconds ago. There is no extract step to schedule, and you never manage a second copy of the data.

<!-- ------------------------ -->
## Configure Snowflake for Cordial Data Jobs
Duration: 10

The second direction of the integration is **Snowflake to Cordial**: Cordial reads data from your Snowflake account and brings it into Cordial with automated **Data Jobs**. This step prepares your Snowflake account so Cordial can connect to it as a source.

### Create a Warehouse for Ingestion

Cordial's jobs run queries in your account, so they need a warehouse. Create a dedicated one:

```sql
USE ROLE ACCOUNTADMIN;

CREATE WAREHOUSE IF NOT EXISTS CORDIAL_INGEST_WH
  WITH WAREHOUSE_SIZE = 'XSMALL'
       WAREHOUSE_TYPE = 'STANDARD'
       AUTO_SUSPEND = 60
       AUTO_RESUME = TRUE;
```

### Create a Role and User for Cordial

Follow the principle of least privilege: create a role with **read-only** access to exactly the tables Cordial should ingest, and a dedicated user used only by Cordial.

```sql
USE ROLE ACCOUNTADMIN;

CREATE ROLE CORDIAL_INGEST_ROLE;

CREATE USER cordial_service
  PASSWORD = '<STRONG_PASSWORD>'
  MUST_CHANGE_PASSWORD = FALSE
  DEFAULT_ROLE = CORDIAL_INGEST_ROLE
  DEFAULT_WAREHOUSE = CORDIAL_INGEST_WH;

GRANT ROLE CORDIAL_INGEST_ROLE TO USER cordial_service;

GRANT USAGE ON WAREHOUSE CORDIAL_INGEST_WH TO ROLE CORDIAL_INGEST_ROLE;
GRANT USAGE ON DATABASE <SOURCE_DB> TO ROLE CORDIAL_INGEST_ROLE;
GRANT USAGE ON SCHEMA <SOURCE_DB>.<SOURCE_SCHEMA> TO ROLE CORDIAL_INGEST_ROLE;
GRANT SELECT ON ALL TABLES IN SCHEMA <SOURCE_DB>.<SOURCE_SCHEMA> TO ROLE CORDIAL_INGEST_ROLE;
GRANT SELECT ON FUTURE TABLES IN SCHEMA <SOURCE_DB>.<SOURCE_SCHEMA> TO ROLE CORDIAL_INGEST_ROLE;
```

Your workforce data is the source for Data Jobs, so `<SOURCE_DB>.<SOURCE_SCHEMA>` should point at the database and schema that hold the tables you want to bring into Cordial - for example a `marketing` schema with a `contacts` table.

### Configure Authentication

Cordial authenticates to Snowflake with one of two methods. **Key-pair authentication is recommended for automated, unattended jobs**, while username and password is the simplest way to get started.

**Option A - Username and password.** Provide the `cordial_service` username and the `<STRONG_PASSWORD>` value when you configure the source in Cordial (step below).

**Option B - Key-pair authentication.** Generate a 2048-bit RSA key pair locally, then register the public key on the user:

```bash
openssl genrsa 2048 | openssl pkcs8 -topk8 -inform PEM -out rsa_key.p8 -nocrypt
openssl rsa -in rsa_key.p8 -pubout -out rsa_key.pub
```

```sql
ALTER USER cordial_service SET RSA_PUBLIC_KEY = '<PUBLIC_KEY_FROM_rsa_key.pub>';
```

Keep `rsa_key.p8` (the private key) safe - it is the credential Cordial will use. Never commit it to source control or paste it into a SQL worksheet.

### Add Snowflake as a Source in Cordial

1. Sign in to Cordial and navigate to the area where data sources and integrations are managed (the exact menu name can vary between releases - see the [Cordial documentation](https://docs.cordial.com/)).
2. Choose to add a **Snowflake** source.
3. Enter your account identifier in `LOCATOR.CLOUD_REGION` format - get it from **Admin > Accounts** in Snowsight (see the [account identifier documentation](https://docs.snowflake.com/en/user-guide/admin-account-identifier)).
4. Enter the warehouse (`CORDIAL_INGEST_WH`), database (`<SOURCE_DB>`), and schema (`<SOURCE_SCHEMA>`).
5. Select the authentication method (key-pair or username/password) and supply the matching credential.
6. Test the connection. When it succeeds, save the source.

> aside positive
> Only grant `SELECT` on the schemas Cordial should read, and use the dedicated `cordial_service` user - not an administrator login. If a data job is ever compromised, you can revoke just that user's access.

<!-- ------------------------ -->
## Create and Run Data Jobs
Duration: 15

Now that Snowflake is configured as a source, you can create **Data Jobs** that read your Snowflake tables and bring the records into Cordial.

To create a Data Job:

1. In Cordial, open the **Data Jobs** area.
2. Select **Create Data Job**.
3. Choose the **Snowflake** source you configured in the previous step.
4. Choose the Cordial object type the job writes to - most commonly **Contacts**.
5. Map source columns to Cordial fields, and select the merge key used to match existing records (for example, `email` or an external ID).
6. Choose the load strategy:
   - **Full refresh** - processes the entire source object set. Use it for a first load or a backfill.
   - **Incremental refresh** - processes only rows that are new or changed since the last run, using a high-water mark such as an updated/created timestamp column. Use it for ongoing, scheduled syncs.
7. Add a **schedule** (for example, hourly or daily) or leave the job to run manually.
8. Save and run the job.

The flow below summarizes the process:

![Configure Snowflake and run Cordial Data Jobs](./assets/data_jobs_flow.png)

After a run, review the job history in Cordial: it shows the run times, the number of records read, how many were created versus updated, and any errors to investigate.

> aside positive
> Start with a **full refresh** to load your baseline, then switch the job to an **incremental refresh** on a schedule. Incremental runs touch only the rows that changed, so ongoing syncs stay fast and inexpensive.

<!-- ------------------------ -->
## Conclusion and Resources
Duration: 2

You've connected Cordial and Snowflake in both directions. Cordial's Snowflake data is now queryable inside your own Snowflake account through a live Secure Data Share - no copies, no ETL. In the other direction, Cordial Data Jobs read tables from your Snowflake account and keep Cordial profiles synchronized with full and incremental refreshes.

Because both legs run through Snowflake - sharing for reads and Data Jobs for writes - the integration stays governed, auditable, and free of brittle file transfers. Marketing analysts can query real-time Cordial activity with any Snowflake tool, while operational data from Snowflake flows into Cordial automatically to power messaging.

### What we've covered
- How to request and accept a Secure Data Share from Cordial's Snowflake Marketplace listing
- How to query shared Cordial datasets (contacts, events, and other available views) from your Snowflake account
- How to configure a Snowflake warehouse, role, user, and key-pair or password authentication for Cordial Data Jobs
- How to create and run Data Jobs for full and incremental refreshes

### Related Resources
- [Cordial](https://cordial.com/) - customer engagement and lifecycle marketing platform
- [Cordial Documentation](https://docs.cordial.com/) - Data Jobs and Snowflake source setup (UI names can vary by release; review for the current navigation)
- [Snowflake Marketplace](https://www.snowflake.com/en/data-cloud/marketplace/) - discover and request the Cordial listing
- [Snowflake secure data sharing](https://docs.snowflake.com/en/user-guide/data-sharing-intro)
- [Consuming listings in the Snowflake Marketplace](https://docs.snowflake.com/en/user-guide/data-marketplace-consuming-improved)
- [Snowflake warehouses overview](https://docs.snowflake.com/en/user-guide/warehouses)
- [Key-pair authentication and key rotation](https://docs.snowflake.com/en/user-guide/key-pair-auth)
- [Snowflake account identifiers](https://docs.snowflake.com/en/user-guide/admin-account-identifier)
- [Sign up for a free Snowflake trial](https://signup.snowflake.com/)

190: Follow the principle of least privilege: create a role with **read-only** access to exactly the tables Cordial should ingest, and a dedicated user used only by Cordial.

215: 
216: Cordial authenticates to Snowflake with one of two methods. **Key-pair authentication is recommended for automated, unattended jobs**, while username and password is the simplest way to get started.

229: ```

53:     * **feedback link:** The URL that the student should be sent to when they click on the feedback link to report a bug in the codelab.
54:     * **analytics account:** This allows you to specify a custom Google Analytics ID for your codelab. If no ID is specified, it defaults to a global codelabs analytics account.
55:     * **tags:** Add relevant tags to make your codelab easily found.
56:     * **authors:** Indicate the author(s) of this specific codelab.
57: 
58: 1. Headers
59: 
60:     Within the steps of your codelab you should use the **Heading 2**, **Heading 3** and **Heading 4** paragraph styles to organize your content. These will get translated to `<h2>`, `<h3>` and `<h4>` tags in the codelab markup.
61: 
62:     Also, if you wish to include some additional administrative information at the beginning of your codelab you can freely use the **Heading 2**, **Heading 3** and **Heading 4** paragraph styles and they will not show up in the codelab as long as they appear before the first **Heading 1**.
63: 
64: 1. Text Styles
65: 
66:     For the most part, it doesn't matter which fonts you use in your Google Doc draft; everything will be formatted using Roboto in the final codelab.
67: 
68:     There are some simple ways that you can add emphasis to certain parts of the text. Bolded and italicized text will be passed through to the codelab markup as `<strong>` and `<em>` tags respectively. Also, passages of text formatted with the `Courier New` font will be passed through as an inline `<code>` tag in the markup.
69: 
70: 1. Responsive Images
71: 
72:     Inline images in your codelab should just work seamlessly. You can re-size them in your codelab document and that width will be applied as a **max-width** on the image in the codelab markup so that images are the same size relative to the text but also scale down appropriately for smaller browsers.
73: 
74: 1. Youtube Videos
75: 
76:     Youtube Videos can be embedded by doing:
77:      - Add an image in the document. The image can be a screenshot of the video for instance but it doesn't really matter since it won't be displayed but replaced by the embedded video.
78:      - Add an "Alt Text" to the image by doing **Cmd+Opt+Y** or **Right click > "Alt Text..."**
79:      - Put a Youtube video link in the **Description** field of the Alt Text. in the format `https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=[video_ID]`
80:     > Specifying a start time is not supported at this time.
81: 
82: 1. Embedded Iframes
83: 
84:     Iframes can be embedded by doing:
85:      - Add an image in the document. The image can be a screenshot of the iframe for instance but it doesn't really matter since it won't be displayed but replaced by the embedded iframe.
86:      - Add an "Alt Text" to the image by doing **Cmd+Opt+Y** or **Right click > "Alt Text..."**
87:      - Put a full URL in the **Description** field of the Alt Text. in the format `https://www.domain.com/watch?foo=bar`. Note that for security reasons, iframe embbedding is limited to an enumerated set of allowable iframe source URLs. Feel free to submit a PR if you'd like to augment that list or tweak your own version of the claat command.
88: 
89: 1. Info Boxes
90: 
91:     For additional information that you would like to specially call-out in your codelab, there are two styles of info boxes:
92: 
93:     1. Positive information like best practices and time saving tips should be formatted as a **single-cell table** with a **light green 3** background.
94: 
95:     2. Negative information like warnings and API usage restrictions should be formatted as a **single-cell table** with a **light orange 3** background.
96: 
97:     It is recommended that you keep your infoboxes clean, concise and focused on a single topic. If you have information which may be useful to know but is not a critical part of the codelab instructions, then you should link to that information from the FAQ section rather than including it as an infobox.
98: 
99: 1. Command-line Snippets
100: 
101:     It's often the case that you will have command-line instructions or log messages which are formatted with a monospaced font and have pre-defined whitespace. You can add these sections to your codelab by creating a **single-cell table** and making sure that all the text is formatted using the **Consolas font**.
102: 
103: 1. Code Snippets
104: 
105:     Code snippets with syntax highlighting can be added by creating a **single-cell table** and making sure that all the text is formatted using the **`Courier New`** font.
106: 
107:     Any additional styles applied to the code will be overridden by the syntax highlighting. This means that you're free to use code highlighting Add-ons in your codelab doc but it will have no effect on how the code is highlighted in the final codelab.
108: 
109:     It is also strongly recommended that you provide a **Heading 3** header directly above your code snippet with the file name. This helps students keep track of where the code is coming from. The codelab framework also uses the file extension of the prior header as a clue for how to highlight the code.
110: 
111:     It is also strongly recommended that you make your **Heading 3** header a hyperlink to the actual file if it is available on GitHub. A GitHub icon will automatically be added to the heading in such cases.
112: 
113: 1. Frequently Asked Questions
114: 
115:     As the author of the codelab, you have developed and tested your code. You've probably run into all sorts of common issues or misconceptions. By linking to frequently asked questions, after each step where they often occur, you will reassure the students that they have everything they need to complete the codelab and avoid having to explain everything inline in your codelab.
116:     FAQs are easy to add. All the author needs to do is provide an unordered list of hyperlinks and preface it with a **Heading 3** header with the exact text: **Frequently Asked Questions**.
117: 
118:     Link icons will be added automatically for stackoverflow.com, developers.google.com, developers.android.com and support.google.com. All links will be configured to open in a new tab.
119: 
120: 1. Download Buttons
121: 
122:     You can make it really easy to get started by including direct download buttons inline in your codelab. In order to add a button to your codelab, simply add a hyperlink and make sure that it is highlighted with a **dark green 1** background.
123: 
124:     Additionally, if the link text begins with the word "Download", a file download icon will be added to the button.
125: 
126: 1. Per-step Time Estimates
127: 
128:     Many participants are not fully committed to completing a codelab when they start it. One of the ways that we can keep them in our codelab is by giving them accurate estimates about how much additional effort is required to complete the codelab at each step.
129: 
130:     In order to add this feature to your codelab, simply annotate each step in your codelab doc with a Duration: which uses **dark grey 1** text.
131: 
132:     That's it. The codelab framework will do everything else for you. If you forget to annotate a step with a duration, the default is 1:00. Also, if the last step of your codelab is just a congratulations page, you should set the duration of that step to **0**.
133: 
134: 1. Conditional Steps
135: 
136:     Sometimes it's useful to have different versions of a codelab for different environments. For example, you might have some steps that only apply to students who take the codelab in a classroom setting while other steps only apply to people who are following the instructions at their own pace online.
137: 
138:     The format is similar to the duration metadata. You simply specify one or more environments with an Environment: which uses **dark grey 1** text. The Duration and/or Environment fields, when present, should be followed by a blank line and should be set in normal text (not in Heading 1, lest they be considered part of the step title).
139: 
140:     If no environment metadata is specified, the default environment is "Web, Kiosk".
141: 
142:     When previewing your codelab, you can change environments using the &env=web or &env=kiosk parameters.
143: 
144: 1. Fragment imports
145: 
146:     It is possible for a codelab to import another doc as a step fragment. For instance, it could be a set of setup instructions shared among multiple codelabs:
147: 
148:     [[**import** [funny dog](https://docs.google.com/document/d/1VkJopEKiqitwFgqFOEU6rpB1VE-R-uYWq4erNHP2TQ4/edit)]]
149: 
150:     The contents of the funny dog document will be inserted in the codelab, replacing import instruction.
151: 
152:     The instruction syntax is:
153: 
154:     *   start with [[ (two square brackets)
155:     *   followed by **import** keyword in bold
156:     *   followed by a link to a doc
157:     *   end with ]] (two square brackets)
158: 
159:     Caveat: The imported doc is limited to content within a step (hence the term "fragment"). Including multiple steps, or even the step title/heading, within the imported doc is not supported.
160: 
161: 1. Resumable Codelabs
162: 
163:     When a user returns to a codelab, they may be returning via a bookmark or a short-link posted online, it usually takes them to the first page of the codelab. In that case, the codelab remembers where they left off and asks them if they wish to resume where they left off. This makes it easier for the user to jump back in and gives us more accurate analytics about how long users spend on each step.
164: 
165:     This is simply part of the framework. There is nothing that you need to do as a codelab author to enable this feature.
166: 
167: 1. Feedback Links
168: 
169:     At the bottom of every step of the codelab there is a link for reporting bugs. This link can be configured using the **Feedback Link** setting in your metadata table.
170: 
171: 1. Inline Surveys
172: 
173:     **NOTE: Surveys cannot be used to collect data that can individually, or in conjunction with other information from this site, help locate and identify a particular user or reveal their sensitive demographics information. Any data collected should be sufficiently anonymized and aggregated. Also, consider that the surveys can possibly send a numerical ID of the selections instead of the actual value itself. Apart from helping on the localization front, this can also help prevent from injecting obvious PII values into GA.**
174: 
175:     As we've seen in previous years, participants consume our codelabs for a wide range of reasons. In order to give us some more insight into how different people consume codelabs, we can ask them some quick multiple choice questions in the early stages of our codelab.
176: 
177:     You can configure these short survey questions to ask whatever you think is relevant to your codelab. In order to include a survey question in your codelab, add a single-cell table with a **light blue 3** background. Format your question with the **Heading 4** paragraph style and provide an **unordered list** of choices.
178: 
179:     The participants' answers will automatically be added as custom variables in Google Analytics which can help you understand things like:
180: 
181:     *   _What is the difference in completion rate between novices and experts?_
182:     *   _What is the average time spent for people who wanted to write code vs. people who just wanted to read?_
183:     *   _Is the bounce rate affected by the students' preference in IDE?_
184: 
185:     Of course, we need to be mindful of our participants' time and concentration and only ask a few key questions. It is _not_ recommended to have a survey after each step.
186: 
187: 1. What you'll learn
188: 
189:     Having a header 2 of "What you'll learn" followed by a bullet point list creates a list of check marks.
190: 
191:     A title of "What we've covered" has the same effect.
192:     
193: 1. YouTube Video Embeds
194: 
195:     Use a video tag like so `<video id="DWAinkJ54AP8"></video>` to embed a video uploaded to YouTube with the URL https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=DWAinkJ54AP8
196: 
197: ## Things to avoid
198: 
199: - **Footers:** Any characters included in the footer (beyond the default page number) result in parsing bugs. For this reason, page footers are not recommended.

(End of file - total 199 lines)

10: # Bidirectional Data Share Between Cordial and Snowflake
11: 
12: <!-- ------------------------ -->
13: ## Overview
14: Duration: 5
15: 
16: Data-driven marketers live in both Snowflake and their lifecycle marketing platform. Analytics, segmentation, and AI models run on the governed, collaborative data platform in Snowflake, while personalized campaigns are orchestrated in Cordial. Historically, keeping these two systems synchronized meant building and maintaining custom ETL jobs, moving files back and forth, or waiting for nightly extracts. This quickstart shows you how to connect them in **both directions** without moving data by hand:
17: 
18: - **Cordial to Snowflake (read side):** Cordial publishes the data stored in your Cordial account as a **Secure Data Share** listing in the Snowflake Marketplace. After you request and accept the share, contacts, events, and other available views appear as a live, read-only database inside your own Snowflake account - with no ETL and no copy of the data.
19: - **Snowflake to Cordial (write side):** Workforce data that lives in your Snowflake account is pulled into Cordial using **Cordial Data Jobs**. You configure Snowflake as a source for Cordial - a warehouse, a role, and a user with either key-pair or password authentication - and then create Data Jobs that run full and incremental refreshes to keep your Cordial profiles up to date.
20: 
21: The diagram below shows the architecture you will build:
22: 
23: ![Bidirectional data share between Cordial and Snowflake](./assets/cordial_bidirectional_data_share_architecture.png)
24: 
25: - **Cordial's Snowflake account** holds the operational data behind your Cordial account (profiles, event streams, campaign activity).
26: - The **Snowflake Marketplace listing** exposes that data through a secure, governed, live share.
27: - **Your Snowflake account** reads the shared database with your own warehouse and query tools, and pushes data back to Cordial through **Cordial Data Jobs**.
28: 
29: ### What is Cordial?
30: Cordial is a customer engagement platform for email, mobile, and other lifecycle messaging. It manages profiles, event streams, and campaign data in Snowflake and provides intelligent orchestration and automation for marketers.
31: 
32: ### What is Snowflake Secure Data Sharing?
33: Snowflake's [secure data sharing](https://docs.snowflake.com/en/user-guide/data-sharing-intro) lets a data provider expose a database, schema, or table to a consumer account without moving or copying the data. The consumer queries the data live in their own account. Listing a share on the [Snowflake Marketplace](https://www.snowflake.com/en/data-cloud/marketplace/) adds discovery, terms, and access control on top of the share itself.
34: 
35: ### What are Cordial Data Jobs?
36: Cordial Data Jobs are Cordial's automated ingestion feature. A Data Job connects to a source (in this guide, your Snowflake account), reads records such as contacts, and creates or updates the corresponding objects inside Cordial. You control the load strategy - **full refresh** or **incremental refresh** - and the schedule.
37: 
38: ### Prerequisites
39: - A [Snowflake](https://signup.snowflake.com/) account (a free trial works) with a role that can create warehouses, users, and roles and import shares (this guide uses `ACCOUNTADMIN`)
40: - A Cordial account with access to the Cordial platform, including the Snowflake listing request flow and **Data Jobs**
41: - Access to [Snowsight](https://docs.snowflake.com/en/user-guide/ui-snowsight-gs), the web interface for running SQL worksheets (the steps below use Snowsight; the same actions work with SQL clients and SnowSQL)
42: 
43: ### What You'll Learn
44: - How to request and accept a Secure Data Share from Cordial's Snowflake Marketplace listing
45: - How to query the shared datasets (contacts, events, and other available views) from your own Snowflake account
46: - How to configure Snowflake as a source for Cordial Data Jobs, including a warehouse, role, user, and key-pair or password authentication
47: - How to create and run Data Jobs for full and incremental refreshes
48: 
49: ### What You'll Need
50: - A Snowflake account with a warehouse you can use for queries
51: - A Cordial account, signed in, with visibility into the Marketplace listing and Data Jobs
52: 
53: ### What You'll Build
54: - A live, read-only connection from your Snowflake account to your Cordial data via the Snowflake Marketplace
55: - An automated ingestion pipeline that reads tables in your Snowflake account and keeps Cordial profiles in sync
56: 
57: <!-- ------------------------ -->
58: ## Request the Secure Data Share
59: Duration: 5
60: 
61: The first direction of the integration is **Cordial to Snowflake**: making the data stored in your Cordial account queryable inside your own Snowflake account. Cordial publishes this data as a listing on the Snowflake Marketplace, and you request access to it.
62: 
63: To request the share:
64: 
65: 1. Sign in to Snowsight and accept the Marketplace terms if you have not already done so: navigate to **Admin > Billing & Terms** and enable the **Snowflake Marketplace**.
66: 2. In the left navigation, select **Data Products > Marketplace**.
67: 3. Search the Marketplace for the **Cordial** listing (for example, "Cordial Secure Data Share").
68: 4. Open the listing and review the available datasets, usage notes, and the terms of the listing.
69: 5. Click **Request** (or **Get**, depending on how Cordial configured the listing).
70: 
71: For a listing that requires approval, Cordial reviews your request and approves it once your account is verified. For an open (auto-publish) listing, the share is provisioned immediately after you click **Get**. You will see a confirmation in Snowsight and the shared database will become ready in your account.
72: 
73: The flow below summarizes the request and accept process:
74: 
75: ![Request and accept the secure data share](./assets/secure_data_share_flow.png)
76: 
77: > aside positive
78: > The Snowflake Marketplace listing is free to request, and accepting it does **not** copy any data. The datasets are live views over Cordial's account, so the data refreshes automatically as your Cordial data changes.
79: 
80: <!-- ------------------------ -->
81: ## Accept the Secure Data Share
82: Duration: 5
83: 
84: Once Cordial has granted access, the inbound share appears in your account and you accept it to materialize the database you will query.
85: 
86: To accept the share:
87: 
88: 1. In Snowsight, select **Data Products > Private Sharing** to see inbound shares from your provider accounts.
89: 2. Find the inbound share from Cordial and select **Get** (also labeled **Create Database** in some releases). Snowflake creates the database in your account automatically.
90: 3. In **Data > Databases**, locate the new database. Record its name and the schema it contains - you will use them when you query the data. The database name is chosen by the provider (for example, `CORDIAL_SHARE`), not by you.
91: 4. Grant read access to the roles and users who should be able to query the data. Run the following as a role with sufficient privileges:
92: 
93: ```sql
94: USE ROLE ACCOUNTADMIN;
95: 
96: GRANT IMPORTED PRIVILEGES ON DATABASE <CORDIAL_SHARED_DB> TO ROLE DATA_ANALYST;
97: ```
98: 
99: 5. Confirm the objects are visible:
100: 
101: ```sql
102: SHOW DATABASES LIKE '%CORDIAL%';
103: SHOW TABLES IN DATABASE <CORDIAL_SHARED_DB>;
104: SHOW VIEWS IN DATABASE <CORDIAL_SHARED_DB>;
105: ```
106: 
107: > aside negative
108: > A shared database is **read-only**. You cannot insert, update, or delete rows in it. Use this share for analytics, segmentation, and activation queries, and use Cordial Data Jobs (covered later in this guide) for the opposite direction.
109: 
110: <!-- ------------------------ -->
111: ## Query the Shared Data
112: Duration: 10
113: 
114: With the share accepted, you can query your Cordial data with standard SQL from your own Snowflake account. Queries run on your warehouse, so first make sure you have one to use.
115: 
116: Create a warehouse if you do not already have one:
117: 
118: ```sql
119: USE ROLE ACCOUNTADMIN;
120: 
121: CREATE WAREHOUSE IF NOT EXISTS ANALYTICS_WH
122:   WITH WAREHOUSE_SIZE = 'XSMALL'
123:        AUTO_SUSPEND = 60
124:        AUTO_RESUME = TRUE;
125: ```
126: 
127: Explore what Cordial shares with you:
128: 
129: ```sql
130: SHOW TABLES  IN DATABASE <CORDIAL_SHARED_DB>;
131: SHOW VIEWS   IN DATABASE <CORDIAL_SHARED_DB>;
132: ```
133: 
134: The listing typically exposes objects such as:
135: 
136: - **Contacts** - the profiles Cordial stores for your audience
137: - **Events** - recorded activity such as email sends, opens, clicks, bounces, and opt-outs
138: - **Views** - pre-aggregated or joined datasets (for example, campaign delivery or unsubscribe summaries)
139: 
140: Query the contacts dataset:
141: 
142: ```sql
143: SELECT contact_id, email, created_at, channel_status
144:   FROM <CORDIAL_SHARED_DB>.<CORDIAL_SHARED_SCHEMA>.contacts
145:   LIMIT 10;
146: ```
147: 
148: Query recent events:
149: 
150: ```sql
151: SELECT contact_id, event_name, event_time, campaign_id
152:   FROM <CORDIAL_SHARED_DB>.<CORDIAL_SHARED_SCHEMA>.events
153:  WHERE event_time >= DATEADD(day, -7, CURRENT_TIMESTAMP())
154:  ORDER BY event_time DESC
155:  LIMIT 100;
156: ```
157: 
158: Views are queried exactly like tables:
159: 
160: ```sql
161: SELECT COUNT(*) AS campaign_sends, COUNT(DISTINCT contact_id) AS recipients
162:   FROM <CORDIAL_SHARED_DB>.<CORDIAL_SHARED_SCHEMA>.campaign_delivery;
163: ```
164: 
165: > aside positive
166: > Because the datasets are shared live rather than copied, queries you run now will reflect activity that happened in Cordial seconds ago. There is no extract step to schedule, and you never manage a second copy of the data.
167: 
168: <!-- ------------------------ -->
169: ## Configure Snowflake for Cordial Data Jobs
170: Duration: 10
171: 
172: The second direction of the integration is **Snowflake to Cordial**: Cordial reads data from your Snowflake account and brings it into Cordial with automated **Data Jobs**. This step prepares your Snowflake account so Cordial can connect to it as a source.
173: 
174: ### Create a Warehouse for Ingestion
175: 
176: Cordial's jobs run queries in your account, so they need a warehouse. Create a dedicated one:
177: 
178: ```sql
179: USE ROLE ACCOUNTADMIN;
180: 
181: CREATE WAREHOUSE IF NOT EXISTS CORDIAL_INGEST_WH
182:   WITH WAREHOUSE_SIZE = 'XSMALL'
183:        WAREHOUSE_TYPE = 'STANDARD'
184:        AUTO_SUSPEND = 60
185:        AUTO_RESUME = TRUE;
186: ```
187: 
188: ### Create a Role and User for Cordial
189: 
190: Follow the principle of least privilege: create a role with **read-only** access to exactly the tables Cordial should ingest, and a dedicated user used only by Cordial.
191: 
192: ```sql
193: USE ROLE ACCOUNTADMIN;
194: 
195: CREATE ROLE CORDIAL_INGEST_ROLE;
196: 
197: CREATE USER cordial_service
198:   PASSWORD = '<STRONG_PASSWORD>'
199:   MUST_CHANGE_PASSWORD = FALSE
200:   DEFAULT_ROLE = CORDIAL_INGEST_ROLE
201:   DEFAULT_WAREHOUSE = CORDIAL_INGEST_WH;
202: 
203: GRANT ROLE CORDIAL_INGEST_ROLE TO USER cordial_service;
204: 
205: GRANT USAGE ON WAREHOUSE CORDIAL_INGEST_WH TO ROLE CORDIAL_INGEST_ROLE;
206: GRANT USAGE ON DATABASE <SOURCE_DB> TO ROLE CORDIAL_INGEST_ROLE;
207: GRANT USAGE ON SCHEMA <SOURCE_DB>.<SOURCE_SCHEMA> TO ROLE CORDIAL_INGEST_ROLE;
208: GRANT SELECT ON ALL TABLES IN SCHEMA <SOURCE_DB>.<SOURCE_SCHEMA> TO ROLE CORDIAL_INGEST_ROLE;
209: GRANT SELECT ON FUTURE TABLES IN SCHEMA <SOURCE_DB>.<SOURCE_SCHEMA> TO ROLE CORDIAL_INGEST_ROLE;
210: ```
211: 
212: Your workforce data is the source for Data Jobs, so `<SOURCE_DB>.<SOURCE_SCHEMA>` should point at the database and schema that hold the tables you want to bring into Cordial - for example a `marketing` schema with a `contacts` table.
213: 
214: ### Configure Authentication
215: 
216: Cordial authenticates to Snowflake with one of two methods. **Key-pair authentication is recommended for automated, unattended jobs**, while username and password is the simplest way to get started.
217: 
218: **Option A - Username and password.** Provide the `cordial_service` username and the `<STRONG_PASSWORD>` value when you configure the source in Cordial (step below).
219: 
220: **Option B - Key-pair authentication.** Generate a 2048-bit RSA key pair locally, then register the public key on the user:
221: 
222: ```bash
223: openssl genrsa 2048 | openssl pkcs8 -topk8 -inform PEM -out rsa_key.p8 -nocrypt
224: openssl rsa -in rsa_key.p8 -pubout -out rsa_key.pub
225: ```
226: 
227: ```sql
228: ALTER USER cordial_service SET RSA_PUBLIC_KEY = '<PUBLIC_KEY_FROM_rsa_key.pub>';
229: ```
230: 
231: Keep `rsa_key.p8` (the private key) safe - it is the credential Cordial will use. Never commit it to source control or paste it into a SQL worksheet.
232: 
233: ### Add Snowflake as a Source in Cordial
234: 
235: 1. Sign in to Cordial and navigate to the area where data sources and integrations are managed (the exact menu name can vary between releases - see the [Cordial documentation](https://docs.cordial.com/)).
236: 2. Choose to add a **Snowflake** source.
237: 3. Enter your account identifier in `LOCATOR.CLOUD_REGION` format - get it from **Admin > Accounts** in Snowsight (see the [account identifier documentation](https://docs.snowflake.com/en/user-guide/admin-account-identifier)).
238: 4. Enter the warehouse (`CORDIAL_INGEST_WH`), database (`<SOURCE_DB>`), and schema (`<SOURCE_SCHEMA>`).
239: 5. Select the authentication method (key-pair or username/password) and supply the matching credential.
240: 6. Test the connection. When it succeeds, save the source.
241: 
242: > aside positive
243: > Only grant `SELECT` on the schemas Cordial should read, and use the dedicated `cordial_service` user - not an administrator login. If a data job is ever compromised, you can revoke just that user's access.
244: 
245: <!-- ------------------------ -->
246: ## Create and Run Data Jobs
247: Duration: 15
248: 
249: Now that Snowflake is configured as a source, you can create **Data Jobs** that read your Snowflake tables and bring the records into Cordial.
250: 
251: To create a Data Job:
252: 
253: 1. In Cordial, open the **Data Jobs** area.
254: 2. Select **Create Data Job**.
255: 3. Choose the **Snowflake** source you configured in the previous step.
256: 4. Choose the Cordial object type the job writes to - most commonly **Contacts**.
257: 5. Map source columns to Cordial fields, and select the merge key used to match existing records (for example, `email` or an external ID).
258: 6. Choose the load strategy:
259:    - **Full refresh** - processes the entire source object set. Use it for a first load or a backfill.
260:    - **Incremental refresh** - processes only rows that are new or changed since the last run, using a high-water mark such as an updated/created timestamp column. Use it for ongoing, scheduled syncs.
261: 7. Add a **schedule** (for example, hourly or daily) or leave the job to run manually.
262: 8. Save and run the job.
263: 
264: The flow below summarizes the process:
265: 
266: ![Configure Snowflake and run Cordial Data Jobs](./assets/data_jobs_flow.png)
267:

1: # Codelabs Site
2: 
3: A site for hosting codelabs content.
4: 
5: 
6: ## Prerequisites
7: 
8: The project requires the following major dependencies:
9: 
10: - [Go](https://golang.org/dl/) language
11: - [Node.js](https://nodejs.org/en/download/) v10+ and [npm](https://www.npmjs.com/get-npm)
12: - [gsutil](https://cloud.google.com/storage/docs/gsutil_install)
13: - [claat](https://github.com/googlecodelabs/tools/tree/master/claat#install)
14: 
15: With Node installed, run `npm install` in the root of the `site` (this folder):
16: 
17: ```text
18: $ npm install
19: ```
20: 
21: (Optional) npm installs binstubs at `./node_modules/.bin/`. When running tasks
22: like `gulp`, you may want to add `./node_modules/.bin/` to your `$PATH` for convenience:
23: 
24: ```text
25: $ export PATH="./node_modules/.bin/:$PATH"
26: ```
27: 
28: This does pose a mild security risk, so please do so at your own risk.
29: 
30: 
31: ## Development
32: 
33: ### Serve
34: 
35: To serve the site in dev mode, run `gulp serve`, passing a path to a directory
36: with the codelabs content as an argument. This will compile all the views and
37: codelabs into the `build/` directory and start a web server to serve that
38: content.
39: 
40: ```text
41: $ gulp serve
42: ```
43: 
44: The output will include the address where the server is running
45: (http://localhost:8000 by default).
46: 
47: You can also serve the completely compiled and minified (prod) version with the
48: `serve:dist` command. Always run this before publishing, as it will show you an
49: replica of what will appear on staging/production.
50: 
51: ```text
52: $ gulp serve:dist
53: ```
54: 
55: ### Views
56: 
57: Views are themed/styled collections of codelabs, served from the same url.
58: Codelab tags are used for selecting codelabs into views. View definitions are
59: stored in `/app/views` directory. Views commonly correspond to events (e.g. NEXT
60: 2018) or abstract themes (e.g. Windows), but we refer to them generically as
61: "views" internally.
62: 
63: #### Add a new view
64: 
65: To add a new view (e.g. to serve codelabs for a particular event):
66: 
67: 1. Create a new folder in `app/views`, which will be the "view id". As the view
68: id will appear in the URL, the name should be sluggified, meaning all lowercase
69: with special characters replaced with dashes.
70: 
71:     ```text
72:     // General example
73:     My Codelab -> my-codelab
74: 
75:     // Always substitute file extensions, otherwise the browser will get confused
76:     Learn underscore.js -> learn-underscore-js
77: 
78:     // Keep other URL-friendly characters when the context warrants
79:     Tracking with utm_source -> tracking-with-utm_source
80:     ```
81: 
82: 1. Add a new file named `view.json` inside this folder. Here is a template
83: `view.json`:
84: 
85:     ```javascript
86:     // app/views/my-event/view.json
87:     {
88:       // Required: page and view title.
89:       "title": "My Event",
90: 
91:       // Required: Text description of the event. This will appear in the view
92:       // landing page.
93:       "description": "",
94: 
95:       // Required: list of string tags by which to include codelabs. Tags are
96:       // specified in the codelab by the codelab author.
97:       "tags": [],
98: 
99:       // Optional: list of string categories by which to include codelabs.
100:       // Categories are specified in the codelab by the codelab author.
101:       "categories": [],
102: 
103:       // Optional: name of a custom stylesheet to include. See also: point below
104:       // about custom styles.
105:       "customStyle": "style.css",
106: 
107:       // Optional: list of regular expressions to exclude particular codelabs.
108:       "exclude": [],
109: 
110:       // Optional: URL to a custom logo for the codelab. If provided, this logo
111:       // must be placed in app/views/<view-id>/ and referenced as such. For
112:       // example, if the event was named "my-event", this logo would exist at
113:       // app/views/my-event/my-event-logo.svg.
114:       //
115:       // Where possible, please use SVG logos. When SVG logos are not available,
116:       // please size images to be 125px high at 72 DPI.
117:       //
118:       // Minify images before uploading using a tool like ImageOptim.
119:       "logoUrl": "/my-event/my-event-logo.svg",
120: 
121:       // Optional: category level to use for iconography
122:       "catLevel": 0,
123: 
124:       // Optional: Method for sorting codelabs.
125:       "sort": "mainCategory",
126: 
127:       // Optional: List of codelab IDs that should be "pinned" at the start.
128:       // This is useful for "getting started" codelabs or when users should
129:       // complete codelabs in a specific order.
130:       "pins": [],
131: 
132:       // Optional: custom google analytics tracking code. By default, all
133:       // codelab views are tracked on the main codelab analytics.
134:       "ga": "",
135: 
136:       // Optional: If true, do not include this view in the list of views on
137:       // the home page. It will still be accessible via the direct URL.
138:       "hidden": false,
139:     }
140:     ```
141: 
142: 1. (Optional) Add a file named `style.css` inside the view folder. If provided,
143: this file will be included in the HTML, allowing for custom styles.
144: 
145:     This file is not included in the main assets bundle, so there will be a
146:     performance decrease as the browser needs to load additional styles.
147:     Furthermore, if the codelab schema were to change, your custom styles may be
148:     broken. Please check with the codelabs team to see if your style changes
149:     make more sense to upstream across all views.
150: 
151: 1. (Optional) Add a file named `index.html` inside the view folder. This allows
152: you to fully customize the view, but comes at the expense of duplication. Please
153: use this sparingly and check with the core team before making drastic changes.
154: 
155: 1. Execute the `serve` command as described above to see the view.
156: 
157: #### Build and serve a single view (deprecated)
158: 
159: The build is very fast, so you should not need to filter by a specific view.
160: Instead, build all views and then visit the appropriate URL. If you still wish
161: to build a single set of views, you can do so with the `--views-filter`
162: parameter:
163: 
164: ```text
165: $ gulp serve --views-filter='^event-*'
166: ```
167: 
168: Note this filter takes a regular expression. By default, all views are built.
169:

171: ## Deployment
172: 
173: Once you build, serve, and verify your labs, you're on your own for publishing the artifacts. There are many ways to publish a static web site and we won't try to cover them all, however, we have included support for deploying your landing pages and codelabs to Google Cloud Storage (GCS).
174: 
175: ### Setup for GCS Support
176: 
177: #### Set  environment variables like this (use your own names):
178: 
179: ```
180: export STAGING_BUCKET=gs://mco-codelabs-staging
181: export PROD_BUCKET=gs://mco-codelabs-prod
182: ```
183: 
184: #### Create staging and production buckets like this (use your own names):
185: 
186: ```
187: 18:42:32 site$ gsutil mb is $STAGING_BUCKET
188: Creating gs://mco-codelabs-staging/...
189: 18:42:47 site$ gsutil mb $PROD_BUCKET
190: Creating gs://mco-codelabs-prod/...
191: ```
192: 
193: #### Setup permissions and web access to your buckets
194: 
195: 1. Make newly uploaded files world-readable and ensure user@ has owner
196: permissions:
197: 
198:     ```text
199:     $ gsutil defacl ch -g all:R -u you@your-domain.com:O $STAGING_BUCKET $PROD_BUCKET
200:     $ gsutil iam ch allUsers:objectViewer $STAGING_BUCKET $PROD_BUCKET
201:     ```
202: 
203:     Add as many `-u user@` as you require. This ensures the users will remain
204:     owners no matter who updates your bucket.
205: 
206: ### Deploy to staging
207: 
208: The following commands perform a "copy" operation, uploading all local files to
209: the staging bucket. The local copy of a file will overwrite the staging copy of
210: the same file. Staging files that do not exist in the local copy will be
211: untouched. To perform a complete "sync" (make staging look exactly like the
212: local copy), specify `--delete-missing` on the publish command.
213: 
214: 1. Compile and minify the build:
215: 
216:     ```text
217:     $ gulp dist
218:     ```
219: 
220: 1. Deploy views to the staging bucket:
221: 
222:     ```text
223:     $ gulp publish:staging:views --staging-bucket=$STAGING_BUCKET
224:     ```
225: 
226: 1. Deploy codelabs to the staging bucket:
227: 
228:     ```text
229:     $ gulp publish:staging:codelabs --staging-bucket=$STAGING_BUCKET
230:     ```
231: 
232: 1. Visit the [staging site](https://mco-codelabs-staging.storage.googleapis.com/index.html) (modify link to match your staging bucket name).
233: 
234: See [#options](#options) for information on how to customize the staging bucket.
235: 
236: ### Deploy to prod
237: 
238: We do not deploy from local to production. Instead, we "promote" a staging build
239: to production.
240: 
241: The following commands perform a "copy" operation, uploading all staging files
242: to the prod bucket. The staging copy of a file will overwrite the prod copy of
243: the same file. Prod files that do not exist in the staging bucket will be
244: untouched. To perform a complete "sync" (make prod look exactly like staging),
245: specify `--delete-missing` on the publish command.
246: 
247: 1. Deploy views from the staging bucket to the production bucket:
248: 
249:     ```text
250:     $ gulp publish:prod:views --staging-bucket=$STAGING_BUCKET --prod-bucket=$PROD_BUCKET
251:     ```
252: 
253: 1. Deploy codelabs from the staging bucket to the production bucket:
254: 
255:     ```text
256:     $ gulp publish:prod:codelabs --staging-bucket=$STAGING_BUCKET --prod-bucket=$PROD_BUCKET
257:     ```
258: 
259: 1. Visit the [production site](https://mco-codelabs-prod.storage.googleapis.com/index.html)  (modify link to match your production bucket name).
260: 
261: See [#options](#options) for information on how to customize the staging and
262: prod bucket.
263: 
264: ### Deploy to custom bucket
265: 
266: This section describes the steps to create and deploy to a custom bucket.
267: Replace `gs://codelabs.mycompany.com` with the name of your bucket. If you want
268: to use GCS directly for serving, the bucket name **must** be a valid domain.
269: 
270: 1. Create a new bucket:
271: 
272:     ```text
273:     $ gsutil mb gs://codelabs.mycompany.com
274:     ```
275: 
276: 1. Make newly uploaded files world-readable and ensure user@ has owner
277: permissions:
278: 
279:     ```text
280:     $ gsutil defacl ch -g all:R -u you@your-domain.com:O gs://codelabs.mycompany.com
281:     $ gsutil iam ch allUsers:objectViewer gs://codelabs.mycompany.com
282:     ```
283: 
284:     Add as many `-u user@` as you require. This ensures the users will remain
285:     owners no matter who updates your bucket.
286: 
287: 1. Set the default main page suffix and not found page:
288: 
289:     ```text
290:     $ gsutil web set -m index.html -e 404.html gs://codelabs.mycompany.com
291:     ```
292: 
293:     This option is only available on bucket names that are valid domains.
294: 
295: 
296: Follow the steps in [deploy to staging](#deploy-to-staging) with a custom
297: `--staging-bucket` parameter. See [#options](#options) for information.
298: 
299: 
300: ### Deploy single view or codelab
301: 
302: Where possible, build and publish the entire website. This will ensure all
303: assets are up-to-date.
304: 
305: To build and publish a set of views to staging:
306: 
307: ```text
308: $ gulp dist --views-filter=^my-event
309: $ gulp publish:staging:views
310: ```
311: 
312: To build and publish a set of codelabs to staging:
313: 
314: ```text
315: $ gulp dist --codelabs-filter=^my-codelab
316: $ gulp publish:staging:codelabs
317: ```
318: 
319: ## Options
320: 
321: `--base-url` - base URL for serving canonical links. This should always include
322: the protocol (http:// or https://) and NOT including a trailing slash. The
323: default value is "https://codelabs.developers.google.com".
324: 
325: `--codelabs-dir` - absolute or relative path on disk where codelabs are stored.
326: Any filters will be applied to these codelabs, and then the resulting selection
327: is symlinked into the build folder. The default value is "." (the current directory).
328: 
329: `--codelabs-filter` - regular expression by which to filter codelabs IDs for
330: inclusion. If a filter is not specified, all codelabs are included.
331: 
332: `--codelabs-namespace` - URL path where codelabs will be served in the web
333: server. The default value is "/codelabs", meaning codelabs will be served at
334: https://URL/codelabs.
335: 
336: `--dry` - Print out steps instead of actually taking them. This only applies  to
337: publish operations.
338: 
339: `--delete-missing` - Delete any files in the destination that are not present
340: at the source (rsync-style behavior).
341: 
342: `--prod-bucket` - name of the GCS bucket to use for production resources. This
343: is only used for publishing.
344: 
345: `--staging-bucket` - name of the GCS bucket to use for staging resources. This
346: is only used for publishing.
347: 
348: `--views-filter` - regular expression by which to filter included views
349: (events). If a filter is not specified, all views are included.
350: 
351: The following options are only relevant when invoking claat:
352: 
353: `--codelabs-env` - environment for which to build codelabs. The default value is
354: "web".
355: 
356: `--codelabs-format` - format in which to build the codelabs. The default value
357: is "html"
358: 
359: `--codelab-source` - Google Doc ID from which to build codelab. This can be
360: specified multiple times to build from multiple sources.
361:

1: # Codelabs command line tool
2: 
3: The program takes an input in form of a resource location,
4: which can either be a Google Doc ID, local file path or an arbitrary URL.
5: It then converts the input into a codelab format, HTML by default.
6: 
7: For more info run `claat help`.

9: ## Install

11: The easiest way is to download pre-compiled binary.
12: The binaries, as well as their checksums are available at the
13: [Releases page](https://github.com/googlecodelabs/tools/releases/latest).

17:     go get github.com/googlecodelabs/tools/claat
18:

20: instructions below.

22: ## Dev workflow

24: **Prerequisites**

26: 1. Install [Go](https://golang.org/dl/) if you don't have it.
27: 2. Make sure this directory is placed under
28:    `$GOPATH/src/github.com/googlecodelabs/tools`.
29: 3. Install package dependencies with `go get ./...` from this directory.
30: 
31: To build the binary, run `make`.
32: 
33: Testing is done with `make test` or `go test ./...` if preferred.

35: Don't forget to run `make lint` or `golint ./...` before creating a new CL.
36: 
37: To create cross-compiled versions for all supported OS/Arch, run `make release`.

The choice is yours. 17: 18: 19: ### Prerequisites 20: - Familiarity with Snowflake and React 21: 22: ### What You’ll Learn 23: - how to connect Snowflake and ThoughtSpot together 24: - how to add ThoughtSpot to a React app 25: 26: ### What You’ll Need 27: - A [Snowflake](https://trial.snowflake.com/) Account 28: - A [ThoughtSpot](https://www.thoughtspot.com/trial?utm=snowtstutorial) Account 29: - [NodeJS](https://nodejs.org/en/download/) Installed 30: 31: ### What You’ll Build 32: - A React web app with ThoughtSpot Everywhere insights backed by Snowflake 33: 34: 35: ## Getting Started 36: 37: To get started, we are going to need a few cloud environments, one for Snowflake and another for ThoughtSpot. Data modeling in ThoughtSpot is similar to how you would go about it in a traditional database. We want to establish relationships between data, the joins, and create some sort of view to make it easier for users to work with the data. Within ThoughtSpot, a view is called a `Worksheet`. Don’t get confused with Snowflake’s definition of worksheets. They are different. If you are more familiar with databases, just remember that a Worksheet in ThoughtSpot is similar to a materialized view in a database. Let’s start by creating ours. 288: 289: If you remember from above, one of the tables we connected to was `Store_sales`. This junction object contains the relationship between stores and items sold. We need to tell ThoughtSpot which fields are the foreign keys in this table. To do so, tap on the `TutorialSnowStore` tile, select `Store_Sales`, then **Joins** from the navigation. We need to create two joins, one from `Store_Sales` to `Sales`, and the other from `Store_Sales` to `Item`. Create your connections like the images below, remembering to set the cardinality field. 290: 291: 292: #### Join 1: Store_Sales to Store 293: 294: ![alt_text](assets/image15.png) 295: 296: 297: 298: #### Join 2: Store_Sales to Item 299: 300: ![alt_text](assets/image21.png) 301: 302: 303: Once you are done, you should see a final configuration like this, with a handy visual ERD for your reference. That’s it. No need to write SQL statements. ThoughtSpot takes care of all the syntax and optimization for you. 304: 305: ![alt_text](assets/image16.png) 306: 307: 308: 309: 310: 311: ## Create the Worksheet 312: 313: 314: ### Using the Visual Designer 315: 316: Now, it is time to create the worksheet that user’s will interact with. Just remember, a worksheet in ThoughtSpot functions very similar to a database view. The good news is that now that we have our modeling complete, creating a Worksheet is really simple. From the top navigation, select **Data**, then **Worksheets**, and finally **New Worksheet**. Select the three tables from Snowflake, using the **Filter by name** box to quickly locate the tables we need. Once select, tap **Close.** 317: 318: ![alt_text](assets/image1.png) 319: 320: 321: With the tables selected, we can create the worksheet by expanding the **Sources** tree on the left, and selecting the columns we need. To keep things simple, we are just going to select them all. If you don’t want to select individual columns, you can also tap on the name of the table, the tap **Add Columns** to add all the columns at once. 322: 323: ![alt_text](assets/image12.gif) 324: 325: 326: 327: ### Using SQL 328: 329: So far we have used the visual designers to create an answer. If you are more familiar with, or have an existing, SQL statement, you can also use this to create a Worksheet using the new SQL based view feature currently available in Beta. To do, select SQL based view from the Data tab, and choose the TutorialSnowStore connection. 330: 331: 332: ![alt_text](assets/image6.png) 333: 334: 335: From here, you can write your query using familiar SQL syntax. For example, if we wanted to create a similar Worksheet from the tutorial steps above, we could write the following statement. 336: 337: 338: ``` 339: SELECT i.i_product_name, s.s_store_name, s.s_state, s.s_country, sales.ss_quantity, sales.ss_net_paid 340: FROM TPCDS_SF10TCL.STORE as s, TPCDS_SF10TCL.item as i, TPCDS_SF10TCL.STORE_SALES as sales 341: WHERE sales.ss_store_sk = s.s_store_sk 342: AND sales.ss_item_sk = i.i_item_sk 343: ``` 344: 345: 346: Go ahead and run the statement to see the results. From here, give your Worksheet a name and tap **Save** to create a Worksheet your users can use to analyze data. The great thing too, is that now that my Worksheet has been created within ThoughtSpot, you can customize it using the visual designer tools as well. This hybrid approach to Worksheet creation works very well for the typical developer who is comfortable with typical sql, but may not be an expert in more advanced grouping, and functions. You can quickly create a worksheet from an existing SQL statement, then tweak the aggregate functions using the visual designer. 347: 348: 349: 350: ![alt_text](assets/image10.gif) 351: 352: 353: 354: ## Visualize the Data with Liveboards 355: 356: For many users, viewing data in charts is the most efficient way of analysing data. The trouble with most charting solutions is that the results is very static. Consider a traditional dashboard to view daily sales. Charts on these dashboards are effectively pre-defined queries. With ThoughtSpot however, charts and dashboards are fully dynamic; they are alive. You can modify the filters with natural language, tap and drill in to view deeper insights, and more. For this tutorial, we are going to create a Liveboard, a dynamic dashboard, to represent product sales by store. Let’s get started. 357: 358: From the top navigation, select **Liveboards**, then tap the **+Liveboard** button in the top right, and name your Liveboard `Snow - Store Sales`. Click **Create**. Your Liveboard is now available alongside any other Liveboards you may have in your environment. Go ahead and tap on `Snow - Store Sales` to open it. 359: 360: 361: 362: ![alt_text](assets/image7.gif) 363: 364: 365: 366: ### Add a Stacked Column Chart 367: 368: Our Liveboard isn’t terribly exciting right now. For our tutorial, this question is “show me all the product sales for all stores”. The ThoughtSpot platform let’s you pose this question using natural language. But don’t worry, if you prefer to use SQL, you can do that too. We will get to that in a moment. def png_chunk(tag, data):

# decode PNG to verify
def read_png(p):
    d = open(p, "rb").read()
    assert d[:8] == b"\x89PNG\r\n\x1a\n"
    pos = 8
    params = {}
    idat = b""
    while pos < len(d):
        ln = struct.unpack(">I", d[pos:pos+4])[0]
        tag = d[pos+4:pos+8]
        chunk = d[pos+8:pos+8+ln]
        if tag == b"IHDR":
            params["w"], params["h"], params["bd"], params["ct"] = struct.unpack(">IIBB", chunk[:10])
        elif tag == b"IDAT":
            idat += chunk
        pos += 12 + ln
    raw = zlib.decompress(idat)
    assert len(raw) == params["h"] * (1 + params["w"] * 3)
    return params

    print("GIF w=%d h=%d ok=%s trailer=%s" % (w, h, d[-1] == 0x3B, d[-1:].hex()))

FR = "/tmp/opencode/genout/frames"
os.makedirs(OUT, exist_ok=True)
os.makedirs(FR, exist_ok=True)

# ---------------------------------------------------------------- helper ---
def frame_dump(name, i, cv):
    path = os.path.join(FR, "%s_%d.rgb" % (name, i))
    with open(path, "wb") as f:
        f.write(bytes(cv.data))
    return path

def gif(name, frames, delays, outdir=None):
    spec = {"out": os.path.join(OUT, name), "frames": []}
    for i, (cv, d) in enumerate(zip(frames, delays)):
        spec["frames"].append({"file": frame_dump(name, i, cv), "w": cv.w, "h": cv.h, "delay": d})
    with open(os.path.join(FR, name + "_spec.json"), "w") as f:
        json.dump(spec, f)

import sys, zlib, struct, os
sys.path.insert(0, "/tmp/opencode")
import gen
from gen import C

def read_png(path):
    d = open(path, "rb").read()
    assert d[:8] == b"\x89PNG\r\n\x1a\n", path
    pos = 8; idat = b""
    while pos < len(d):
        ln = struct.unpack(">I", d[pos:pos+4])[0]
        tag = d[pos+4:pos+8]
        chunk = d[pos+8:pos+8+ln]
        if tag == b"IHDR":
            w, h, bd, ct = struct.unpack(">IIBB", chunk[:10])
        elif tag == b"IDAT":
            idat += chunk
        pos += 12 + ln
    raw = zlib.decompress(idat)
    px = bytearray()
    stride = w * 3
    for r in range(h):
        f = raw[r * (stride + 1)]
        assert f == 0
        px += raw[r * (stride + 1) + 1: (r + 1) * (stride + 1)]
    return w, h, px

for f in sorted(os.listdir(gen.OUT)):
    if f.endswith(".png"):

import sys, zlib, struct, os

def read_png(path):
    d = open(path, "rb").read()
    assert d[:8] == b"\x89PNG\r\n\x1a\n", path
    pos = 8; idat = b""
    while pos < len(d):
        ln = struct.unpack(">I", d[pos:pos+4])[0]
        tag = d[pos+4:pos+8]
        chunk = d[pos+8:pos+8+ln]
        if tag == b"IHDR":
            w, h, bd, ct = struct.unpack(">IIBB", chunk[:10])
        elif tag == b"IDAT":
            idat += chunk
        pos += 12 + ln
    raw = zlib.decompress(idat)
    px = bytearray()
    stride = w * 3
    for r in range(h):
        f = raw[r * (stride + 1)]
        assert f == 0
        px += raw[r * (stride + 1) + 1: (r + 1) * (stride + 1)]
    return w, h, px

ThoughtSpot follows a similar philosophy for analysis: **anyone** should be able to ask questions of that data and get answers in seconds. With the ThoughtSpot Everywhere developer tools you can embed those search-driven insights directly into your own web application, backed by live data in Snowflake. This tutorial walks you through the full journey, end to end: - **Connect** a ThoughtSpot free trial to Snowflake. - **Model** your Snowflake data into user-friendly worksheets. - **Search** your data with natural language. - **Analyze** it with the AI-powered Ask Sage and SpotIQ features. - **Embed** live analytics into a simple application using the ThoughtSpot Everywhere Embed SDK. The diagram below shows the architecture you will build: ![ThoughtSpot and Snowflake embedded analytics architecture](./assets/ThoughtSpot_arch.png) ### What is ThoughtSpot? ThoughtSpot is an AI-powered analytics platform. It connects directly to your data warehouse, lets users ask questions in plain English, and presents the results as visualizations, Liveboards, and AI-generated insights. Its developer platform, **ThoughtSpot Everywhere**, exposes the same analytics through embeddable SDKs and REST APIs. ### What is Snowflake? Snowflake is a governed cloud data platform. In this tutorial you use the [Snowflake sample data](https://docs.snowflake.com/en/user-guide/sample-data) from the free trial to give ThoughtSpot something to analyze. ### What You'll Learn - How to sign up for Snowflake and ThoughtSpot free trials - How to connect a ThoughtSpot trial to Snowflake, including using Partner Connect - How to create a worksheet and model your data in ThoughtSpot - How to build a Liveboard, search in natural language, and use Ask Sage and SpotIQ - How to embed a Liveboard into a simple application with the ThoughtSpot Everywhere Embed SDK ### What You'll Need - A [Snowflake](https://signup.snowflake.com/) free trial account - A [ThoughtSpot](https://www.thoughtspot.com/trial?utm=snowtstutorial) free trial account - [Node.js](https://nodejs.org/en/download/) and npm installed locally (for the embedded application step) ### What You'll Build - A live analytics application that embeds a ThoughtSpot Liveboard backed by Snowflake sample data ## Get Started Duration: 10 To get started you need a couple of cloud environments: one for Snowflake and one for ThoughtSpot. Both platforms offer free trials you can sign up for online, and both include sample datasets so you can follow along without loading your own data. ### Sign Up for a Snowflake Free Trial Open the [Snowflake free trial signup page](https://signup.snowflake.com/), enter the details required, and continue. Follow the steps, then check your email for an activation link. Once logged in, open the **Worksheets** area and use the **+** button to create a new worksheet. Name it `Snowflake + ThoughtSpot Tutorial`. In Snowsight a worksheet is a space where you can write SQL to interrogate data - we will use it to confirm our connection works. Before we can query the sample data we need to set the worksheet **Context** - the warehouse, database, and schema Snowflake uses for the query. Click each field in the Context selector and choose the values below: | Context field | Value | | --- | --- | | Warehouse | `COMPUTE_WH` | | Database | `SNOWFLAKE_SAMPLE_DATA` | | Schema | `TPCDS_SF10TCL` | ![Setting the Snowflake worksheet context](./assets/image5.gif) Now run a quick test query to make sure everything is configured.
